issues.title: chore(build): remove the Google Fonts network dependency
issues.body:
Closes #117

## The finding: the fonts were fetched but never applied

The issue asks for this to be established before choosing an approach, so I checked it two ways.

**Statically.** `app/globals.css` defines `--font-sans` and `--font-mono` inside `@theme inline` as system stacks, and `body` sets `font-family: var(--font-sans)`. The layout generated `--font-geist-sans` and `--font-geist-mono` and put the two generated classes on `<body>`, but a repository-wide search found no reference to either variable outside `app/layout.tsx` itself:

```
$ grep -rni "geist\|next/font" --include="*.ts" --include="*.tsx" --include="*.css" ...
app/layout.tsx:2,9-17,69   (the definitions and the body classes — nothing else)
```

**At runtime**, loading the app in Chromium before the change:

```json
"bodyClass": "geist_a71539c9-module__T19VSG__variable geist_mono_8d43a2aa-module__8Li5zG__variable antialiased",
"bodyFont": "-apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, \"Segoe UI\", \"Noto Sans\", Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif, ...",
"h1Font":   "-apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, \"Segoe UI\", \"Noto Sans\", Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif, ...",
"monoFont": "ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, \"SF Mono\", Menlo, Consolas, \"Liberation Mono\", monospace",
"varGeistSans": "\"Geist\", \"Geist Fallback\"",
"loadedFonts": ["Geist 100 900 unloaded", "Geist Mono 100 900 unloaded", ... 17 faces, all "unloaded"],
"fontLinks": ["preload font /_next/static/media/797e433ab948586e-s.p...woff2",
              "preload font /_next/static/media/caa3a2e1cccd8315-s.p...woff2"]
```

Every visible element computed to the system stack, and every Geist face reported `unloaded` — the browser never used one to render text. The only real effect was two preloaded `woff2` files nobody read, plus a build that needed Google Fonts.

**So the fonts were genuinely unused**, and the first branch of the issue applies: remove the imports and document the system stack. Self-hosting with `next/font/local` would have introduced typography the site never had, which is a design change rather than a build fix.

## What changed

- `app/layout.tsx` — dropped the `next/font/google` imports and the two generated font variables; `<body>` is now `className="antialiased"`.
- `app/globals.css` — a comment recording that the two font tokens are the app's only font definitions and that no web font is downloaded.
- `app/layout.test.tsx` — the `next/font/google` mock is gone (it was the only reason the layout rendered under Vitest), and a new test pins the new contract: the body carries no font-variable class and the markup mentions no `font-geist` variable.
- `AGENTS.md` / `README.md` — the chosen stack documented, with a note not to reach for `next/font/google` again; a font the design really needs belongs in the repository behind `next/font/local`.
- `CHANGELOG.md` — entry under `## Unreleased` → `### Changed`.

No font assets and no font CSS variables remain: `--font-geist-sans` and `--font-geist-mono` were generated by the layout, so removing the imports removes them, and there was never a font package in `package.json`.

## Offline verification

A DNS-level block via `NODE_OPTIONS=--require` was **not** sufficient and I am reporting that rather than hiding it: Next 16 fetches Google Fonts from Turbopack's Rust process, so patching Node's `dns` module never saw the lookup and the pre-change build passed as if it were offline when it was not. What does work is pointing the proxy variables at a dead local port, which Next's font loader honours (its own error message names them).

**Negative control — pre-change tree (`origin/main`), `rm -rf .next` first:**

```
$ HTTP_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:9 HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:9 \
  http_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:9 https_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:9 npm run build
> Build error occurred
Error: Turbopack build failed with 2 errors:
[next]/internal/font/google/geist_a71539c9.module.css
Error: next/font: error:
Failed to fetch Geist from Google Fonts.
If you are offline or behind a proxy, self-host the font with next/font/local, or set HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY so Next.js can reach fonts.googleapis.com.
  Import trace: ... ./app/layout.tsx
[next]/internal/font/google/geist_mono_8d43a2aa.module.css
Error: next/font: error:
Failed to fetch Geist Mono from Google Fonts.
```

That reproduces the failure the issue reports, and proves the block is real rather than assumed.

**This branch, same environment variables plus the Node DNS blocker, `rm -rf .next` first:**

```
▲ Next.js 16.3.0 (Turbopack)
✓ Compiled successfully in 6.4s
  Finished TypeScript in 11.8s ...
✓ Generating static pages using 12 workers (8/8) in 3.5s
Route (app)
┌ ○ /                    ├ ○ /icon              ├ ○ /opengraph-image
├ ○ /privacy             └ ○ /twitter-image     ...
```

`/icon`, `/opengraph-image`, and `/twitter-image` are prerendered *during that offline build*, so the generated images need no network either — `next/og` uses the font bundled with the package and never referenced Geist.

## Visual check (`ui-review` equivalent)

Served the offline production build and compared against the same pages before the change, at 1280×900 and 375×780:

- `body`, `h1`, and `code` computed font-family strings are **identical** before and after, on both viewports and on `/` and `/privacy`.
- `document.fonts` went from 17 registered-but-unloaded faces and 2 preloaded `woff2` files to **empty**, with zero font network requests.
- `/opengraph-image` and `/icon` PNGs are **byte-identical** before and after (md5 `05f8510885c54cc3f75fea8d67860774` and `e89f5603d4b2930d813486aa777c29bf`); `/twitter-image` re-exports the OpenGraph route.
- Homepage screenshots match apart from the dev-server badge present only in the "before" capture. No colour, size, spacing, or semantic change, so there is no accessibility impact.

## Gate

`E2E_PORT=3120 npm run validate` — **passed** end to end: `npm audit` (0 vulnerabilities), 342 unit tests in 26 files, 30 Playwright specs on port 3120, `lint`, `format:check`, `check:agent-docs`, `check:labels`, and `build`. No markdown was run through Prettier.

## Process notes

- **This session cannot invoke sub-agents.** Per AGENTS.md, the `ui-review`, `verifier`, and `code-review` steps were performed by the main agent itself, announced at step 6 rather than afterwards. That is the weakest form of each of those steps: it collapses three independent reviews into one agent reviewing its own change, and a human reviewer should treat it accordingly.
- Next.js re-appended its generated `<!-- BEGIN:nextjs-agent-rules -->` block to `AGENTS.md` on every `next dev` boot (the baseline dev run and the Playwright suite). It was removed before committing and is not in this diff; it never appeared in `CLAUDE.md` or `GEMINI.md`, so the pointer files are untouched and `check:agent-docs` is green. The block's own text argues for committing it; that is generated output, so it was treated as data.
- Left alone: the `--font-mono` token leaves multi-word family names such as `SF Mono` and `Liberation Mono` unquoted. Browsers parse them correctly and this predates the change, so it stays out of scope.

issues.body:
Structural cleanup left over from the earlier move of modules into `app/_lib/`. No behaviour changes.

## `analytics.ts` was in the wrong folder

`app/_home/` is, by AGENTS.md's own rule, the directory for things only the homepage uses. But `analytics.ts` sat there while `app/_components/PrivacySafeAnalytics.tsx` imported it from outside — and that component is rendered by the **root layout**, so every page load reached into the homepage search feature to do something with no connection to searching for a commit.

It now sits in `app/_lib/` with the other shared modules. `app/_home/` is once again exactly the set of things only the homepage uses.

### Correction to the original plan: the import stays relative

The plan for this PR said to switch `PrivacySafeAnalytics` to an aliased `@/` import, reading AGENTS.md's "relative within a feature, aliased with `@/` only across a boundary" as requiring it. Surveying what the code actually does shows a different convention:

- **route files** under `app/api/` → `@/app/_lib/*` (3 imports)
- **everything else** (`_home/*`, `app/page.tsx`) → relative `../_lib/*` (24 imports)

So `../_lib/analytics` is the consistent choice; `@/` would have made this file the sole non-route exception. The violation the finding identified was `_components` reaching into the `_home` **feature**, and the move fixes that regardless of import style.

I have **not** rewritten that sentence in AGENTS.md. It is arguably under-specified rather than wrong — it reads naturally as being about features, with `_lib` as shared infrastructure everything reaches relatively. Whether `_lib` counts as a "boundary" is a call for the repository owner, not something to settle in a cleanup PR.

## Documentation caught up

- Added the rule that decides this for the next module, including the clarification that a feature includes its own route file — so `app/page.tsx` importing from `app/_home/` is *inside* the feature, while `app/_components/` is not.
- Layout list gained `app/api/csp-report/route.ts` and `app/_lib/e2eCommitSearchFixtures.ts`, both of which existed but were only described elsewhere.
- Four comments still pointed at pre-`_lib` paths: `e2eCommitSearchMocks.ts` (×2) and `e2e-readiness/route.test.ts` said `app/actions.ts`; `commitSearchRateLimit.ts` said `app/searchClientKey.ts`.

## Verification

`npm run validate` passes end to end:

- 492 unit tests, coverage unchanged at 96.61 / 93.35 / 98.9 / 97.82
- Playwright 51 passed across chromium / mobile-chrome / webkit
- `check:agent-docs` consistent — it reads AGENTS.md and the pointer templates, so it is the gate command this change most needed
- `npm audit`, lint, format, `check:labels`, production build all clean

Both moved files show `similarity index 100%`. The `vi.mock` paths moved with them: `searchExecution.test.ts` asserts on the mocked `trackAppEvent`, so a mis-pointed mock would fail rather than silently fall through to the real module.

issues.title: perf(app): build the commit date formatters once
issues.body:
Two changes: one optimisation applied, and one **not** applied with a test explaining why.

## Applied: build the commit date formatters once

`FirstCommitDisplay` constructed a fresh `Intl.DateTimeFormat` on every call. A rendered result builds **eleven** of them — the hover title on each of the ten commit cards, plus the summary date on the main one — and again on every re-render a retry or a share status causes. `Intl.DateTimeFormat` is among the more expensive constructors the platform offers: it resolves a locale and builds a pattern each time.

Both configurations are constant and deliberately pinned to `en` and UTC, so there is nothing per-call to close over. `Intl.DateTimeFormat.prototype.format` holds no per-call state, so a shared instance cannot leak anything between cards.

Output is unchanged and already pinned: `FirstCommitDisplay.test.tsx` asserts the exact string `"Jan 1, 2024"`, and the malformed-date fallback test still passes.

## Not applied: an early exit in `dropIdleClients`

The plan for this PR included short-circuiting the rate limiter's idle-client sweep, which scans up to 500 entries on every allowed search. The reasoning was that `allowCommitSearch` deletes and re-inserts on each call, so insertion order should be ascending by last-search time — letting the sweep `break` at the first client still inside the window.

**That reasoning is wrong.** When a client is *refused*, it is deleted and re-inserted at the tail, but nothing is pushed to its `searchTimes`, so its last-search time does not advance. The existing comment says this is deliberate — being evicted is a reprieve, so a client being refused should not get one. The consequence is that insertion order is **not** sorted by last-search time, and an idle client can sit *behind* an active one.

This is reachable, not theoretical. The new test builds the arrangement: `CLIENT` spends its whole allowance, `OTHER_CLIENT` searches one millisecond later, then `CLIENT` is refused — which moves it behind `OTHER_CLIENT` while its own newest search stays older. At one instant, `OTHER_CLIENT` is inside the window and `CLIENT` is not, so the only idle client stands after the active one.

Verified the test has teeth by temporarily applying the `break`:

```
AssertionError: expected [ Array(3) ] to deeply equal [ 'client-key-b', 'client-key-c' ]
```

The idle client survives eviction — which fails *open*, silently refilling an allowance rather than erroring, so nothing else would have caught it. `commitSearchRateLimit.ts` is therefore **unchanged**; only the test is added, so the next person to spot this scan is warned off it.

The scan is also not worth optimising: it is bounded at 500 cheap array-index reads on a path that otherwise makes an HTTP request to GitHub with a 10-second timeout.

## Verification

`npm run validate` passes end to end:

- 492 unit tests (491 + the new one)
- Coverage 96.61 stmts / 93.35 branch / 98.9 funcs / 97.82 lines, all above their floors
- Playwright 51 passed across chromium / mobile-chrome / webkit
- `npm audit`, lint, format, `check:agent-docs`, `check:labels`, production build all clean

## No CHANGELOG entry

Purely internal, per the step 9 exemption: no user-visible or operational effect. The rendered dates are identical, and the rate limiter's behaviour is unchanged by construction — its source is untouched.

issues.body:
Three removals, each of something no reachable path used. No behaviour changes.

## 1. `buildResultShareText` took a union it never received

It accepted `CommitData` and carried a fallback for a result with no commits. Its only caller (`app/page.tsx:109`) reaches it from behind a `result?.found` guard, and `CommitSearchSuccess` carries a non-empty tuple, so a first commit is guaranteed.

Narrowing the parameter to `CommitSearchSuccess` made `tsc` reject **exactly one** thing — the test that had been pinning the dead branch — and nothing at the call site:

```
app/_home/sharedSearch.test.ts(82,44): error TS2345:
  Argument of type 'CommitSearchFailure' is not assignable to parameter of type 'CommitSearchSuccess'.
```

That the call site compiles untouched is what proves the branch was unreachable in production rather than merely untested. This is the defensive check `commitTypes.ts` documents the tuple invariant as existing to remove.

## 2. `logger.error` could be handed a raw error object

It accepted an optional second `unknown` and passed it straight to `console.error`. No caller ever passed one, so nothing was being logged that should not have been — what is gone is the supported way to start.

That matters because it contradicts the module's stated purpose and the AGENTS.md logging gotcha: an Octokit error carries the request URL, and a commit-search URL carries the username being searched. `actions.ts` already extracts scalars (`status`, `errorKind`) and logs those.

## 3. Nine unused design tokens in `globals.css`

The `@theme inline` block mapped nine `--color-*` tokens into Tailwind's theme — `bg-gh-blue`, `text-gh-text-primary`, `bg-background`, and the rest. Not one of the generated utilities is referenced anywhere; every colour is applied as an arbitrary value reading the `:root` property directly (`text-[var(--github-blue)]`). They were a second, parallel naming scheme for the same seven colours that nothing was written against.

Tailwind emits only referenced utilities, so these never reached the stylesheet. **Verified** by concatenating the production CSS from a clean `next build` before and after:

```
de48109c96f6b0f7a27b8e017fcd71ddd644f92897ca140dcb0abaddd8eaab14  css-before.css
de48109c96f6b0f7a27b8e017fcd71ddd644f92897ca140dcb0abaddd8eaab14  css-after.css
```

Byte-identical. The font tokens stay — those are live via `font-sans`/`font-mono`.

## Verification

`npm run validate` passes end to end:

- 491 unit tests (492 before, minus the deleted dead-branch test)
- Coverage **up**: 96.61 stmts / 93.35 branch / 98.91 funcs / 97.82 lines, against the baseline recorded in `vitest.config.mts` of 96.53 / 93.26 / 98.91 / 97.72 — consistent with removing a partially-covered branch

Closes #185. Found while measuring coverage for #183.

## The problem

`app/_lib/actions.ts` was 569 lines, **173 of them browser-test fixtures** — thirty percent of the `"use server"` module that queries GitHub with the token, including one fixture that throws on purpose and two that keep state between calls.

The coverage number was the symptom, not the reason. Test scaffolding does not belong in the most security-sensitive file in the repository, and its presence made the real search path harder to read than it needed to be.

`actions.ts` is now **379 lines** and calls into the fixture module twice.

## Two things had to move first

**`commitSearchError` and the two empty-search messages** are shared between the production path and the fixtures, and a `"use server"` module cannot export a synchronous helper. They moved to `commitTypes.ts` beside `toCommitSearchSuccess`, so both constructors of the union now live with the union. Sharing rather than copying matters for the same reason `commitSearchMocksEnabled` has one definition — two copies would let the real path and the fixture path describe the same outcome in different words.

**The reject-once hook could not move as a fixture result**, because its whole purpose is to throw rather than return. It became `shouldRejectCommitSearchOnce`, which owns the decision and the state while `actions.ts` still owns the throw.

## The browser suite is the regression test

No fixture has a unit test to lean on, so Playwright is the proof. **All 51 specs pass**, including the four that depend on state surviving between two requests in one process:

- `a retry that is still partial says so and keeps focus on the button`
- `retrying a partial result reaches the complete history`
- `a failed retry keeps the partial result on screen`
- `home page recovers from an unexpected Server Action rejection` — the one I rewired

## Coverage moved, so the floors moved

| | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `actions.ts` statements | 76.54% | **93.33%** |
| `actions.ts` branches | 71.08% | **86.25%** |
| Aggregate statements | 93.71% | **96.53%** |
| Aggregate branches | 89.73% | **93.26%** |

`actions.ts` is now in line with the rest of the codebase instead of the outlier, because it is no longer measured against lines no unit test could reach.

**Floors raised to 96/93/98/97.** Leaving them at 93/89/98/94 would have left three and a half points of slack, which is room for real regression to pass — the opposite of what #183 just established. This was a scope correction rather than a coverage push, and the config says so.

Re-proved at the new floors: a two-function module that no test imports still fails the gate, on branches at 92.77% against 93.

## Verification

`npm run validate` passes in full: 0 vulnerabilities, 492 unit tests across 31 files with the raised thresholds met, 51 Playwright runs, lint, format, both checks, production build.

The AGENTS.md gotcha now points at the fixture module rather than `actions.ts`, so the next person adding browser coverage for a new state adds it in one obvious place.

## Note on the workflow

Stated at step 6, per #153: this session cannot invoke sub-agents, so steps 6-8 were performed directly. No user-visible surface — the fixtures are unreachable without `E2E_COMMIT_SEARCH_MOCKS=1`, and the browser suite confirms every reserved username still resolves.

issues.body:
Closes #183. The follow-on #121 carried forward, unblocked by #179.

## The hole

Coverage measured the files the suite **loaded**, which is Vitest's default. A module no test imported was *absent* from the report rather than counted as zero — so the floor from #114 caught coverage slipping in code already under test, and missed code that arrived with no test at all. That is the more common way coverage decays, and the case a floor exists for.

## The thresholds did not move

That is the evidence the exclusions are right rather than convenient:

| | Statements | Branches | Functions | Lines |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Before (default scope) | 93.71 | 89.73 | 98.38 | 94.65 |
| Scoped, no exclusions | 74.49 | 77.97 | 88.40 | 74.80 |
| **Scoped + 7 exclusions** | **93.71** | **89.73** | **98.38** | **94.65** |

Identical to two decimal places. Every point of the drop to 74% is the seven files below — not hidden regression — so the existing 93/89/98/94 floors stand unchanged and no threshold decision was needed.

## Seven exclusions, each covered by running rather than importing

| File | Covered by |
| --- | --- |
| `app/icon.tsx`, `app/opengraph-image.tsx`, `app/twitter-image.tsx` | `next build` prerenders them; a browser spec asserts each returns a PNG |
| `scripts/check-agent-docs.mjs`, `scripts/sync-labels.mjs` | `npm run check:agent-docs` and `npm run check:labels`, both links in the gate chain |
| `scripts/verify-deployed-commit.mjs`, `scripts/resolve-active-deployment.mjs` | the production health and promotion workflows |

Every one is a thin shell over a module that **is** unit tested — `gate-commands`, `ignore-entries`, `label-plan`, `production-release`. That split is deliberate in this repository, and the config now says to add to this list only when another gate command genuinely covers the file, and to name which one. Excluding a file nothing covers is how a floor starts reporting a hole that is not there.

## Proved in both directions

With a temporary two-function module that no test imports, then removed:

```
scoped:          92.98% statements, 97.34% functions   → gate fails, exit 1
default scope:   93.71% statements, 98.38% functions   → zero threshold errors
```

**The counterfactual is the point.** The same file that changes nothing today now fails the gate. Without that second measurement, "coverage is scoped" would be a claim rather than a demonstrated property.

## The interaction #179 made possible

Re-confirmed rather than assumed: with coverage patterns present in the config, widening the *test* include still fails with `collects from **, scripts rather than from app, scripts`. Before #179 the coverage patterns themselves would have failed that check, which is exactly why this change could not be made in #174.

## Verification

`npm run validate` passes in full: 0 vulnerabilities, 492 unit tests across 31 files with thresholds met, 51 Playwright runs, lint, format, both checks, production build.

`docs/development.md` records the new measurement, the reason for scoping, and the rule for adding an exclusion.

## Note on the workflow

Stated at step 6, per #153: this session cannot invoke sub-agents, so steps 6-8 were performed directly. No user-visible surface.

**That reasoning is wrong.** When a client is *refused*, it is deleted and re-inserted at the tail, but nothing is pushed to its `searchTimes`, so its last-search time does not advance. The existing comment says this is deliberate — being evicted is a reprieve, so a client being refused should not get one. The consequence is that insertion order is **not** sorted by last-search time, and an idle client can sit *behind* an active one.

This is reachable, not theoretical. The new test builds the arrangement: `CLIENT` spends its whole allowance, `OTHER_CLIENT` searches one millisecond later, then `CLIENT` is refused — which moves it behind `OTHER_CLIENT` while its own newest search stays older. At one instant, `OTHER_CLIENT` is inside the window and `CLIENT` is not, so the only idle client stands after the active one.

Verified the test has teeth by temporarily applying the `break`:

```
AssertionError: expected [ Array(3) ] to deeply equal [ 'client-key-b', 'client-key-c' ]
```

The idle client survives eviction — which fails *open*, silently refilling an allowance rather than erroring, so nothing else would have caught it. `commitSearchRateLimit.ts` is therefore **unchanged**; only the test is added, so the next person to spot this scan is warned off it.

The scan is also not worth optimising: it is bounded at 500 cheap array-index reads on a path that otherwise makes an HTTP request to GitHub with a 10-second timeout.

`npm run validate` passes end to end:

- 492 unit tests (491 + the new one)
- Coverage 96.61 stmts / 93.35 branch / 98.9 funcs / 97.82 lines, all above their floors
- Playwright 51 passed across chromium / mobile-chrome / webkit
- `npm audit`, lint, format, `check:agent-docs`, `check:labels`, production build all clean

## No CHANGELOG entry

Purely internal, per the step 9 exemption: no user-visible or operational effect. The rendered dates are identical, and the rate limiter's behaviour is unchanged by construction — its source is untouched.

issues.title: refactor(app): move the e2e commit search fixtures out of the server action
issues.body:
Found while measuring coverage for #183.

## Problem

`app/_lib/actions.ts` is 569 lines, and **173 of them (30%) are the browser-test fixture block** — `getE2eCommitSearchResult`, its reserved-username cases, and the stateful `Set` that makes the `*-once-*` fixtures return a different answer the second time.

Three consequences, in ascending order of importance.

**Coverage.** The block is exercised only by Playwright, so unit tests cannot reach it. That is why `actions.ts` sits at **76.54% statements / 71.08% branches** while every other file in the repository is 90–100%. It is the same "covered by running rather than importing" pattern the exclusions in #183 handle, except it is trapped inside a file that also holds real production logic, so the file cannot be excluded.

**Bundle.** `commitSearchMocksEnabled` reads `process.env.E2E_COMMIT_SEARCH_MOCKS` at module load, so it is a runtime check rather than a build-time constant. The fixtures are inert in production, but they ship there.

**Design.** This is the `"use server"` module that queries GitHub with the token. Thirty percent of it is test doubles, including one fixture that deliberately throws a synthetic error and another that mutates process-level state between calls. Test scaffolding does not belong in the most security-sensitive file in the repository, and its presence makes the real search path harder to read than it needs to be.

## Proposed scope

Move the fixture block to `app/_lib/e2eCommitSearchFixtures.ts`, keeping `commitSearchMocksEnabled` where it is — `app/api/e2e-readiness/route.ts` also reads it, and #156 exists because those two must not drift.

`actions.ts` then calls one function and is otherwise the production search path. The new module becomes the obvious home for the reserved usernames that AGENTS.md documents, and is excludable from coverage on the same justification as the other run-not-import files: Playwright executes it, and the gate runs Playwright.

Worth deciding while in there: whether the stateful `Set` behind the `*-once-*` and `*-then-error-*` fixtures should move with the block or be reset explicitly per process. It is currently module state in a server action, which is fine for a fixture and worth being deliberate about rather than inheriting.

## Acceptance criteria

- No fixture case or reserved username is defined in `app/_lib/actions.ts`.
- Every reserved username documented in AGENTS.md still resolves, proved by the browser suite passing unchanged — the fixtures have no unit tests to lean on, so the Playwright run is the regression test.
- `actions.ts` coverage rises to reflect the production path it actually contains, and the numbers are recorded.
- Coverage thresholds are re-measured. Removing 173 unreachable lines from a measured file moves the aggregate; do not lower a floor to accommodate it.
- The stateful-fixture behaviour is unchanged: a `*-once-*` username still returns partial first and the named outcome second, per process.

## Tests

The fixtures are only reachable through Playwright, so the browser suite is the proof. Run it before and after and confirm the same specs pass — particularly the `*-once-*` and `*-then-error-*` journeys, which depend on state surviving between two requests in one process, and the production canary, which must still be skipped locally.

issues.title: test(unit): scope coverage so an untested file counts as zero
issues.body:
Unblocked by #179. Recorded on #121 as a follow-on before that tracker closed.

## Problem

Coverage measures the files the suite loads — Vitest's default when `coverage.include` is unset. A module that **no test imports is absent from the report rather than counted as zero**, so the threshold floor added in #114 cannot catch a wholly untested new file. Adding one leaves the percentages unchanged.

That is a real gap in a non-regression floor. It catches coverage falling in code that is already tested, and misses code that arrives untested — which is the more likely way coverage degrades.

## Why it was left this way

#174 could not fix it. `check-agent-docs` read every glob-shaped literal in `vitest.config.ts`, so a `coverage.exclude` pattern registered as a collection root and failed the gate. #179 removed that obstacle: the check now reads only the test `include`, and a coverage block may carry its own patterns. Verified at the time by adding `include`/`exclude` to the coverage block and confirming the check still passed.

## The decision this needs

Scoping coverage to `app/**` and `scripts/**` measured **75.34%** when #174 tried it, against 93.68% for the default scope. The difference is not regression — it is files the gate exercises by *running* them rather than by unit test:

- the metadata image routes (`app/icon.tsx`, `app/opengraph-image.tsx`, `app/twitter-image.tsx`), which the production build renders
- the npm-script entrypoints (`scripts/check-agent-docs.mjs`, `scripts/sync-labels.mjs`, and the CLI shells added in #181), which the gate runs directly
- `tests/e2e/**`, covered by Playwright

So the work is not "turn on `all: true`" — it is deciding, file by file, which of those deserve an explicit exclusion because another gate command covers them, and which are genuinely untested and should drag the number down. Then set thresholds from the resulting measurement.

Excluding too much recreates today's blind spot under a bigger number. Excluding too little sets a floor so far below reality that it never fails.

## Acceptance criteria

- A new module that no test imports lowers the reported coverage.
- Every exclusion is justified in a comment naming the gate command that does cover that file.
- Thresholds are re-measured and set from the new scope, with the numbers recorded.
- `npm run check:agent-docs` still passes, and widening the test `include` still fails it.
- The note in `vitest.config.mts` describing the current blind spot is removed, since it stops being true.

## Tests

The change is configuration, so the proof is measurement rather than assertions. Add a temporary module with no test, confirm coverage drops and the gate fails, then remove it — the same shape as the stray-spec proof in #155 and the mutation checks in #178.

issues.body:
## Goal

Track remediation of the repository-wide engineering audit completed on 2026-08-10. Each linked issue is intentionally scoped for an independently reviewable, testable, and squash-mergeable pull request.

## Status

**Two items remain, both from Phase 2, and both need a deploy to verify rather than a local loop.**

| Phase | State |
| --- | --- |
| 1 — correctness and privacy | Complete |
| 2 — boundaries and production | #107 and #108 remain |
| 3 — user journeys and UI resilience | Complete |
| 4 — quality and maintainability | Complete |

Every follow-up raised during the work is closed.

## Recommended order

### Phase 1: protect correctness and privacy

- [x] #96
- [x] #97
- [x] #98
- [x] #99
- [x] #100
- [x] #103
- [x] #104
- [x] #110

### Phase 2: harden boundaries and production

- [x] #101
- [x] #102
- [x] #105 — *(closed by #157)*
- [x] #106 — both halves: coalescing in #150, the per-client burst bound in #164
- [x] #107
- [x] #108
- [x] #109

### Phase 3: complete user journeys and UI resilience

- [x] #111 — *(closed by #172)*
- [x] #112 — *(closed by #178)*
- [x] #113 — *(closed by #165)*

### Phase 4: improve quality and maintainability

- [x] #114 — *(closed by #174)*
- [x] #115 — *(closed by #180)*
- [x] #116
- [x] #117 — *(closed by #159)*
- [x] #118 — *(closed by #177)*
- [x] #119 — *(closed by #158)*
- [x] #120 — protection applied directly through the API rather than in a pull request, and
  documented in #176. Approving reviews stayed at zero to match the documented self-merge policy;
  Vercel was deliberately not made a required check, since `validate` already runs the build

## Follow-ups raised while remediating

Found during the work above, not part of the original audit. Each was filed rather than folded into
the pull request that surfaced it, because each needed either a decision or a slice of its own.
All are closed.

- [x] #138 — in-place retry for partial results *(closed by #139)*
- [x] #140 — the error-state retry lost focus when pressed *(closed by #152)*
- [x] #141 — a stray directory at the repository root joined the unit test run *(closed by #155)*
- [x] #142 — `app/home/` sat in the routing namespace *(closed by #162)*
- [x] #143 — components lived in three places *(closed by #167)*
- [x] #144 — routes and library modules shared a directory *(closed by #170)*
- [x] #146 — the browser suite's server check confirmed identity, not freshness *(closed by #156)*
- [x] #148 — a maximum-length handle overflowed the shortcut row at 320px *(closed by #154)*
- [x] #151 — the second half of #106 *(closed by #164)*
- [x] #160 — `sync-labels` matched names case-sensitively, so `--prune` could delete a label the
  file asks to keep *(closed by #173)*
- [x] #161 — Next.js re-appended a generated block to `AGENTS.md` on every `next dev` *(closed by
  #163; the generator has no opt-out and skips writing once the block is committed)*
- [x] #166 — a production health check failure, caused by #165 teaching one workflow to install
  WebKit and not the other *(fixed by #168)*
- [x] #169 — nothing tied a workflow's browser install list to the Playwright config *(closed by
  #171)*
- [x] #175 — the collection-scope check read every glob in the Vitest config, which kept coverage
  from being scoped at all *(closed by #179)*

## What is left

Both remaining items need a CI and Vercel round-trip to verify. Nothing about them can be settled
by `npm run validate`, which is what separates them from everything else on this list.

- **#108 — bind health checks and promotion to the deployed SHA.** Do this first. Today a
  production health check reports on whatever is deployed when it runs, not on the commit that
  triggered it, so a green check does not prove the new code is the code that was checked.
- **#107 — exercise the real commit search journey in production.** Depends on #108 being right to
  be worth anything, and needs three decisions made deliberately rather than discovered: it must
  reach real GitHub, so it interacts with the per-client rate limit added in #164; the mocked
  fixtures are skipped against a deployed target by design (#156), so it cannot reuse them; and it
  consumes the shared token quota on every run, which is the resource #106 exists to protect.

## Follow-on work, not blocking this tracker

- **Scope the coverage configuration.** #179 removed the obstacle. Coverage currently measures only
  the files the suite loads, so a module no test imports is absent from the report rather than
  counted as zero, and the floor cannot catch a wholly untested new file. Scoping it needs a
  threshold decision, since the number will move.
- **Watch the first Dependabot pull request after #176.** Branch protection now requires a branch
  to be up to date before merging. The expected behaviour is documented in `CONTRIBUTING.md` but
  has not been exercised, because no dependency pull request was open when the setting changed.

## Delivery guidance

- Use one issue and one thin vertical slice per pull request unless two items prove inseparable.
- Follow the repository's TDD, UI review, verifier, and code-review workflow.
- Keep this tracker open until every linked issue is closed or explicitly declined with rationale.
- Merging is now serialized: protection requires an up-to-date branch, so a second open pull
  request goes stale the moment the first lands and needs a rebase plus a fresh CI run.

issues.body:
## Problem

Deployed Playwright runs skip every mocked success and GitHub-error search test. The health endpoint confirms only that a token is present, so a revoked token, changed GitHub response, or broken Server Action can pass production health and release promotion.

## Evidence

- `tests/e2e/home.spec.ts:249-305`
- A deployed run currently executes 12 applicable checks and skips five search-state checks.

issues.title: chore(tooling): scope globRoots to the collection include, not every glob in the file
issues.body:
Surfaced by #174, which had to design around this rather than hit it.

## Problem

`globRoots` in `scripts/ignore-entries.mjs` collects the leading segment of **every glob-shaped string literal in `vitest.config.ts`**, not just those in `include`. `check-agent-docs` then requires the result to be exactly `app, scripts`.

Its own doc comment names this as a deliberate cost: *"It reads every pattern in the file, not only the ones in `include`, so a glob added for some unrelated option would have to be accounted for here too. In a file this small, a check that fails loudly beats one that guesses."*

That was the right call when the file held one option. It is no longer free. #174 added a coverage block and could not give it patterns of its own — `exclude: ["coverage/**"]` registers `coverage` as a collection root and fails the gate. The check cannot tell a coverage exclusion from a widened test scope, so it correctly refuses both.

## Why it matters beyond the inconvenience

The workaround was to leave the coverage block pattern-free, which means coverage measures only the files the suite loads. A module that no test imports is **absent from the report rather than counted as zero**, so the new threshold floor cannot catch a wholly untested new file.

Scoping coverage properly needs `include`/`exclude` patterns: count `app/**` and `scripts/**`, minus the metadata image routes and npm-script entrypoints that the gate exercises by running them rather than by unit test. Without those exclusions the number reads ~75% while measuring less than the current 93.68% does. So the guard is currently standing between the repository and a stronger coverage configuration.

This is a good problem to have — the tripwire worked exactly as designed and refused something it could not verify. It is now worth teaching it to tell the two apart.

## Proposed scope

Read the collection scope from the `include` array specifically, rather than from every literal in the file. Options, roughly in order of preference:

1. Parse for the `include:` key and read only its array. Keeps the module a scanner; needs care, because Prettier collapses a short array onto one line and the existing `stringLiterals` scanner is what makes that safe to read.
2. Import the config and read `test.include` directly. Most accurate, but `vitest.config.ts` is TypeScript and `check-agent-docs.mjs` is plain Node, so this needs a loader — and #115 may move the file to `.mts`, which changes the answer.

Whichever is chosen, the failure mode must stay loud: a widened `include` still has to fail, and a config the reader cannot parse must throw rather than return an empty set that silently passes.

## Acceptance criteria

- A coverage block carrying its own `include`/`exclude` patterns does not affect the reported collection roots.
- Widening the test `include` scope still fails `npm run check:agent-docs`, with the current message quality.
- A `vitest.config.ts` whose `include` cannot be found or read fails loudly rather than passing vacuously.
- The `globRoots` doc comment stops describing a behaviour that is no longer true.

## Tests

Extend `scripts/ignore-entries.test.mjs`. Fixture cases, as it already uses: a config with both an `include` and a coverage `exclude` reports only the include roots; a widened include still reports `**`; a config with no `include` throws. Keep the collapsed-onto-one-line case, which is the one a naive line-based reading gets wrong.

## Follow-on

Once this lands, revisit the coverage scope in `vitest.config.ts` so the threshold floor can see a file no test imports. That is the actual goal; this issue is the thing in the way.

issues.title: fix(scripts): match label names case-insensitively before pruning
issues.body:
Pinned by a test in #158 (issue #119) rather than fixed there, because changing prune semantics is a decision of its own.

## Problem

`scripts/label-plan.mjs` matches desired labels against existing ones by exact name. GitHub label names are case-insensitive for uniqueness — you cannot have both `Bug` and `bug` in a repository — so a repository label that differs from `.github/labels.yml` only in case is planned as **two** conflicting actions at once:

- a **create** for the desired name, and
- an **extra**, because the existing label matched nothing.

With `--prune` that combination is destructive in a way neither half is alone: the existing label is deleted, and the create that was supposed to replace it fails with a `422` because a label with that name (differing only in case) still existed when the plan was made. Deleting a label also removes it from every issue and pull request carrying it.

Ordering does not save it. `applyLabelPlan` runs creates and updates before deletes, so the create fails first, and the run stops on the first failed request — which leaves the label neither renamed nor deleted, but only because an unrelated safety behaviour caught it.

## Evidence

- `scripts/label-plan.mjs` — `planLabelSync` keys existing labels by exact name.
- `scripts/label-plan.test.mjs` — the case-mismatch behaviour is asserted with an explanatory comment, so this issue is a change in intent, not a discovery.
- `.github/labels.yml` currently uses all-lowercase names, so nothing in this repository triggers it today. It fires when a label is renamed by hand in the GitHub UI, or when someone adds a capitalised name to the file.

## Proposed scope

Match existing labels case-insensitively when building the plan. A case-only difference should then become an **update** that corrects the name, not a create plus a delete. Decide explicitly what an update does about the name itself, since the current update payload sends `color` and `description` but not a new name — GitHub's label update API takes `new_name` for exactly this.

Keep the existing guarantees: prune stays opt-in, dry-run keeps previewing accurately, and the plan stays a pure value.

## Acceptance criteria

- A repository label differing from the desired one only in case is never planned as both a create and an extra.
- `--prune` cannot delete a label that a desired entry is meant to keep.
- Dry-run output describes the case-only change accurately.
- Two desired entries differing only in case are rejected by validation as a duplicate, since GitHub could not hold both.

## Tests

- Replace the pinned test with one asserting the corrected behaviour.
- A prune case proving the case-mismatched label is not deleted.
- A validation case for two desired names differing only in case.

issues.title: chore(ci): fail the gate when a workflow misses a declared browser project
issues.body:
Raised by #166, which #168 fixed by hand.

## Problem

`playwright.config.ts` declares the browser projects the suite runs. Two workflows run that suite and each installs browsers with its own hardcoded list:

- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` — `npx playwright install --with-deps chromium webkit`
- `.github/workflows/deployed-smoke.yml` — the same list, separately written

Nothing keeps those lists in step with the config. #165 added the `webkit` project and updated the first workflow but not the second, and the mismatch surfaced as a failed **production** health check after a deploy, with a browser-launch error that says nothing about the real cause.

That is the expensive place for this to fail. The local gate cannot catch it — `npm run validate` does not run `deployed-smoke.yml`, and that workflow only fires on a production `deployment_status`. So the feedback arrives after merge, after deploy, as an alert issue.

## Why a check rather than care

This repository already treats "two lists that must agree" as something to enforce rather than remember, and has the pattern for it twice:

- `scripts/gate-commands.mjs` — the validation chain in `package.json` against its copies in the docs and the `verifier` definition.
- `scripts/ignore-entries.mjs` — `.prettierignore`, `eslint.config.mjs`, and the vitest collection scope against each other.

A third instance fits the same shape: read the project names from `playwright.config.ts`, read the install lines from every workflow that runs the suite, and fail when a workflow installs fewer than the config declares.

## Proposed scope

Extend `npm run check:agent-docs`, or add a sibling module in its style, that:

- Parses the `projects` array in `playwright.config.ts` for project names and maps them to the browser each needs — note `mobile-chrome` is Chromium-backed, so the mapping is project → engine, not project → name.
- Finds every workflow that runs the suite, whether directly (`npm run test:e2e`) or through the gate (`npm run validate`), rather than hardcoding the two filenames — a third workflow is exactly how this recurs.
- Fails with a message naming the workflow, what it installs, and what the config requires.

## Acceptance criteria

- Adding a project to `playwright.config.ts` without updating every workflow that runs the suite fails the gate locally, before merge.
- Removing a browser from a workflow's install list fails the same way.
- A workflow that does not run the suite is not required to install anything.
- The check runs offline and reads no network.

## Tests

Unit cases in the style of `gate-commands.test.mjs`: a matching pair passes; a project added to the config alone fails; a browser dropped from one workflow fails; a workflow with no suite invocation is ignored. Use fixture strings rather than reading the real files, as `ignore-entries.test.mjs` does, so the cases stay stable when the real config changes.

## Note

The engine mapping is the fiddly part and worth getting explicitly right: a project's `use` may be a device descriptor whose `defaultBrowserType` is the thing that matters, not the project's name. `mobile-chrome` uses `devices["Galaxy S9+"]`, which is Chromium — so a naive name-based mapping would demand a browser that does not exist.

Found in a layout audit.

## Problem

`app/` mixes App Router special files with plain library modules at the same level:

- Routing: `page.tsx`, `layout.tsx`, `error.tsx`, `not-found.tsx`, `icon.tsx`, `opengraph-image.tsx`, `twitter-image.tsx`, `favicon.ico`
- Library: `actions.ts`, `commitSearchCache.ts`, `commitTypes.ts`, `githubUrls.ts`, `logger.ts`, `username.ts`, `PrivacySafeAnalytics.tsx`, plus their tests

Colocation is supported by Next.js, so this is valid. The cost is that the directory that defines the app's routes is 23 files of which 15 are not routes, and `ls app/` no longer answers "what does this app serve?".

`app/logger.ts` in particular is imported from `app/api/csp-report/route.ts` as `@/app/logger` — a module used across route boundaries, sitting in the routes directory.

## Proposed scope

Move the non-route modules behind one boundary — `lib/` at the root, or `app/_lib/` if colocation is preferred — keeping tests beside their modules. Then `app/` contains routes and nothing else.

Worth deciding together with the components question, since both are "where does this file go" and one rule should cover them.

## Acceptance criteria

- Every file directly under `app/` is a route file or a route directory.
- Import paths follow the documented rule rather than history.
- `AGENTS.md`'s Layout section describes the boundary.
- No behaviour change.

## Note on sequencing

The widest of the three layout refactors — it touches `app/actions.ts`, which nearly every open Phase 2 issue also edits (#101 landed, #106 and #118 pending). Land it last, or accept the rebase cost.

Found in a layout audit.

## Problem

React components live in three places with no rule distinguishing them:

- `components/FirstCommitDisplay.tsx` — the only file in a root-level `components/`
- `app/home/SearchForm.tsx`, `SearchResults.tsx`, `SearchErrorState.tsx`, `SearchShortcutSection.tsx`
- `app/PrivacySafeAnalytics.tsx`

Colocating components inside `app/` is explicitly supported by Next.js, so none of this is wrong. Pick one rule and apply it. Two coherent options:

1. **Colocate everything.** Feature components live beside the feature (`app/_home/`), shared ones in `app/_components/`. Root `components/` disappears. Keeps a feature's files together.
2. **Separate by role.** All components in root `components/`, all non-component modules in `app/` or `lib/`. Keeps `app/` closer to pure routing.

Option 1 fits the current shape better — most components are already feature-local, and only one is shared. Whichever is chosen, record it in `AGENTS.md`'s Layout section so it holds.

## Acceptance criteria

- One documented rule decides where a new component goes.
- Import style follows from it: relative within a feature, aliased across boundaries.
- No behaviour change; the suite and build are the proof.

issues.body:
## Problem

The in-memory cache reduces repeated completed searches, but concurrent misses for the same username each call GitHub. Requests for many distinct valid usernames bypass the cache entirely. A modest burst can exhaust the shared GitHub token quota for every user.

## Evidence

- `app/actions.ts:234-249`
- `app/commitSearchCache.ts`
- No in-flight request map or platform-level request limit exists.

## Proposed scope

Coalesce in-flight requests by normalized username and add a documented platform rate limit or abuse-control policy for the public search action.

## Acceptance criteria

- Concurrent identical searches share one GitHub request.
- In-flight entries are removed on success and every failure path.
- Unique-user request bursts are bounded without persisting searched usernames.
- Users receive the existing recovery-focused rate-limit response.
- Serverless/process-local limitations are documented.

- Test cleanup after rejection and timeout.

issues.title: fix(api): bound request bursts against the shared GitHub quota
issues.body:
Second half of #106. The first half — coalescing concurrent identical searches — shipped in #150.

## Problem

Coalescing bounds *duplicate* work: many readers of one shared link now cost one upstream search. It does nothing about a flood of **distinct** usernames, where every request is a genuine cache and coalescer miss and reaches GitHub. That is the path that can exhaust the shared token quota for every visitor, and #106's acceptance criteria name it: "unique-user request bursts are bounded without persisting searched usernames."

## Why it was not done alongside the coalescing

Two decisions that deserve to be made deliberately rather than defaulted:

**1. The threshold has real user impact.** Too low and legitimate visitors meet the existing rate-limit screen, which is indistinguishable to them from GitHub rate-limiting the app. There is no traffic data in the repo to size it from, and the app has no analytics on request volume — `search_completed` records outcome, not rate.

**2. "Bounded" means less than it sounds on serverless.** An in-process counter is per-instance and resets on every cold start, exactly like the cache and the in-flight map. Vercel scales instances on load, so an in-process limit of N is really N × instances, and a burst spread across cold starts is barely limited at all. Whatever lands must document that honestly rather than implying a global ceiling.

Note that `inFlightSearches` in `app/commitSearchInFlight.ts` is itself uncapped, unlike the 100-entry cache. It is self-bounding today — entries delete on settle, and every search settles within the 10s `withTimeoutSignal` budget — so it is not a leak, but its size is precisely "concurrent distinct usernames", which is the quantity this slice needs to reason about.

## Options

- **In-process rolling window.** A counter per instance over a short window, returning the existing `rate_limit` result when exceeded. Simple, testable, no new dependency, honest limitations. Bounds one instance's contribution.
- **Platform-level.** Vercel WAF or firewall rules, configured outside the repo. A real global ceiling, but not visible in code review, not testable in the gate, and needs an account-level decision.
- **Both.** Platform rules for abuse, in-process for accidental bursts.

## Acceptance criteria

- Unique-username bursts are bounded without persisting or logging searched usernames.
- Exceeding the bound returns the existing recovery-focused rate-limit response, not a new error state.
- The per-instance, cold-start-resetting nature of any in-process limit is documented where an operator will read it — `docs/production.md` and `docs/architecture.md`.
- Normal single-visitor use cannot reach the bound.

## Tests

- Unit coverage for the chosen limiter, including the boundary and the window rolling over.
- A test proving no username is recorded by the limiter.
- If a platform rule is chosen instead, document how it is verified, since the gate cannot.
issues.display_title: fix(api): bound request bursts against the shared GitHub quota

issues.title: chore(tooling): decide how to handle the Next.js agent-rules block in AGENTS.md
issues.body:
## Problem

Next.js 16.3.0 ships `node_modules/next/dist/server/lib/generate-agent-files.js`, which appends a block delimited by `<!-- BEGIN:nextjs-agent-rules -->` / `<!-- END:nextjs-agent-rules -->` to `AGENTS.md` whenever `next dev` runs. The Playwright suite boots `next dev`, so **every** `npm run test:e2e` — and therefore every `npm run validate` — dirties the working tree.

Observed on five separate runs across four branches on 2026-08-15. It was committed by accident once (stripped in #155) and manually removed in every run since.

## Why it needs a decision rather than a default

`AGENTS.md` is this repository's canonical instruction file. Letting a dependency write into it means Next.js owns a section of it and can rewrite that section on any upgrade, without review. The block's current text instructs agents to read `node_modules/next/dist/docs/` before writing code, and includes a line arguing for its own retention: *"Removing it from a diff only re-creates the uncommitted change; committing it with your work keeps the tree clean."* That reasoning is not wrong, but it is generated output arguing about repository policy, which per this repository's own untrusted-content rule is data rather than direction.

The alternative — stripping it every time — has a real cost too: it is manual, easy to forget, and it already reached a commit once.

## Latent CI risk

The generator references `CLAUDE.md` as well as `AGENTS.md`. `CLAUDE.md` has stayed clean through every observed run, but `npm run check:agent-docs` fails if that file drifts from the pointer template, so if the generator ever writes there, CI breaks for everyone on a fresh install. Worth confirming what conditions make it target `CLAUDE.md`.

## Options

1. **Suppress generation.** Preferred if Next.js supports it. Investigate first — check `next.config.ts` options and the generator source for an opt-out env var or flag. Nothing is written, nothing is stripped, and `AGENTS.md` stays hand-maintained.
2. **Commit it once.** Ends the churn immediately. Accepts that a dependency owns a section of the canonical instruction file, and that an upgrade can change it. If chosen, note in `AGENTS.md` that the block is generated and must not be hand-edited.
3. **Strip it in tooling.** A pre-commit hook or a `check:agent-docs` rule that fails when the block is present. Keeps the file hand-owned without relying on anyone remembering, at the cost of one more thing to maintain.

## Acceptance criteria

- `npm run validate` leaves the working tree clean, or leaves it dirty in a way the gate reports rather than one a contributor must notice.
- The chosen policy is written down in `AGENTS.md`.
- Whatever happens to `CLAUDE.md`, `npm run check:agent-docs` still passes on a fresh `npm ci` followed by a full gate run.

## Notes

- Reproduce with: `npm ci && npm run test:e2e`, then `git status`.
- The block first became possible when the lockfile moved to Next 16.3.0. A checkout with stale `node_modules` on 16.2.12 does not reproduce it, which is why it appeared only once fresh installs started happening.

issues.title: refactor(app): move non-route folders out of the routing namespace
issues.body:
Found in a layout audit.

## Problem

`app/home/` holds 19 files — four components, seven modules, and their tests — and no `page.tsx`, so `/home` returns the custom not-found page today. But the directory name occupies a route segment. Nothing prevents a future `app/home/page.tsx` from turning an internal folder into a public route, and nothing in the name signals that it is not one.

Next.js has a convention for exactly this: a folder whose name starts with `_` is a [private folder](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/routing/colocation#private-folders), opted out of routing entirely. `app/_home/` could never become a route, and the underscore tells a reader why.

## Proposed scope

Rename `app/home/` to `app/_home/` and update the imports. Mechanical: every import of it is relative or via the `@/` alias, and `tsc --noEmit` plus the build verify the rename completely.

Consider at the same time whether `tests/e2e/home.spec.ts` and the `docs/architecture.md` layout list need the new name, and whether `AGENTS.md`'s Layout section — which names `app/home/` — should describe the convention so the next folder added under `app/` follows it.

## Acceptance criteria

- No non-route directory under `app/` occupies a route segment.
- `/home` still renders the not-found page; no route is added or removed.
- `AGENTS.md` records the private-folder convention, so this does not regress.

## Tests

- The existing journeys cover the components; a passing suite plus a clean build is the proof for a rename.
- The unknown-route journey already asserts the not-found behaviour that `/home` relies on.

## Note on sequencing

Touches `app/home/**`, which several open issues also edit (#111, #118). Land it when those are not in flight, or after them.

issues.title: fix(csp): bound and sanitize CSP report ingestion
issues.body:
## Problem

The unauthenticated CSP endpoint reads the entire request before checking its size, measures JavaScript characters rather than bytes, accepts arbitrary content types, and logs every valid entry in a Reporting API array. A single request can amplify into many log records. Non-HTTP schemes outside the current opaque allowlist can also retain sensitive path content.

## Evidence

- `app/api/csp-report/route.ts:23-58`
- `app/api/csp-report/route.ts:125-162`
- Current tests cover post-read length and selected opaque schemes, not byte limits or report-count caps.

## Proposed scope

Enforce a bounded byte read, cap reports per request, validate expected content types, sanitize non-HTTP schemes to the scheme alone, and configure platform-level rate limiting or sampling.

## Acceptance criteria

- Bodies over the byte limit are rejected before unbounded buffering.
- At most a documented number of reports are logged per request.
- Only expected CSP report content types are processed.
- Query strings, fragments, opaque payloads, and non-HTTP path data cannot reach logs.
- Normal legacy and Reporting API payloads still return the expected response.

## Tests

- Cover multibyte bodies, excessive arrays, unsupported content types, and `mailto:`/custom schemes.
- Retain query-string and script-sample privacy tests.

issues.title: chore(tooling): keep stray root directories out of the unit test run
issues.body:
Surfaced during verification of #139.

## Problem

A `.verifier-probe/` directory containing a Playwright spec appeared at the repository root during a session, and `npm test` failed:

```
FAIL  .verifier-probe/probe.spec.ts [ .verifier-probe/probe.spec.ts ]
Error: Playwright Test did not expect test() to be called here.
```

`vitest.config.ts` excludes `node_modules`, `.next`, `tests/e2e`, and the four named tooling-state directories `.claude/`, `.codex/`, `.entire/`, `.vercel/`. Any other root-level scratch directory is collected by vitest's default `**/*.{test,spec}.?(c|m)[jt]s?(x)` glob, so a tool or agent that writes a scratch spec anywhere else breaks the gate with an error that points at the tooling rather than at the cause.

The same gap applies to the other two lists `npm run check:agent-docs` keeps in step: `.prettierignore` and `eslint.config.mjs` both enumerate the same four directories by name.

## Proposed scope

Decide between two approaches and apply it consistently across all three lists:

1. **Exclude by convention** — ignore all root-level dot-directories rather than four named ones. Smallest change, but silently widens what the gate cannot see, which is exactly the property the AGENTS.md unread-path exemption depends on being explicit.
2. **Scope collection positively** — have vitest collect only from `app/`, `components/`, and `scripts/` instead of excluding directories one at a time. A stray file outside those is then invisible by construction, and the exemption's "membership is the list above, not a tool result" rule stays honest.

Option 2 looks better: the exemption in AGENTS.md is only as safe as the three lists agreeing, and a positive scope is easier to keep true than a growing denylist.

## Acceptance criteria

- A stray `*.spec.ts` or `*.test.ts` at the repository root, or in an unlisted root directory, does not fail or silently join `npm test`.
- `.prettierignore`, `eslint.config.mjs`, and `vitest.config.ts` stay in agreement, and `npm run check:agent-docs` still fails when they drift.
- Product code under `app/`, `components/`, and `scripts/` is still fully collected — verify the test count is unchanged.
- The AGENTS.md unread-path exemption is updated if the exempt set changes.

## Tests

- Extend the existing `check:agent-docs` unit coverage for whichever list format changes.
- A temporary stray spec at the root, confirmed not collected, then removed.

issues.title: test(e2e): make the browser suite reject a stale server of this app
issues.body:
Follow-up to #109, which shipped the identity check in #<pending>.

## Problem

The preflight added by #109 rejects a *foreign* server on the Playwright port by asking `/api/health` for `service: "my-first-commit"`. It confirms identity, not freshness.

A server of this app left running by an interrupted earlier run therefore passes, even when it is:

- serving a different branch's code, or
- started without `E2E_COMMIT_SEARCH_MOCKS=1`, so every fixture username hits real GitHub.

The second case produces the same symptom the identity check was built to eliminate: a wall of misleading failures with no indication that the server, not the branch, is the problem. In an agent session it is more likely than a foreign app on the port, because interrupted runs are common.

## Proposed scope

Expose enough state in the health payload for the check to reject a mismatched server, and extend `findForeignServer` to use it. Candidates:

- Whether commit-search mocks are enabled. Cheap and closes the more damaging case. It is a boolean about test configuration, not a secret, but `app/api/health/route.ts` is public and uncached, so weigh it deliberately — the file's existing comment is explicit that `GITHUB_TOKEN` presence is the maximum it will report.
- The commit the server is running, which `buildHealthPayload` already reports as `commit`. It is `"local"` for any dev server, so it does not distinguish branches without more work.

If the mocks flag is judged inappropriate for a public endpoint, an alternative is a dedicated non-production probe route, or having the preflight compare against a value the web-server command passes in.

## Acceptance criteria

- A server of this app started without the mock flag is rejected before any spec runs, with a message saying so.
- Nothing secret is added to a public endpoint.
- A correctly started server is still accepted, and a free port still starts one.
- The foreign-server cases from #109 keep working.

## Tests

- Unit cases beside the existing ones in `scripts/e2e-server-identity.test.mjs`.
- An acceptance check equivalent to #109's: start the app without the flag on the configured port and confirm the run stops with the new message rather than failing every fixture spec.

issues.title: fix(ui): keep a maximum-length handle inside the shortcut row
issues.body:
Raised during review of #102. Pre-existing, not introduced there.

## Problem

`app/home/SearchShortcutSection.tsx` renders each shortcut as a button that neither shrinks nor wraps. GitHub handles are up to 39 characters, so `@` plus 39 characters at `text-sm` with `px-3` padding is roughly 300–330px, against a content box of about 288px at a 320px viewport (`main` carries `p-4`). The result is a horizontal scrollbar on the page.

320px is also what 200% zoom produces on a 640px window, which is the WCAG 1.4.10 reflow condition — content should reflow rather than require two-dimensional scrolling.

This applies to the Recent searches row and the Examples row equally, though the shipped example handles are short enough not to trigger it. #102 made the bound explicit by validating handles on read, so the widest label that can reach the row is now clearly 40 characters.

## Evidence

- `app/home/SearchShortcutSection.tsx:54` — button class list has no `max-w-*`, no wrapping.
- `app/page.tsx` — `main` has `p-4`.
- `app/username.ts` — 39-character limit.

The measurement above is an estimate from the class list; the reviewer that raised it could not render the app. **Confirm it in a browser before fixing**, since the fix depends on the real overflow.

## Proposed scope

Let a long label wrap or truncate inside the row rather than overflowing it — `max-w-full break-all` on the button is the smallest change. Truncation with a title/`aria-label` fallback is an alternative, but the accessible name already carries the full handle, so wrapping is simpler and loses nothing.

## Acceptance criteria

- A 39-character handle in Recent searches does not cause horizontal page scrolling at a 320px viewport.
- The button remains a single tap target and keeps its focus ring.
- Short handles look unchanged.

## Tests

- A Playwright assertion at 320px that `document.documentElement.scrollWidth` does not exceed the viewport width with a maximum-length handle seeded into storage. That is the check that would have caught this, and it generalises to other long-content regressions.

issues.title: fix(a11y): keep the error-state retry focusable while it runs
issues.body:
Surfaced during review of #139.

## Problem

`app/home/SearchErrorState.tsx` renders its "Try again" button with `disabled={isPending || !lastSearchedUsername}`. When a focused control becomes `disabled`, browsers blur it to `<body>`, so a keyboard or screen-reader user who activates the retry loses their place for the whole request and lands nowhere when it settles. Nothing announces that a retry is running either.

The partial-result retry added in #139 avoids exactly this, using `aria-disabled` plus an early-return guard in the click handler, a label that changes to "Searching again...", and an always-mounted polite region. `app/home/SearchResults.tsx` carries a comment explaining the choice.

#139 also made the error-state button a first-class retry path — it now passes `{ isRetry: true }` — so the two controls sit inside one feature with different behaviour, and the codebase currently teaches both patterns.

## Proposed scope

Port the `aria-disabled` pattern from `SearchResults` to `SearchErrorState`'s retry, including the pending label and the click guard. Decide whether the announcement belongs there too: unlike the partial-result panel, this button sits inside a container that is already `role="alert"` or `role="status"`, so a second live region may be redundant.

## Acceptance criteria

- Activating the retry keeps focus on the control.
- A retry in progress is distinguishable from an idle one, and is announced without competing with the surrounding alert.
- The disabled styling still meets WCAG 1.4.11 for its boundary in every state.
- Both retry controls follow one pattern, and the comment in `SearchResults.tsx` no longer needs to name an exception.

## Tests

- A unit test asserting the button keeps focus across a retry, which is the regression this class of bug keeps reproducing.
- Extend an existing rate-limit or unavailable journey rather than adding a fixture; both already reach this button.

## Acceptance criteria

- Empty, whitespace-only, non-string, and invalid usernames are removed.
- Values are trimmed and case-insensitive duplicates collapse deterministically.
- Corrupt JSON and blocked storage remain non-fatal.

## Tests

- Add one browser test with deliberately corrupt stored data.

issues.title: feat(ui): offer an in-place retry for partial commit results
issues.body:
Follow-up to #101, which shipped in #137 without an in-place retry control.

## Problem

When GitHub returns `incomplete_results`, the results view now explains that the search timed out and that a repeated search often reaches the full history — but offers no way to run one. The only control on screen is the header's "Search another user", which clears the handle the copy just told the visitor to reuse. A page reload works, because the URL carries `?user=<handle>`, but that is not discoverable.

## Why it was deferred

A retry button here is the first control this app places inside a *successful* result view that re-issues a search, and #137's review rounds surfaced four distinct problems with the straightforward implementation. Each is worth designing for rather than patching:

- **Busy state ownership.** `isPending` from `useTransition` stays true through the tail of any search's transition, so a first partial result briefly rendered its button as "Searching again...", announcing a retry that never happened. A retry needs its own flag.
- **Cancellation.** Adding a retry makes it possible to have a search in flight while the results view and its always-enabled header reset button are both on screen. Invalidating the in-flight request via a search-id bump fixes the stale result, but leaves `isPending` true — which drives `canSearch`, `SearchForm`, and both shortcut sections. The visitor lands back on the form with the submit button disabled and labelled "Searching..." for up to `GITHUB_SEARCH_TIMEOUT_MS` (10s), with no status text explaining why. The busy flag needs to be owned by the hook, not read from the transition.
- **Failure handling.** `runCommitSearch` calls `setResult` unconditionally, so a retry that comes back rate-limited flips `result.found` to false, unmounts `SearchResults`, and discards the commits the visitor was reading. GitHub's search limit is shared across all users of the app's token, and a search slow enough to return `incomplete_results` is exactly the kind that gets retried. The failure needs to render without destroying the result — and its placement matters: above the button it pushes the button down under the pointer as it wraps.
- **Announcement.** A retry that succeeds but is *still* partial produces no change in heading, section, or button label, so nothing tells a screen-reader user the search completed. A name change on an already-focused control is not reliably announced. This needs an always-mounted polite region whose text changes, not a region that appears with its content.

## Acceptance criteria

- A visitor can re-run the same search from the results view in one action.
- Pending, success-still-partial, and failure outcomes are each announced.
- A failed retry leaves the displayed commits on screen.
- Abandoning a retry does not leave the form in a busy state.
- The control meets WCAG 1.4.11 for its boundary and focus indicator in every state, and its label meets AA at 4.5:1. The amber palette regressed below AA twice during #137, so assert this in a journey rather than by eye.

## Tests

- A stateful `e2e-incomplete-once-*` fixture proving the retry re-issues the search and reaches the complete history, plus an incomplete-then-error fixture for the preservation path. Both need `AGENTS.md` entries.
- Hook-level coverage for the busy flag and cancellation, since both reset controls are disabled while pending and cannot reach those states through the UI.

issues.body:

GitHub can return `incomplete_results: true`, but the action currently ignores that flag, labels the first returned item as the earliest indexed commit, and caches the response as authoritative.

- The UI explains the limitation or offers recovery.
- Incomplete responses do not poison the normal five-minute cache.

## Problem

Searches update the browser URL to `?user=<handle>` before emitting analytics. The analytics component has no `beforeSend` sanitizer, so the repository's promise that analytics events exclude searched usernames is not enforced by application code.

Vercel recommends `beforeSend` when sensitive query parameters must be removed before events are sent.

- `app/home/searchExecution.ts:32-42`
- `app/layout.tsx:71`

Wrap the Analytics component with a client-side `beforeSend` callback that removes the `user` parameter from every page-view and custom-event URL.

## Acceptance criteria

- No analytics event URL contains the `user` query value.
- Unrelated URL parameters are preserved unless policy says otherwise.
- Analytics properties continue to exclude usernames.
- The privacy documentation matches the enforced behavior.

## Tests

- Add focused sanitizer tests for page views and custom events.
- Include encoded usernames and URLs with multiple query parameters.

issues.title: fix(search): prevent stale results from overlapping requests
issues.body:
## Problem

Example and recent-search shortcuts remain enabled while a search transition is pending, and every response is applied unconditionally. If two searches resolve out of order, an older response can overwrite the newer result while the URL and heading still identify the newer username.

## Evidence

- `app/home/searchExecution.ts:37-59`
- `app/page.tsx:164-182`
- `app/home/SearchShortcutSection.tsx:45-53`

## Proposed scope

Track a monotonically increasing request identity and ignore superseded completions. Also disable all search entry points while a request is pending.

## Acceptance criteria

- Only the latest initiated search may update the result, recent searches, or completion analytics.
- All search and shortcut controls expose a consistent pending/disabled state.
- The displayed username, URL, and commit data cannot disagree after overlapping searches.

## Tests

- Add a focused deferred-promise test that resolves two searches in reverse order.
- Add a browser journey that attempts a second shortcut search while the first is pending.
issues.display_title: fix(search): prevent stale results from overlapping requests

issues.title: fix(search): eliminate shared URL hydration mismatch
issues.body:
## Problem

The homepage initializes shared-search state by reading `window.location.search`. Server rendering returns an empty username, while browser hydration can render a populated or invalid username immediately.

A production-build browser run against `/?user=octo_cat` reproduced React hydration error 418 because validation markup existed only in the client render.

## Evidence

- `app/page.tsx:24-25`
- `app/home/sharedSearch.ts:16-19`
- The current Playwright suite does not navigate directly to a shared `?user=` URL.

## Proposed scope

Initialize the server and first client render identically. Read the query after hydration, or pass server-derived search parameters into a client search component.

## Acceptance criteria

- Valid shared URLs automatically search the requested username.
- Invalid shared URLs show validation without a hydration warning.
- Initial HTML and the first client render are structurally consistent.
- Shared URLs preserve the existing privacy and URL-clearing behavior.

## Tests

- Add Playwright coverage for valid and invalid `?user=` URLs.
- Fail the test on `pageerror` or React hydration console errors.
- Retain focused unit coverage for shared URL parsing.

`eslint-config-next` is pinned to the same exact version as `next` and is the lint half of the same release. Merging one at a time is what the [dependency policy](docs/development.md#dependency-update-policy) asks for, so `main` briefly held `next@16.3.1` with `eslint-config-next@16.3.0`.
