issues.title: docs(agents): describe the import convention the code follows
issues.body:
Resolves the one item left open by #192. Documentation only — no code changes, and the convention itself is unchanged.

## The rule described neither half of the codebase

AGENTS.md said imports were "relative within a feature, aliased with `@/` only across a boundary". Measured against the code:

| Form | Count | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@/app/_lib/*` | 3 | exactly the route files under `app/api/` |
| `../_lib/*`, `./_lib/*` | 29 | everything else under `app/` |

All 29 relative imports cross out of their own folder, so "relative within a feature" was not what was happening; and the 3 aliased ones are not a boundary category, they are a location.

## What actually decides it is depth

A route file sits three levels down. Its relative path to a shared module is `../../_lib/logger`, which counts directories rather than naming anything and silently resolves to a different place if the route ever moves — so route files use `@/app/_lib/logger`. Everything else is at most one directory from `_lib`, where the relative form is the readable one.

The rule now says that, which makes it checkable against the code rather than a principle nothing obeys. The old sentence is quoted in the new paragraph so the correction is legible to someone who remembers the previous wording.

## Verification

`PASS (unread-paths)` — every modified path (`AGENTS.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`) is a `*.md` file, which is exactly the exempt set in step 7 of AGENTS.md. Ran `npm run check:agent-docs`, which reports the docs consistent and is the one gate command that reads these paths; here it verifies the change rather than merely re-checking repository state, since the change edits AGENTS.md.

Skipped `npm audit`, `test:coverage`, `test:e2e`, `lint`, `format:check`, `check:labels`, and `build`: `.prettierignore` excludes `*.md` wholesale, ESLint does not lint Markdown, Vitest collects only from `app/` and `scripts/`, and the remaining three read source, `package.json`, and `.github/labels.yml`. CI runs the complete gate on this PR regardless.

## Note on the counts

An earlier version of this PR said 27 total / 24 relative. Those were correct when measured during #192 but stale by the time they were written down — the analytics move in that PR added five relative imports. Recounted before committing: 32 total, 29 relative, 3 aliased.

issues.title: test(e2e): reject a stale server of this app on the Playwright port
issues.body:
Closes #146

## Problem

The preflight from #109 confirms identity, not freshness. A server of this app left behind by an interrupted run answers `/api/health` with the right `service` name and is adopted. When that run started it without `E2E_COMMIT_SEARCH_MOCKS=1`, every reserved `e2e-*` username reaches real GitHub and nearly every spec fails for a reason that has nothing to do with the branch — the same misleading wall of failures the identity check was built to remove. In an agent session that is more likely than a foreign app on the port.

## The candidate that cannot work

The issue offers "have the preflight compare against a value the web-server command passes in". I checked it before discarding it, and it cannot close this case.

The damaging server is one the preflight did **not** start. `reuseExistingServer` means `playwright.config.ts`'s `webServer.command` never ran for that process, so any value this side injects describes the current run's *intent*, and comparing it against itself proves nothing about the process actually listening. A side channel does not rescue it either: a nonce written to a file by the run that started the server is still on disk after that run is interrupted, so the stale server would pass on the strength of its own leftover nonce. One process cannot read another's environment, so the server has to report its own configuration. That leaves the two remaining candidates.

## Choosing between them

**(a) report the flag in `/api/health`.** The honest case for it: in a real production deployment the mock flag is never set, so the field reads `false` forever and discloses nothing. It costs one line and no new route.

**(b) a dedicated route that does not exist outside development.** Chosen.

`app/api/health/route.ts` is public and uncached, and its comment does not merely say "don't print the token" — it fixes the endpoint's ceiling at what a production operator needs, which is why `githubToken` reports presence and nothing else. A commit-search mocks flag is not that; it is harness configuration, useful to nothing running in production.

The objection to (a) is therefore not the byte, it is the precedent. Accepting "always false in production, so it leaks nothing" as sufficient reason to hang test state off a public endpoint makes that the standing argument for the next flag — and the next one will not necessarily be always-false. The comment in that file is the boundary; spending it on a convenience is what erodes it.

(b) removes the need for the argument. `/api/e2e-readiness` returns `404` whenever `NODE_ENV` is `production`, which covers `next start` and every Vercel deployment, preview included. On a deployed server the answer is not merely uninteresting — the question cannot be asked. What stays reachable is a development server answering one boolean about that developer's own shell. `/api/health` is unchanged, so nothing at all was added to a public endpoint.

The cost is one route file and one extra preflight request, sent only after identity has passed. Identity still runs first, so a foreign server keeps getting the #109 message rather than a confusing complaint about a probe it was never going to serve.

`app/e2eCommitSearchMocks.ts` gives the flag one definition shared by the route and `app/actions.ts`, so the probe cannot report ready while the server action disagrees about what "enabled" means — reporting ready and then serving live GitHub is precisely the failure this PR exists to prevent.

## Acceptance check

A dev server started on the configured port **without** the flag, then the suite run against it. Real output:

```
$ npx next dev -H 127.0.0.1 -p 3120        # note: no E2E_COMMIT_SEARCH_MOCKS
$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3120/api/e2e-readiness
{"service":"my-first-commit","commitSearchMocks":false}

$ E2E_PORT=3120 npx playwright test
Error: Port 3120 is in use by my-first-commit, but it was started without E2E_COMMIT_SEARCH_MOCKS=1, so the reserved e2e-* usernames would reach real GitHub instead of the fixtures and nearly every spec would fail for a reason that has nothing to do with this branch. This is usually a server left behind by an interrupted run. Stop whatever is using port 3120 and run the suite again, or point this run at a free port with E2E_PORT=<port>. The process is left alone on purpose: the port may belong to another checkout, a colleague, or another agent's session.

   at globalSetup.ts:16
```

Zero specs ran. Before this change that server produced a full suite of fixture failures.

The production gate was verified against the real build rather than argued for. `next build && next start` on the same port:

```
$ curl -s -w "HTTP %{http_code}" http://127.0.0.1:3120/api/e2e-readiness
HTTP 404

$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3120/api/health
{"status":"ok","service":"my-first-commit","timestamp":"...","environment":"local","commit":"local","checks":{"siteUrl":{"configured":false,"value":null},"githubToken":{"configured":false}}}
```

The health payload is byte-for-byte what it was. And a production-mode server on the port is itself rejected, with its own reason:

```
Error: Port 3120 is in use by my-first-commit, but it does not serve /api/e2e-readiness (HTTP 404). That route is missing from builds older than this check, and absent from production builds on purpose, so this server could not be confirmed as one started for this suite. ...
```

Both servers were stopped afterwards; nothing else is ever killed.

## Tests

Unit cases beside the existing ones in `scripts/e2e-server-identity.test.mjs`: a mocks-enabled server accepted; a mocks-disabled server rejected naming the flag; a missing probe route; each "nothing is listening" code still treated as a free port; a dropped connection, a silent server, and a non-JSON body; a payload that omits the flag treated as *not* enabled rather than assumed; the two probes disagreeing about identity. On `findLocalServerProblem`: a correct server accepted with both probes sent, a stale one rejected, a foreign one rejected **without** the readiness probe being sent, and a free port left free. Plus a guard that `READINESS_PATH` still points at a route that exists, since it is a string in one file and a directory name in the other.

`app/api/e2e-readiness/route.test.ts` covers the enabled and disabled payloads, that `"true"` is not accepted where `app/actions.ts` requires `"1"`, the production `404`, and that the payload carries nothing beyond the service name and the one flag.

The #109 cases are untouched and still pass: `findForeignServer` was not modified, only called first.

## Gate

`E2E_PORT=3120 npm run validate` — **pass**, complete, in CI order: `npm audit`, `npm test`, `npm run test:e2e` (30 passed), `npm run lint`, `npm run format:check`, `npm run check:agent-docs`, `npm run check:labels`, `npm run build`.

The first run failed in `build`: three TypeScript errors from typing the env parameter as a weak type with one optional named property, which `NodeJS.ProcessEnv` does not satisfy. Fixed with an index-signature type, focused tests rerun, then the whole gate rerun from the top on the fixed state — the pass above is that second, complete run.

## Docs

The E2E gotcha in `AGENTS.md` said the check "checks identity, not freshness", which this change makes false; it now describes both probes and keeps the one limitation that is still real — neither probe can tell which branch a server is running. `docs/development.md` and `docs/architecture.md` match, and the layout list names the new route. `CHANGELOG.md` gets an `Unreleased` → `Changed` entry, hand-formatted.

## Review steps

**This session could not invoke sub-agents, so steps 6–8 of `AGENTS.md` were performed by this agent itself and are not sub-agent output.** Stated here rather than left implied, because it collapses three independent reviews into one agent reviewing its own change and supplies no second opinion.

- **`ui-review` equivalent** — no user-visible surface. No component, style, markup, or copy shown to a visitor changed. The one new route serves JSON to a test harness and does not exist in production.
- **`verifier` equivalent** — the complete gate above, run in full on the committed state, plus the two acceptance checks against real servers.
- **`code-review` equivalent** — self-review of the branch diff and every untracked file. Findings acted on: the env parameter typing (caught by the gate, fixed and reverified); a `new URL(relative, import.meta.url)` in the path guard that silently resolved against the jsdom document instead of the `file:` base and made the assertion meaningless — replaced with `fileURLToPath` and commented; and `timedOutProblem` hard-coding `/api/health` in a message the readiness probe also emits, now parameterised with the old call sites unchanged.

## Deliberately out of scope

The other half of #146's problem statement — a stale server running a *different branch* — is not addressed. `commit` is `"local"` on every dev server, so distinguishing branches needs a mechanism this PR does not build. Both docs now say so plainly instead of implying the check is complete.

issues.title: test(unit): add coverage thresholds and time-contract tests
issues.body:
Closes #114

## What this does

Two halves, both about things the suite could not previously tell you.

**Coverage.** `@vitest/coverage-v8` is installed, the gate's unit step is now
`npm run test:coverage` (`vitest run --coverage`), and thresholds live in `vitest.config.ts`. The
gate runs the suite once, instrumented, so coverage is produced by the same command locally and in
CI rather than by a second job. `npm test` still exists uninstrumented for a fast single-file loop.

**Time contracts.** The five-minute cache TTL and the ten-second search deadline are now tested on
a fake clock. No test waits on real time; the whole unit suite still finishes in about 20 seconds.

## Measured coverage and the thresholds

Measured on this branch (the numbers the report prints):

| Metric | Measured | Floor set |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Statements | 93.68% | 93% |
| Branches | 89.58% | 89% |
| Functions | 98.30% | 98% |
| Lines | 94.66% | 94% |

Each floor is the whole percent below its measurement — under a point of slack. That is deliberate
on both sides: aspirational numbers would fail on day one, and a floor at 60% could never fail. At
this setting a handful of newly uncovered lines, or one new uncovered function, fails the gate,
while a refactor that moves a few lines around does not.

Coverage measures the files the suite loads, which is Vitest's default when `coverage.include` is
unset. The trade-off is stated in `vitest.config.ts` and in the development guide rather than left
for a reader to discover: a module that **no** test imports is absent from the report rather than
counted as zero, so the floors cannot catch a wholly untested new file. Scoping coverage to the two
collection roots instead would pull in the metadata image routes and the two npm-script
entrypoints, which the gate exercises by running them rather than by unit test; the floor would then
read 75% while measuring less than it does now.

`coverage/` was already in `.gitignore` and `.prettierignore`. It was **not** in
`eslint.config.mjs`, and a coverage run left `npm run lint` reporting a warning about a generated
file, so `coverage/**` is now in `globalIgnores` alongside the tooling-state directories.
`git status --untracked-files=all` is clean after a coverage run.

## The `check:agent-docs` interaction

`globRoots` in `scripts/ignore-entries.mjs` collects the leading segment of every glob-shaped
string literal in `vitest.config.ts` and `check-agent-docs.mjs` requires the result to be exactly
`app, scripts`. A coverage block containing any pattern therefore fails that check.

I did not change the check. The coverage block carries **no glob patterns at all**: `provider`,
`reporter`, and `thresholds` only, with Vitest's default `coverage/` report directory and its
default include/exclude behaviour. That leaves `test.include` the only thing in the file that
answers "what does the unit run reach?", which is exactly what the guard is asserting. A comment in
`vitest.config.ts` records why the block must stay pattern-free.

Proof the guard still bites, run on this branch:

- Widening the collection scope by hand — `include: ["app/**/...]` to `["**/...]` —
  makes `npm run check:agent-docs` exit **1** with
  `vitest.config.ts collects from **, scripts rather than from app, scripts`.
- Adding a coverage pattern by hand — `exclude: ["coverage/**"]` inside the coverage block — exits
  **1** the same way, with `collects from app, coverage, scripts rather than from app, scripts`.
  (`exclude: ["**/*.config.*"]` produces `**, app, scripts`.)
- Both were reverted; the check passes on the committed state and the working tree is clean.

## Proving the ten-second timeout actually fires

The old test injected an `AbortError` into the Octokit mock, which proves the error is normalized
but would pass just as well if `withTimeoutSignal` never set a timer. It is kept, renamed in intent
by a comment, because normalization is still worth pinning.

The new test makes the search hang the way a request with no response does: the mock returns a
promise that settles only when the `AbortSignal` it was handed fires. Then, on fake timers:

- advance to 9,999 ms — the search has been called once, `signal.aborted` is `false`, and the
  `getCommits` promise has not settled;
- advance the last 1 ms — `signal.aborted` is `true` and the promise resolves to the timeout state
  with the `github_commit_search_timeout` warning.

A second test asserts `vi.getTimerCount()` is 0 after a search that answers in time, so the abort
timer is cleared rather than left pending.

Mutation checks, run locally and reverted:

- `GITHUB_SEARCH_TIMEOUT_MS` 10,000 → 1,000 fails the deadline test.
- dropping `clearTimeout` fails the timer-count test.
- cache TTL 5 min → 1 min fails 4 boundary tests.
- caching every result regardless of `errorKind` fails 7 cacheability tests.

## Cache contracts

`app/_lib/commitSearchCache.test.ts` gains: the boundary in both directions (served at TTL − 1 ms,
gone at TTL), that a read refreshes eviction order without extending the lifetime, that a rewrite
starts a fresh deadline, that an empty result **is** cached and expires on the same deadline, and
that every other failure kind — `rate_limit`, `timeout`, `unavailable`, `validation`, `unknown`,
and a result with no kind at all — is never cached and never evicts a good entry.

The expiry tests call the cache without the `now` argument, so they exercise the `Date.now()`
default the server action actually uses; the existing tests pass timestamps in and never reach it.

## Gate

`E2E_PORT=3110 npm run validate` — **exit 0** on the rebased commit: 0 vulnerabilities, 468 unit
tests in 30 files with the coverage thresholds met, 45 Playwright tests across the three browser
projects, lint, format, `check:agent-docs`, `check:labels`, and the production build. Port 3110
throughout, because another suite was using the default 3100. The working tree is clean afterwards,
including after a coverage run.

The branch was rebased onto `main` after #173 landed; the coverage numbers above are the
post-rebase measurement, and the gate result is from the rebased state.

## Sub-agents

This session cannot invoke sub-agents, so steps 6-8 of `AGENTS.md` were performed by me rather than
by `ui-review`, `verifier`, and `code-review`. I said so on reaching step 6, not here. Concretely:

- **ui-review**: no user-visible surface. This change touches tests, configuration, documentation,
  and a dev dependency; no component, style, markup, or copy changed.
- **verifier**: I ran the complete gate myself with `E2E_PORT=3110`, plus the mutation checks above.
- **code-review**: I reviewed the branch diff and every staged, unstaged, and untracked file
  (`git status --short --untracked-files=all`) myself.

That collapses three independent reviews into one agent reviewing its own change, and is the
weakest form of each step. Worth a human eye on the threshold numbers in particular.

## Not done here

- Thresholds are global, not per-file. `app/_lib/actions.ts` at ~78% statements is the lowest file
  and would fail a per-file floor set from the global one; raising it is test work, not
  configuration work, and belongs in its own change.
- `playwright-report/` and `test-results/` are ignored by Git and Prettier but not by ESLint, the
  same gap `coverage/**` just closed. Left alone as unrelated to this issue.

issues.title: test(scripts): cover label sync planning and prune behavior
issues.body:
Closes #119

## What

`scripts/sync-labels.mjs` mixed validating `.github/labels.yml`, planning creates and updates, and deleting labels, all behind a CLI shell that exits the process and talks to GitHub. CI ran only the offline `--check` path, so the branch that deletes repository labels — which removes them from every issue and pull request that carries them, irreversibly — had no tests.

Validation, reconciliation planning, reporting, and applying now live in `scripts/label-plan.mjs` as pure functions over plain data, following the split `gate-commands.mjs` and `ignore-entries.mjs` already use. The script keeps the side effects only: arguments, file reading, the token and repository, Octokit, printing, and the exit code.

- `validateLabels(labels, labelsFile)` returns every problem as a line instead of exiting at the first.
- `planLabelSync({ desired, existing, prune })` returns `{ created, updated, unchanged, deleted, extra }`. `deleted` is empty unless `prune` is set, so a prune-less plan has nothing to delete rather than merely not deleting.
- `formatPlanReport({ owner, repo, plan, dryRun, prune })` returns the report lines.
- `applyLabelPlan(plan, { owner, repo, request, dryRun })` sends the plan through an injected `request` with Octokit's signature — testable with a recorder, and it reads nothing but the plan.

## Coverage

54 new tests, no GitHub writes and no network:

- **Validation** — duplicate names, blank names, non-mapping entries, colour format (uppercase, `#`, wrong length, non-hex, whitespace), description required and the 100-character limit at the boundary, and all problems reported rather than the first.
- **YAML numbers** — parses a fixture with `js-yaml` and pins the asymmetry: `123456`, `5319e7`, and `000000` come back as numbers (`5319e7` as `53190000000`), while `e10c02` stays a string. That is what makes an unquoted colour silently wrong in only some rows.
- **Planning** — create, update on drifted colour or description, unchanged, GitHub's uppercase colours and `null` descriptions, extras, all buckets at once, no input mutation, and that a plan carries only the three fields GitHub is sent.
- **Prune** — never planned without the flag; only extras are ever in `deleted`; a name differing only in case is planned as a create plus an extra, which is documented in a test rather than changed.
- **Dry run** — conditional wording throughout, and the deletion line lists exactly the names a real run would delete. `applyLabelPlan` sends nothing at all in a dry run.
- **Applying** — exact route and parameters for POST, PATCH (including `new_name`), and DELETE; nothing for unchanged labels; no DELETE for a plan that kept its extras; creates and updates before deletions; and a stop at the first failed request.

`npm run check:labels` is untouched and stays in `validate` as the CLI smoke check; `npm run check:agent-docs` passes, since neither the `validate` chain nor the way `check:labels` is invoked changed.

## Behaviour notes

Two deliberate differences from the old script: a create sends `name`, `color`, `description` rather than spreading whatever else the YAML entry carried, and an unparseable label file is now reported under the same `is invalid:` heading as every other problem.

## Verification

`E2E_PORT=3130 npm run validate` — pass. `npm audit` 0 vulnerabilities, 27 unit files / 395 tests (up from 26 / 341, exactly the 54 added), 30 Playwright tests, lint, `format:check`, `check:agent-docs`, `check:labels`, and `next build` all green.

## Process

This session cannot invoke sub-agents, so the `ui-review`, `verifier`, and `code-review` work in steps 6–8 of AGENTS.md was done by the implementing agent itself rather than by those sub-agents. That is one agent reviewing its own change, not three independent reviews. The change touches `scripts/` and `CHANGELOG.md` only and has no user-visible surface, so the ui-review equivalent has nothing to review and returns no findings.

issues.title: fix(scripts): match label names case-insensitively before pruning
issues.body:
Closes #160

## Problem

`planLabelSync` matched desired labels against existing ones by exact name. GitHub label names are unique *without regard to case* — a repository cannot hold both `Bug` and `bug` — so a repository label differing from `.github/labels.yml` only in case was planned as two conflicting actions at once: a **create** for the desired name, and an **extra**, because the existing label matched nothing.

Under `--prune` that pair is destructive in a way neither half is alone. The existing label is deleted, and deleting a label removes it from every issue and pull request carrying it. The create meant to replace it fails with a `422`, because a label differing only in case still existed when the plan was made.

Nothing in this repository reaches it today: every name in `.github/labels.yml` is lowercase. It fires when a label is renamed by hand in the GitHub UI, or when a capitalised name is added to the file. `.github/labels.yml` is untouched here; the failing cases are fixtures.

## Change

- **`planLabelSync` matches on a lowercased key.** A case-only difference is now an update, never a create plus an extra. The prune scan uses the same key, so a label a desired entry matches is never `extra` and therefore never `deleted`.
- **An update carries `currentName`.** `updated` entries are `{ name, color, description, currentName }`, where `name` is what the file wants and `currentName` is what GitHub has. `created` and `unchanged` are unchanged.
- **The dry-run report shows both names** when they differ: `would update: Bug -> bug`. A colour-only or description-only update still prints one name.
- **`validateLabels` rejects two desired entries differing only in case**, with a message naming the entry it collides with. An exact duplicate keeps its existing message.

## Decision: yes, an update renames

The issue asked for this to be decided explicitly. **An update now sends `new_name`, and it sends the desired name rather than the current one.**

The payload already sent `new_name: label.name`, but `label.name` was also what addressed the request, so the field was a no-op that happened to look like a rename. `applyLabelPlan` now addresses the `PATCH` to `currentName` and sends the desired name as `new_name`.

Not renaming was the alternative, and it fails the point of the fix. Matching case-insensitively without renaming makes `Bug` match `bug` forever: it is no longer extra, so prune will not remove it, and no update corrects it, so `.github/labels.yml` becomes permanently unenforceable for that label — the file would say `bug` and the repository would say `Bug` with nothing left to reconcile them. Renaming is also the non-destructive option: the label keeps its identity, and with it every issue and pull request carrying it, which is exactly what the delete-and-recreate path destroyed. GitHub's label update API takes `new_name` for this case, and a rename differing only in case is an update of the same label, not a conflict with itself.

`applyLabelPlan` keeps a `currentName ?? name` fallback so a plan built without one renames nothing rather than sending `name: undefined`.

## How prune is proven safe

Three ways, all of them fixtures — no network, no token:

1. `planLabelSync` unit test with `prune: true`: `Bug` on GitHub against `bug` in the file yields `deleted: []` and `extra: []`, with the label in `updated`.
2. A mixed case: `BUG` and `Feature` matched by desired `bug` and `feature`, alongside a genuinely unlisted `wontfix`. Only `wontfix` is deleted, so the fix does not blunt prune.
3. An end-to-end `applyLabelPlan` test over a real `planLabelSync` output with `prune: true`, asserting the exact request sequence is a single `PATCH` addressed to `Bug` with `new_name: bug` — no `POST`, no `DELETE`.

The same plan run through the CLI's own reporter, for the record:

```
scottdensmore/my-first-commit (dry run, nothing changed)
  would create: docs
  would update: Bug -> bug
  unchanged: 0
  would delete: wontfix
--- requests a real run would send ---
POST   /repos/{owner}/{repo}/labels           {"name":"docs"}
PATCH  /repos/{owner}/{repo}/labels/{name}    {"name":"Bug","new_name":"bug"}
DELETE /repos/{owner}/{repo}/labels/{name}    {"name":"wontfix"}
```

## The pinned test

`scripts/label-plan.test.mjs` asserted the old behaviour deliberately, with a comment explaining it — the "an existing test pins the old contract" case AGENTS.md step 4 warns about, which would not have failed on its own. It is replaced by a test asserting the corrected behaviour, inside the same red/green loop. Two more existing tests that pinned the old `updated` entry shape were updated in the same pass.

**Tests: 442 before, 451 after** (`scripts/label-plan.test.mjs`: 54 → 63). Ten added, one removed, three updated in place.

## Guarantees kept

Prune is still opt-in and still the only thing that fills `deleted`. `planLabelSync` is still a pure function over plain data that mutates neither input. Nothing in `label-plan.mjs` touches the network or calls `process.exit`. `npm run check:labels` is unchanged and still passes; no `package.json` script changed.

## Verification

`E2E_PORT=3120 npm run validate` — **complete gate, passed in full**: `npm audit`, 451 unit tests, 45 Playwright tests across chromium/mobile-chrome/webkit, eslint, `prettier --check`, `check:agent-docs`, `check:labels`, `next build`.

## Sub-agents

Sub-agents were unavailable in this session, so AGENTS.md steps 6-8 were performed by the main agent itself and are reported as such rather than implied to have run. This collapses three independent reviews into one agent reviewing its own change, and supplies no second opinion.

- **`ui-review` equivalent:** this change has no user-visible surface — no route, component, markup, style, or interaction, and nothing under `app/`. The only human-facing output is the maintainer-facing CLI report, whose rename wording was checked. No findings, none invented.
- **`verifier` equivalent:** the complete gate above, on the state that entered review.
- **`code-review` equivalent:** the branch diff plus `git status --short --untracked-files=all` (clean). Three points considered and resolved: `nameKey` would throw on a non-string name, but `sync-labels.mjs` validates before planning and `existing` comes from GitHub; two existing labels differing only in case would collapse in the lookup map, which GitHub cannot produce, so guarding it would be untestable; the `currentName ?? name` fallback is documented and exercised by existing tests. No blockers, no should-fix.

## Left alone

`.github/labels.yml` — every name in it is already lowercase, and the fix is proven with fixtures. `docs/labels.md` gained a short subsection describing the matching rule and the validation it implies.

issues.title: fix(api): bound search bursts per client
issues.body:
Second half of #106. The first half — coalescing concurrent identical searches — shipped in #150. Leaves #106 open for the owner to close.

Closes #151

## What this bounds

Coalescing bounds *duplicate* work. It does nothing about a flood of **distinct** usernames, where every request is a genuine cache and coalescer miss and reaches GitHub. This adds a rolling window over exactly that traffic.

## Per client, not globally

The issue frames the threshold as unanswerable without traffic data. That is true of a global counter — which is also the version that meets legitimate visitors with the rate-limit screen precisely when the app is busiest, the objection the issue raises.

A per-client window targets the one caller behaving unlike a person, so the threshold can sit far above any human's pace and stops being a guess. A busy day cannot turn it on ordinary visitors, because no visitor shares an allowance with anyone else.

**30 searches per rolling 60 seconds, per client.** Sustained, that is one distinct valid GitHub handle typed every two seconds for a full minute. A visitor clicking every recent-search shortcut they have stored produces five requests and then stops to read one. It is also the documented authenticated GitHub search ceiling (verified against [GitHub's rate-limit docs](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/rate-limits-for-the-rest-api): 30 requests/minute authenticated for search endpoints other than code search, 10/minute unauthenticated), so a client past it is by itself able to spend the whole shared per-minute allowance.

Only searches that can still reach GitHub are counted — an answer the cache already holds is free — so the limit applies to the traffic that actually costs the shared quota.

## This is a cost, not a quota guarantee

Stated plainly in the code, in `AGENTS.md`, and in both operator documents:

- The window is a `Map` in one server instance, like the cache and the in-flight map. A limit of 30 is really **30 × instances**.
- A cold start resets it, so a burst spread across cold starts is barely limited.
- It therefore **cannot** defend the shared 30/min ceiling and is not documented as if it does. The cache and the coalescing from #150 are what actually remove upstream calls. A real global ceiling is a Vercel Firewall rule — account-level configuration, not code — and `docs/production.md` says where it would go.

## Privacy

The app advertises no server-side storage of searches, and `app/logger.ts` takes scalar fields only.

**What is retained, per client, until it has been quiet for longer than the window (60s):**

- A salted SHA-256 hash of the forwarded client address.
- The timestamps of that client's searches inside the current 60-second window — at most 30.

Nothing else. The searched username never reaches the limiter at all: `app/commitSearchRateLimit.ts` is handed an opaque key by `app/searchClientKey.ts` and has nothing else to store, log, or key on. The refusal log event carries `limit` and `windowMs` and nothing that identifies a client or a search. No address is stored, no username is stored, and the two are never held together.

The salt is 32 random bytes per process, never persisted. **What a memory dump would reveal:** the salt, those hashes, and those timestamps. With the salt, an investigator could confirm whether an address they *already suspected* was among the clients active in the last minute. They could not read the addresses out, correlate them across instances or across a restart, or learn anything whatsoever about what was searched.

**Bounding the map.** Idle clients are dropped as the window passes them, and the map is capped at 500 clients. A map keyed by client is a memory-exhaustion vector otherwise — trading one abuse problem for another.

## The forwarded header is untrusted input

The key comes from `x-vercel-forwarded-for`, falling back to `x-forwarded-for`. Vercel sets both and overwrites `x-forwarded-for` from the connecting socket specifically to prevent spoofing, so on this deployment neither is attacker-controlled; `x-vercel-forwarded-for` is preferred because a proxy placed in front of Vercel could not overwrite that one either.

Behind some other proxy that forwards the header verbatim, a spoofer **can**:

- Split their own traffic across fabricated addresses for a fresh allowance each, weakening the limit to the cost of forging headers.
- Spend another client's allowance by sending that client's address, refusing them for up to one window.

A spoofer **cannot**:

- Exhaust memory. Idle entries are dropped, the map is capped, and an over-long header value is truncated rather than rejected, so an absurd value cannot buy an unlimited lane.
- Deny service through eviction. Eviction only ever *forgets* a client, which refills an allowance; inheriting one would be the dangerous direction, and there is a test pinning it.
- Learn who has searched, what was searched, or read any stored key back.

Blast radius of the one real attack: one minute, one instance, one address the attacker had to know already.

## No new error state

Exceeding the bound returns the existing `rate_limit` kind, so `getResultMessage`, `canRetryCommitSearch`, the alert panel, and the **Try again** button all apply unchanged — the visitor sees exactly the screen GitHub's own rate limiting produces. Only the unrendered `error` string and the log event differ, so neither blames GitHub for a limit this app applied. `result.error` is not displayed for this kind; the panel's copy comes from the error kind.

## Tests

`app/commitSearchRateLimit.test.ts`, `app/searchClientKey.test.ts`, and a `per-client burst limit` block in `app/actions.test.ts`:

- The boundary: exactly the limit passes, the next is refused.
- The window rolling over, and sliding one slot at a time as the oldest search ages out — which also proves a refused search is not recorded, so hammering does not push the unblock time out.
- **Human-paced use cannot reach the bound**: one search every three seconds without a pause for thirty minutes, all allowed; and twenty repeated bursts of five recent-search shortcut clicks 400ms apart, all allowed.
- Per-client isolation: one client's flood does not refuse another.
- The map stays capped under 5,000 distinct keys, and an evicted client is forgotten rather than blocked.
- No username is retained: what the limiter holds after a search is the client hash and nothing containing the username or the raw address.
- The refusal log contains no identifier and no username.
- A cached repeat search does not spend the allowance.
- A request with no forwarded address is not limited rather than being bucketed with everyone else, since one shared bucket is the global counter this deliberately is not.

## Verification

`E2E_PORT=3110 npm run validate` — **pass, in full**: `npm audit` 0 vulnerabilities · 428 unit tests in 29 files · 32 Playwright specs · lint · format:check · check:agent-docs · check:labels · production build. Tree clean afterwards, with the committed `nextjs-agent-rules` block untouched.

**Review honesty:** this session could not invoke the `ui-review`, `verifier`, or `code-review` sub-agents. Per `AGENTS.md`, the implementing agent did the equivalent work itself and said so on reaching step 6. Those three steps were one agent reviewing its own change, which is the weakest form of each of them and is not the second opinion they exist to provide. The complete gate above did run in full.

The ui-review equivalent found no user-visible surface to review: the change adds no UI and reuses an existing result state whose panel, copy, retry affordance, and ARIA behavior are untouched.

## Out of scope, deliberately

The cache, the coalescer, and the error UI are unchanged. `inFlightSearches` remains uncapped — it is still self-bounding, since entries delete on settle within the 10s timeout budget.

issues.title: fix(csp): bound and sanitize CSP report ingestion
issues.body:
Closes #105

`/api/csp-report` is unauthenticated, so every cost it accepts is a cost any anonymous caller can impose. It read the whole body before measuring it, measured JavaScript characters rather than bytes, parsed any content type it was handed, and wrote one log record per entry of a Reporting API array.

## What changed

**Bounded byte read, before buffering.** `readBoundedBody()` refuses an oversized `Content-Length` before a byte is read. That header can be absent or simply untrue, so the body stream is then read chunk by chunk with a running byte count, and cancelled the moment the count passes 16 KB. The limit counts bytes, not characters: a 6,000-character multibyte body is 18,000 bytes and was previously accepted. Oversized bodies answer `413`.

**A cap on reports per request.** At most **10** violations are logged from one POST — the number is documented in the runbook and at the constant. A Reporting API array is a batch, so without a cap one request could turn into a log record per entry. The overflow is counted in a single `csp_report_truncated` event carrying `received` and `logged`.

**Content types.** Only `application/csp-report` (`report-uri`) and `application/reports+json` (Reporting API) are read, matched case-insensitively and ignoring parameters such as `; charset=utf-8`. Anything else answers `415` without the body being touched.

**Non-HTTP schemes.** The opaque-scheme allowlist became an http(s) allowlist: any scheme other than `http:` and `https:` is reduced to the scheme alone, so `mailto:` addresses and paths from app-specific schemes cannot reach logs, joining the `data:`, `blob:`, `javascript:`, and `filesystem:` payloads already dropped. Query strings, fragments, `original-policy`, and `script-sample` are still never logged, and the tests pinning that are unchanged.

Normal legacy and Reporting API payloads still return `204` with the same fields — the existing tests for both shapes pass untouched.

## Rate limiting is not in this PR

The issue also asks to "configure platform-level rate limiting or sampling". That is Vercel account configuration, not repository code, and the app is serverless with no shared state, so per-instance counting would not hold across instances. Rather than invent infrastructure, `docs/production.md` gains a **Rate Limiting CSP Reports** section saying where it belongs (a Vercel Firewall rule scoped to the path, or lower reporting sampling) and that nothing in the app reads it. The bounds in this PR cap what one request can cost, not how many requests arrive.

## Tests

New unit coverage: a multibyte body that passes a character check and fails a byte check, a declared oversized body proven unread via `request.bodyUsed`, a lying `Content-Length` where the streamed body is proven to be abandoned mid-read (the test counts chunks the route pulled), a 25-entry array capped at 10 with the truncation event, rejected content types, an accepted content type with parameters, and `mailto:`/`my-app:` reduction. One Playwright test posts an oversized body and a wrong content type against the real server, so the streaming path is exercised in the Next.js runtime rather than only in the unit harness.

## Verification

`E2E_PORT=3110 npm run validate` passed end to end on the committed state: 0 vulnerabilities, 348 unit tests, 31 Playwright tests, lint, format check, agent-docs, labels, and the production build. The non-default port avoids other suites running concurrently on this machine.

## Review sub-agents

This session could not invoke sub-agents, so the AGENTS.md steps 6-8 work was done in the main agent and is stated here rather than implied: `ui-review` — no user-visible surface (API route, tests, docs; browsers discard CSP report responses); `verifier` — the complete gate above; `code-review` — a self-review of the branch diff, which produced one fix (a rejected `reader.cancel()` no longer downgrades a `413` to a `204`), after which the gate was rerun in full. A self-review cannot supply the second opinion those steps exist to provide, so this diff is worth a human read.

Next.js 16.3.0's `generate-agent-files.js` appended its `nextjs-agent-rules` block to `AGENTS.md` on every `next dev` boot during the Playwright runs. It is generated output and is not committed; it never appeared in `CLAUDE.md` or `GEMINI.md`.

issues.title: chore(tooling): scope unit test collection to product code
issues.body:
Closes #141

## What changed

`vitest.config.ts` now collects unit tests **positively** — from `app/`, `components/`, and `scripts/` — instead of running the default whole-tree glob minus a list of directories to skip. This is option 2 from the issue, adopted as recommended; no reason was found that it does not work.

- `vitest.config.ts`: `exclude` (7 entries) replaced by a root-anchored `include` of the three product-code roots. `tests/e2e/`, `node_modules`, `.next`, and the four tooling-state directories are all out of scope by construction rather than by name.
- `scripts/ignore-entries.mjs`: new `globRoots(source)`, which yields the directory each glob-shaped string literal is anchored to (`"app/**/*.test.ts"` → `app`). An unanchored pattern yields `**`, `.`, or an empty segment — values no root list contains — so a widened scope fails loudly instead of passing.
- `scripts/check-agent-docs.mjs`: `.prettierignore` and `eslint.config.mjs` are still checked entry by entry for the four tooling-state directories. `vitest.config.ts` moved out of `IGNORE_LISTS` and is checked by its scope: the collected roots must be exactly `app`, `components`, `scripts`.
- `AGENTS.md` and `.claude/agents/verifier.md`: the unread-path exemption is reworded. **The exempt set is unchanged** (`*.md` plus the repository-root tooling-state directories); only the reason Vitest cannot see them changed. Both files also now say that being outside the unit-test scope is *not* on its own a reason for the exemption — every path outside the three roots is — so `.github/hooks/` and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` still get no exemption.
- `CHANGELOG.md`: entry under `## Unreleased` → `### Changed`.

### Why the format change was safe for the drift check

The three lists still have to agree, and `npm run check:agent-docs` still fails when they drift — it just asks Vitest a different question. Verified both directions by hand:

- Deleting `".codex/**"` from `eslint.config.mjs` → `eslint.config.mjs no longer ignores .codex. …` (exit 1).
- Widening one include pattern to `"**/*.{test,spec}.?(c|m)[jt]s?(x)"` → `vitest.config.ts collects from **, components, scripts rather than from app, components, scripts. …` (exit 1). Deleting `include` entirely gives `no named root` and fails the same way.

`globRoots` has nine new unit tests in `scripts/ignore-entries.test.mjs`, written before the implementation and confirmed red for the expected reason (`globRoots is not a function`) first.

## Test counts

| | Test files | Tests |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before (`origin/main`) | 25 | 309 |
| After | 25 | **318** |

The 9 added tests are exactly the new `globRoots` cases. No product test was dropped: the file count is identical and the collected file list is unchanged.

## Stray-spec proof

Before the change, with three scratch specs present, `npx vitest list --filesOnly` collected `stray-probe.test.ts` and `.verifier-probe/probe.spec.ts` alongside the 25 real files, and `npm test` failed with `Playwright Test did not expect test() to be called here` — the exact failure in the issue.

After the change, with the same three probes in the tree:

```
$ ls stray-probe.test.ts .verifier-probe/probe.spec.ts scratch-dir/probe.spec.ts
$ npm test
 Test Files  25 passed (25)
      Tests  318 passed (318)
$ npx vitest list --filesOnly | grep -i probe
none
```

A nested `app/.claude/probe.test.ts` is still collected, before and after, so the "root-level only" sentence in the exemption stays true. All probes were removed; `git status --short --untracked-files=all` is clean apart from the seven changed files.

## Verification

`E2E_PORT=3110 npm run validate` — **passed end to end**: `npm audit`, `npm test` (25 files / 318 tests), `npm run test:e2e` (30 Playwright tests passed on port 3110), `npm run lint`, `npm run format:check`, `npm run check:agent-docs`, `npm run check:labels`, `next build`. Prettier was never run over markdown.

## Review disclosure

Sub-agents could not be invoked in this session, so per AGENTS.md the implementing agent performed the `ui-review`, `verifier`, and `code-review` work itself and is saying so rather than implying the sub-agents ran. This is self-review and does not provide the second opinion those steps exist for.

- **ui-review equivalent:** no user-visible surface. The change touches test-collection config, a check script, its unit tests, and docs; no app route, component, or style is affected.
- **verifier equivalent:** the complete gate above, plus the two drift simulations.
- **code-review equivalent:** self-review of the branch diff and all untracked files. One known limit is documented in the `globRoots` doc comment rather than fixed: it reads every glob literal in the file, not only the ones inside `include`, so a glob added for an unrelated Vitest option would have to be accounted for in `COLLECTION_ROOTS` too. In a 26-line config a loud false failure beats a parser, and it matches the existing "tripwire, not a parser" scope of that module.

## Out of scope

Nothing unrelated was changed. Noted but deliberately left alone: `npm test` prints a Vite warning that `vitest.config.ts` uses ESM syntax in a file loaded as CommonJS (`configLoader: 'native'`), which predates this branch.

issues.title: chore(build): remove the Google Fonts network dependency
issues.body:
Closes #117

## The finding: the fonts were fetched but never applied

The issue asks for this to be established before choosing an approach, so I checked it two ways.

**Statically.** `app/globals.css` defines `--font-sans` and `--font-mono` inside `@theme inline` as system stacks, and `body` sets `font-family: var(--font-sans)`. The layout generated `--font-geist-sans` and `--font-geist-mono` and put the two generated classes on `<body>`, but a repository-wide search found no reference to either variable outside `app/layout.tsx` itself:

```
$ grep -rni "geist\|next/font" --include="*.ts" --include="*.tsx" --include="*.css" ...
app/layout.tsx:2,9-17,69   (the definitions and the body classes — nothing else)
```

**At runtime**, loading the app in Chromium before the change:

```json
"bodyClass": "geist_a71539c9-module__T19VSG__variable geist_mono_8d43a2aa-module__8Li5zG__variable antialiased",
"bodyFont": "-apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, \"Segoe UI\", \"Noto Sans\", Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif, ...",
"h1Font":   "-apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, \"Segoe UI\", \"Noto Sans\", Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif, ...",
"monoFont": "ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, \"SF Mono\", Menlo, Consolas, \"Liberation Mono\", monospace",
"varGeistSans": "\"Geist\", \"Geist Fallback\"",
"loadedFonts": ["Geist 100 900 unloaded", "Geist Mono 100 900 unloaded", ... 17 faces, all "unloaded"],
"fontLinks": ["preload font /_next/static/media/797e433ab948586e-s.p...woff2",
              "preload font /_next/static/media/caa3a2e1cccd8315-s.p...woff2"]
```

Every visible element computed to the system stack, and every Geist face reported `unloaded` — the browser never used one to render text. The only real effect was two preloaded `woff2` files nobody read, plus a build that needed Google Fonts.

**So the fonts were genuinely unused**, and the first branch of the issue applies: remove the imports and document the system stack. Self-hosting with `next/font/local` would have introduced typography the site never had, which is a design change rather than a build fix.

## What changed

- `app/layout.tsx` — dropped the `next/font/google` imports and the two generated font variables; `<body>` is now `className="antialiased"`.
- `app/globals.css` — a comment recording that the two font tokens are the app's only font definitions and that no web font is downloaded.
- `app/layout.test.tsx` — the `next/font/google` mock is gone (it was the only reason the layout rendered under Vitest), and a new test pins the new contract: the body carries no font-variable class and the markup mentions no `font-geist` variable.
- `AGENTS.md` / `README.md` — the chosen stack documented, with a note not to reach for `next/font/google` again; a font the design really needs belongs in the repository behind `next/font/local`.
- `CHANGELOG.md` — entry under `## Unreleased` → `### Changed`.

No font assets and no font CSS variables remain: `--font-geist-sans` and `--font-geist-mono` were generated by the layout, so removing the imports removes them, and there was never a font package in `package.json`.

## Offline verification

A DNS-level block via `NODE_OPTIONS=--require` was **not** sufficient and I am reporting that rather than hiding it: Next 16 fetches Google Fonts from Turbopack's Rust process, so patching Node's `dns` module never saw the lookup and the pre-change build passed as if it were offline when it was not. What does work is pointing the proxy variables at a dead local port, which Next's font loader honours (its own error message names them).

**Negative control — pre-change tree (`origin/main`), `rm -rf .next` first:**

```
$ HTTP_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:9 HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:9 \
  http_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:9 https_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:9 npm run build
> Build error occurred
Error: Turbopack build failed with 2 errors:
[next]/internal/font/google/geist_a71539c9.module.css
Error: next/font: error:
Failed to fetch Geist from Google Fonts.
If you are offline or behind a proxy, self-host the font with next/font/local, or set HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY so Next.js can reach fonts.googleapis.com.
  Import trace: ... ./app/layout.tsx
[next]/internal/font/google/geist_mono_8d43a2aa.module.css
Error: next/font: error:
Failed to fetch Geist Mono from Google Fonts.
```

That reproduces the failure the issue reports, and proves the block is real rather than assumed.

**This branch, same environment variables plus the Node DNS blocker, `rm -rf .next` first:**

```
▲ Next.js 16.3.0 (Turbopack)
✓ Compiled successfully in 6.4s
  Finished TypeScript in 11.8s ...
✓ Generating static pages using 12 workers (8/8) in 3.5s
Route (app)
┌ ○ /                    ├ ○ /icon              ├ ○ /opengraph-image
├ ○ /privacy             └ ○ /twitter-image     ...
```

`/icon`, `/opengraph-image`, and `/twitter-image` are prerendered *during that offline build*, so the generated images need no network either — `next/og` uses the font bundled with the package and never referenced Geist.

## Visual check (`ui-review` equivalent)

Served the offline production build and compared against the same pages before the change, at 1280×900 and 375×780:

- `body`, `h1`, and `code` computed font-family strings are **identical** before and after, on both viewports and on `/` and `/privacy`.
- `document.fonts` went from 17 registered-but-unloaded faces and 2 preloaded `woff2` files to **empty**, with zero font network requests.
- `/opengraph-image` and `/icon` PNGs are **byte-identical** before and after (md5 `05f8510885c54cc3f75fea8d67860774` and `e89f5603d4b2930d813486aa777c29bf`); `/twitter-image` re-exports the OpenGraph route.
- Homepage screenshots match apart from the dev-server badge present only in the "before" capture. No colour, size, spacing, or semantic change, so there is no accessibility impact.

## Gate

`E2E_PORT=3120 npm run validate` — **passed** end to end: `npm audit` (0 vulnerabilities), 342 unit tests in 26 files, 30 Playwright specs on port 3120, `lint`, `format:check`, `check:agent-docs`, `check:labels`, and `build`. No markdown was run through Prettier.

## Process notes

- **This session cannot invoke sub-agents.** Per AGENTS.md, the `ui-review`, `verifier`, and `code-review` steps were performed by the main agent itself, announced at step 6 rather than afterwards. That is the weakest form of each of those steps: it collapses three independent reviews into one agent reviewing its own change, and a human reviewer should treat it accordingly.
- Next.js re-appended its generated `<!-- BEGIN:nextjs-agent-rules -->` block to `AGENTS.md` on every `next dev` boot (the baseline dev run and the Playwright suite). It was removed before committing and is not in this diff; it never appeared in `CLAUDE.md` or `GEMINI.md`, so the pointer files are untouched and `check:agent-docs` is green. The block's own text argues for committing it; that is generated output, so it was treated as data.
- Left alone: the `--font-mono` token leaves multi-word family names such as `SF Mono` and `Liberation Mono` unquoted. Browsers parse them correctly and this predates the change, so it stays out of scope.

issues.title: refactor(app): move analytics out of the homepage feature
issues.body:
Structural cleanup left over from the earlier move of modules into `app/_lib/`. No behaviour changes.

## `analytics.ts` was in the wrong folder

`app/_home/` is, by AGENTS.md's own rule, the directory for things only the homepage uses. But `analytics.ts` sat there while `app/_components/PrivacySafeAnalytics.tsx` imported it from outside — and that component is rendered by the **root layout**, so every page load reached into the homepage search feature to do something with no connection to searching for a commit.

It now sits in `app/_lib/` with the other shared modules. `app/_home/` is once again exactly the set of things only the homepage uses.

### Correction to the original plan: the import stays relative

The plan for this PR said to switch `PrivacySafeAnalytics` to an aliased `@/` import, reading AGENTS.md's "relative within a feature, aliased with `@/` only across a boundary" as requiring it. Surveying what the code actually does shows a different convention:

- **route files** under `app/api/` → `@/app/_lib/*` (3 imports)
- **everything else** (`_home/*`, `app/page.tsx`) → relative `../_lib/*` (24 imports)

So `../_lib/analytics` is the consistent choice; `@/` would have made this file the sole non-route exception. The violation the finding identified was `_components` reaching into the `_home` **feature**, and the move fixes that regardless of import style.

I have **not** rewritten that sentence in AGENTS.md. It is arguably under-specified rather than wrong — it reads naturally as being about features, with `_lib` as shared infrastructure everything reaches relatively. Whether `_lib` counts as a "boundary" is a call for the repository owner, not something to settle in a cleanup PR.

## Documentation caught up

- Added the rule that decides this for the next module, including the clarification that a feature includes its own route file — so `app/page.tsx` importing from `app/_home/` is *inside* the feature, while `app/_components/` is not.
- Layout list gained `app/api/csp-report/route.ts` and `app/_lib/e2eCommitSearchFixtures.ts`, both of which existed but were only described elsewhere.
- Four comments still pointed at pre-`_lib` paths: `e2eCommitSearchMocks.ts` (×2) and `e2e-readiness/route.test.ts` said `app/actions.ts`; `commitSearchRateLimit.ts` said `app/searchClientKey.ts`.

## Verification

`npm run validate` passes end to end:

- 492 unit tests, coverage unchanged at 96.61 / 93.35 / 98.9 / 97.82
- Playwright 51 passed across chromium / mobile-chrome / webkit
- `check:agent-docs` consistent — it reads AGENTS.md and the pointer templates, so it is the gate command this change most needed
- `npm audit`, lint, format, `check:labels`, production build all clean

Both moved files show `similarity index 100%`. The `vi.mock` paths moved with them: `searchExecution.test.ts` asserts on the mocked `trackAppEvent`, so a mis-pointed mock would fail rather than silently fall through to the real module.

Two changes: one optimisation applied, and one **not** applied with a test explaining why.

## Applied: build the commit date formatters once

`FirstCommitDisplay` constructed a fresh `Intl.DateTimeFormat` on every call. A rendered result builds **eleven** of them — the hover title on each of the ten commit cards, plus the summary date on the main one — and again on every re-render a retry or a share status causes. `Intl.DateTimeFormat` is among the more expensive constructors the platform offers: it resolves a locale and builds a pattern each time.

Both configurations are constant and deliberately pinned to `en` and UTC, so there is nothing per-call to close over. `Intl.DateTimeFormat.prototype.format` holds no per-call state, so a shared instance cannot leak anything between cards.

Output is unchanged and already pinned: `FirstCommitDisplay.test.tsx` asserts the exact string `"Jan 1, 2024"`, and the malformed-date fallback test still passes.

## Not applied: an early exit in `dropIdleClients`

The plan for this PR included short-circuiting the rate limiter's idle-client sweep, which scans up to 500 entries on every allowed search. The reasoning was that `allowCommitSearch` deletes and re-inserts on each call, so insertion order should be ascending by last-search time — letting the sweep `break` at the first client still inside the window.

**That reasoning is wrong.** When a client is *refused*, it is deleted and re-inserted at the tail, but nothing is pushed to its `searchTimes`, so its last-search time does not advance. The existing comment says this is deliberate — being evicted is a reprieve, so a client being refused should not get one. The consequence is that insertion order is **not** sorted by last-search time, and an idle client can sit *behind* an active one.

This is reachable, not theoretical. The new test builds the arrangement: `CLIENT` spends its whole allowance, `OTHER_CLIENT` searches one millisecond later, then `CLIENT` is refused — which moves it behind `OTHER_CLIENT` while its own newest search stays older. At one instant, `OTHER_CLIENT` is inside the window and `CLIENT` is not, so the only idle client stands after the active one.

Verified the test has teeth by temporarily applying the `break`:

```
AssertionError: expected [ Array(3) ] to deeply equal [ 'client-key-b', 'client-key-c' ]
```

The idle client survives eviction — which fails *open*, silently refilling an allowance rather than erroring, so nothing else would have caught it. `commitSearchRateLimit.ts` is therefore **unchanged**; only the test is added, so the next person to spot this scan is warned off it.

The scan is also not worth optimising: it is bounded at 500 cheap array-index reads on a path that otherwise makes an HTTP request to GitHub with a 10-second timeout.

## Verification

`npm run validate` passes end to end:

- 492 unit tests (491 + the new one)
- Coverage 96.61 stmts / 93.35 branch / 98.9 funcs / 97.82 lines, all above their floors
- Playwright 51 passed across chromium / mobile-chrome / webkit
- `npm audit`, lint, format, `check:agent-docs`, `check:labels`, production build all clean

## No CHANGELOG entry

Purely internal, per the step 9 exemption: no user-visible or operational effect. The rendered dates are identical, and the rate limiter's behaviour is unchanged by construction — its source is untouched.

issues.body:
Three removals, each of something no reachable path used. No behaviour changes.

## 1. `buildResultShareText` took a union it never received

It accepted `CommitData` and carried a fallback for a result with no commits. Its only caller (`app/page.tsx:109`) reaches it from behind a `result?.found` guard, and `CommitSearchSuccess` carries a non-empty tuple, so a first commit is guaranteed.

Narrowing the parameter to `CommitSearchSuccess` made `tsc` reject **exactly one** thing — the test that had been pinning the dead branch — and nothing at the call site:

```
app/_home/sharedSearch.test.ts(82,44): error TS2345:
  Argument of type 'CommitSearchFailure' is not assignable to parameter of type 'CommitSearchSuccess'.
```

That the call site compiles untouched is what proves the branch was unreachable in production rather than merely untested. This is the defensive check `commitTypes.ts` documents the tuple invariant as existing to remove.

## 2. `logger.error` could be handed a raw error object

It accepted an optional second `unknown` and passed it straight to `console.error`. No caller ever passed one, so nothing was being logged that should not have been — what is gone is the supported way to start.

That matters because it contradicts the module's stated purpose and the AGENTS.md logging gotcha: an Octokit error carries the request URL, and a commit-search URL carries the username being searched. `actions.ts` already extracts scalars (`status`, `errorKind`) and logs those.

## 3. Nine unused design tokens in `globals.css`

The `@theme inline` block mapped nine `--color-*` tokens into Tailwind's theme — `bg-gh-blue`, `text-gh-text-primary`, `bg-background`, and the rest. Not one of the generated utilities is referenced anywhere; every colour is applied as an arbitrary value reading the `:root` property directly (`text-[var(--github-blue)]`). They were a second, parallel naming scheme for the same seven colours that nothing was written against.

Tailwind emits only referenced utilities, so these never reached the stylesheet. **Verified** by concatenating the production CSS from a clean `next build` before and after:

```
de48109c96f6b0f7a27b8e017fcd71ddd644f92897ca140dcb0abaddd8eaab14  css-before.css
de48109c96f6b0f7a27b8e017fcd71ddd644f92897ca140dcb0abaddd8eaab14  css-after.css
```

Byte-identical. The font tokens stay — those are live via `font-sans`/`font-mono`.

## Verification

`npm run validate` passes end to end:

- 491 unit tests (492 before, minus the deleted dead-branch test)
- Coverage **up**: 96.61 stmts / 93.35 branch / 98.91 funcs / 97.82 lines, against the baseline recorded in `vitest.config.mts` of 96.53 / 93.26 / 98.91 / 97.72 — consistent with removing a partially-covered branch
- Playwright 51 passed across chromium / mobile-chrome / webkit, including the clipboard and copy-result journeys that exercise the share text
- `npm audit`, lint, format, `check:agent-docs`, `check:labels`, production build all clean

No user-visible change: the stylesheet is byte-identical, and the share text is unchanged for every reachable input.

issues.body:
Closes #185. Found while measuring coverage for #183.

## The problem

`app/_lib/actions.ts` was 569 lines, **173 of them browser-test fixtures** — thirty percent of the `"use server"` module that queries GitHub with the token, including one fixture that throws on purpose and two that keep state between calls.

The coverage number was the symptom, not the reason. Test scaffolding does not belong in the most security-sensitive file in the repository, and its presence made the real search path harder to read than it needed to be.

`actions.ts` is now **379 lines** and calls into the fixture module twice.

## Two things had to move first

**`commitSearchError` and the two empty-search messages** are shared between the production path and the fixtures, and a `"use server"` module cannot export a synchronous helper. They moved to `commitTypes.ts` beside `toCommitSearchSuccess`, so both constructors of the union now live with the union. Sharing rather than copying matters for the same reason `commitSearchMocksEnabled` has one definition — two copies would let the real path and the fixture path describe the same outcome in different words.

**The reject-once hook could not move as a fixture result**, because its whole purpose is to throw rather than return. It became `shouldRejectCommitSearchOnce`, which owns the decision and the state while `actions.ts` still owns the throw.

## The browser suite is the regression test

No fixture has a unit test to lean on, so Playwright is the proof. **All 51 specs pass**, including the four that depend on state surviving between two requests in one process:

- `a retry that is still partial says so and keeps focus on the button`
- `retrying a partial result reaches the complete history`
- `a failed retry keeps the partial result on screen`
- `home page recovers from an unexpected Server Action rejection` — the one I rewired

## Coverage moved, so the floors moved

| | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `actions.ts` statements | 76.54% | **93.33%** |
| `actions.ts` branches | 71.08% | **86.25%** |
| Aggregate statements | 93.71% | **96.53%** |
| Aggregate branches | 89.73% | **93.26%** |

`actions.ts` is now in line with the rest of the codebase instead of the outlier, because it is no longer measured against lines no unit test could reach.

**Floors raised to 96/93/98/97.** Leaving them at 93/89/98/94 would have left three and a half points of slack, which is room for real regression to pass — the opposite of what #183 just established. This was a scope correction rather than a coverage push, and the config says so.

Re-proved at the new floors: a two-function module that no test imports still fails the gate, on branches at 92.77% against 93.

## Verification

`npm run validate` passes in full: 0 vulnerabilities, 492 unit tests across 31 files with the raised thresholds met, 51 Playwright runs, lint, format, both checks, production build.

The AGENTS.md gotcha now points at the fixture module rather than `actions.ts`, so the next person adding browser coverage for a new state adds it in one obvious place.

## Note on the workflow

Stated at step 6, per #153: this session cannot invoke sub-agents, so steps 6-8 were performed directly. No user-visible surface — the fixtures are unreachable without `E2E_COMMIT_SEARCH_MOCKS=1`, and the browser suite confirms every reserved username still resolves.

issues.body:
Closes #183. The follow-on #121 carried forward, unblocked by #179.

## The hole

Coverage measured the files the suite **loaded**, which is Vitest's default. A module no test imported was *absent* from the report rather than counted as zero — so the floor from #114 caught coverage slipping in code already under test, and missed code that arrived with no test at all. That is the more common way coverage decays, and the case a floor exists for.

## The thresholds did not move

That is the evidence the exclusions are right rather than convenient:

| | Statements | Branches | Functions | Lines |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Before (default scope) | 93.71 | 89.73 | 98.38 | 94.65 |
| Scoped, no exclusions | 74.49 | 77.97 | 88.40 | 74.80 |
| **Scoped + 7 exclusions** | **93.71** | **89.73** | **98.38** | **94.65** |

Identical to two decimal places. Every point of the drop to 74% is the seven files below — not hidden regression — so the existing 93/89/98/94 floors stand unchanged and no threshold decision was needed.

## Seven exclusions, each covered by running rather than importing

| File | Covered by |
| --- | --- |
| `app/icon.tsx`, `app/opengraph-image.tsx`, `app/twitter-image.tsx` | `next build` prerenders them; a browser spec asserts each returns a PNG |
| `scripts/check-agent-docs.mjs`, `scripts/sync-labels.mjs` | `npm run check:agent-docs` and `npm run check:labels`, both links in the gate chain |
| `scripts/verify-deployed-commit.mjs`, `scripts/resolve-active-deployment.mjs` | the production health and promotion workflows |

Every one is a thin shell over a module that **is** unit tested — `gate-commands`, `ignore-entries`, `label-plan`, `production-release`. That split is deliberate in this repository, and the config now says to add to this list only when another gate command genuinely covers the file, and to name which one. Excluding a file nothing covers is how a floor starts reporting a hole that is not there.

## Proved in both directions

With a temporary two-function module that no test imports, then removed:

```
scoped:          92.98% statements, 97.34% functions   → gate fails, exit 1
default scope:   93.71% statements, 98.38% functions   → zero threshold errors
```

**The counterfactual is the point.** The same file that changes nothing today now fails the gate. Without that second measurement, "coverage is scoped" would be a claim rather than a demonstrated property.

## The interaction #179 made possible

Re-confirmed rather than assumed: with coverage patterns present in the config, widening the *test* include still fails with `collects from **, scripts rather than from app, scripts`. Before #179 the coverage patterns themselves would have failed that check, which is exactly why this change could not be made in #174.

## Verification

`npm run validate` passes in full: 0 vulnerabilities, 492 unit tests across 31 files with thresholds met, 51 Playwright runs, lint, format, both checks, production build.

`docs/development.md` records the new measurement, the reason for scoping, and the rule for adding an exclusion.

## Note on the workflow

Stated at step 6, per #153: this session cannot invoke sub-agents, so steps 6-8 were performed directly. No user-visible surface.

issues.body:
Closes #107. The last item on the #121 tracker.

## Why fixtures were not enough

Every search test uses fixtures. That is what makes them deterministic, and it is also what makes them blind to the failures that only happen in production: a revoked token, a changed GitHub response, a Server Action broken there and nowhere else.

`/api/health` reports that a token is **present**, never that it works. So all of that could pass production health and be promoted to a release — which, after #108, is a release tag that now claims the commit was proven healthy.

## What it does

One spec runs the whole path against real infrastructure — browser → Server Action → GitHub → a rendered commit — and asserts **a commit in the timeline**, not just a heading, so a success shell with no result does not pass. It also checks the commit links out to `github.com`, which is the evidence the result came from GitHub at all.

## Scoped to one search per deployment

It is a canary, not a suite:

- **Untagged**, so it runs on Chromium only rather than once per browser project.
- **No workflow step configures it.** It skips unless `PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL` is set, which makes it automatically part of the production health check and any manual run against a deployed URL — and never part of local CI, where the fixtures already cover this ground for free.

Every additional search spends the shared GitHub quota that the burst limiting from #106 exists to protect, so the count is the point rather than an oversight.

## Two judgment calls

**A partial result passes.** GitHub returning `incomplete_results` is its own load shedding, not a fault of this app, and failing on it would make the canary flap for a reason no deploy can fix. An empty result, an error state, or a heading with no commit still fails.

**The handle is overridable.** `torvalds` by default, for having the largest and most reliably indexed history on the platform, with `E2E_CANARY_USERNAME` to change it. The assertion depends on GitHub's commit search index — the one part of this check that nothing in this repository controls — so if that index stops returning results, the fix should be a variable rather than an edit to the spec.

## Verified against the real deployment, in three directions

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Against production | passes in ~5s |
| Against a handle with no indexed commits | **fails** on the missing result heading |
| Locally, no `PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL` | reports as skipped |

The middle row is the one that matters: it is the proof the canary is not passing vacuously, and it is the acceptance criterion asking that it fail for a broken GitHub response.

The full deployed suite goes from 20 passing to **21**, the single addition being this canary on one browser. Locally the gate reports `1 skipped`, so it costs local CI nothing.

## Docs

`docs/manual-qa.md` had claimed the commit-search states are not covered against a deployed target. That is now only true of the *mocked* states, and the line was corrected rather than left to mislead — a plain successful search in production no longer needs testing by hand.

The runbook documents the canary, the one-search-per-deploy reasoning, the override, and how to run it manually.

## Verification

`npm run validate` passes in full: 0 vulnerabilities, 492 unit tests across 31 files with thresholds met, 51 Playwright runs plus 1 skipped, lint, format, both checks, production build.

## Note on the workflow

Stated at step 6, per #153: this session cannot invoke sub-agents, so steps 6-8 were performed directly. No user-visible surface.

issues.title: fix(release): bind health checks and promotion to the deployed SHA
issues.body:
Closes #108.

## Two checks that answered the wrong question

**The health run never asked what it was testing.** It points Playwright at a mutable alias, so a green suite meant *something healthy was serving that URL* — not that the commit which triggered the run was serving it. A deployment still in flight, or a failed one leaving the previous build live, both produced a pass.

**Promotion asked which commit was newest, not which was live.** The superseded guard compared the deployed commit against the tip of `main`. Those are different questions: `main` advances at merge, while a deployment becomes live later and may never. A newer commit still deploying — or one that failed — suppressed the release of the commit genuinely in production, and **that release was never cut at all.**

## What changed

The health job now verifies the deployment **before any spec runs**, for the same reason the Playwright global setup checks the port first: a run against the wrong build otherwise produces a wall of results describing code that is not deployed.

The promotion guard resolves the active deployment through the deployments API — newest whose latest status is `success` — and **stops rather than guessing** when none has succeeded. Superseded deployments are still skipped, for the reason they always were.

## Three details that would each have broken it quietly

**The comparison has to be by prefix.** `/api/health` abbreviates to seven characters (`getShortCommit` slices), so equality against a 40-character deployment SHA would reject *every* run rather than the wrong ones — a check that fails always is as useless as one that passes always.

**`local` is refused outright.** That is what the route returns when `VERCEL_GIT_COMMIT_SHA` is unset, so it identifies no deployment. Treating it as a value to compare would let an unconfigured build pass.

**A prefix under seven characters is refused.** At one or two characters a prefix match means almost nothing, and accepting it would make the check decorative.

## Verified against real infrastructure, not just fixtures

Both CLI shells were run against the live deployment:

```
$ node scripts/verify-deployed-commit.mjs https://my-first-commit-eta.vercel.app <correct-sha>
…is serving c53813f, which is the commit this run expects.          exit 0

$ node scripts/verify-deployed-commit.mjs https://my-first-commit-eta.vercel.app 000…0
The deployment at this URL is serving c53813f, but this run expected 0000000…   exit 1

$ GITHUB_TOKEN=… node scripts/resolve-active-deployment.mjs scottdensmore/my-first-commit Production
c53813f4e669bdc367363af59d244c6f8d0a9a36                             exit 0
```

The deployments API and `/api/health` agree on which commit is live. **That agreement is the invariant**, and the runbook now documents how to check it by hand.

## Structure

Decisions are pure and unit tested — 20 cases covering matching, mismatched, active, superseded, in-flight, failed, and the no-successful-deployment case. The network lives in two thin CLI shells, following `sync-labels.mjs`, which keeps the logic testable without a token.

`setup-node` is pinned in the promotion job rather than left to the runner's default; the scripts need no dependencies, so there is no install step.

## Verification

`npm run validate` passes in full: 0 vulnerabilities, 492 unit tests across 31 files with thresholds met, 51 Playwright runs, lint, format, both checks, production build. Both workflow files were parsed to confirm the new steps are wired as intended.

**This is the first change today whose real behaviour only appears after a deploy.** The health verification runs on the next `deployment_status`, and the promotion guard on the run after that — worth watching both rather than assuming.

## Note on the workflow

Stated at step 6, per #153: this session cannot invoke sub-agents, so steps 6-8 were performed directly. No user-visible surface.
