issues.body:
Closes #115. Unblocked by #179, which taught the collection check to read the config by scope rather than by every glob in it.

## Two mismatches

**Types against runtime.** `@types/node` was pinned to major **22** while `.nvmrc` and `engines.node` both say **24**. The types described a different runtime than the one executing — the kind of mismatch that reports an API as missing when it exists, or accepts one that does not, quietly and only where the two majors differ. Now `^24.13.3`.

**Module format against file extension.** `vitest.config.ts` uses `import.meta.url`, but as `.ts` it was loaded through a CommonJS compatibility path that printed this on **every test run**:

```
(!) Your Vite config uses features that are unsupported by `configLoader: 'native'` …
  - ESM syntax in a file loaded as CommonJS (vitest.config.ts:1:1)
```

Vite has said that path becomes the error rather than the warning in a future major. Renamed to `vitest.config.mts`; the warning is gone from the gate output, and the `@` alias built from `import.meta.url` plus the jsdom setup both still resolve, which the 472-test suite proves by passing.

## The hazard in the rename

`check-agent-docs` reads that file **by name** to verify unit collection stays scoped. Renaming without updating the check leaves the gate hunting for a file that no longer exists — which fails in a way that looks like the check is broken rather than like a rename is incomplete.

Both moved in this commit, and the drift guard was re-proved afterwards on the renamed file:

```
vitest.config.mts collects from **, scripts rather than from app, scripts
```

Six other files referenced the old name in prose — `AGENTS.md`, the verifier definition, `docs/development.md`, two scripts, and the Playwright global setup. All updated, so nothing points at a path that is gone.

## Lockfile

Carries `@types/node` and its transitive `undici-types`, and nothing else. No packages added or removed.

## Verification

`npm run validate` passes in full: 0 vulnerabilities, 472 unit tests across 30 files with coverage thresholds met, 51 Playwright runs, lint, format, both checks, production build. `npx tsc --noEmit` is clean under the new type definitions.

Worth noting the gate output is now free of that deprecation warning, which has printed on every run in this repository for some time.

issues.title: chore(tooling): scope globRoots to the collection include
issues.body:
Closes #175. Unblocks scoping the coverage configuration, which #174 could not do.

## What was wrong

`globRoots` took the leading directory of **every** glob-shaped literal in `vitest.config.ts`. Fine while the file held one option; a problem the moment a coverage block wanted patterns of its own, because `exclude: ["coverage/**"]` registered `coverage` as a collection root and failed the gate.

Correctly, too — a whole-file read genuinely cannot tell a coverage pattern from a widened test scope. But the cost was real: #174 had to leave the coverage block pattern-free, which is why a module no test imports is currently absent from the report rather than counted as zero.

## What it does now

Reads only the collection array, and only the one belonging to the **test** object. A coverage block may carry its own `include`, so tracking which object a key sits in is what makes the two distinguishable rather than merely differently named.

**Brackets are counted over tokens, not raw text.** A collection pattern contains them — `[jt]` inside `?(c|m)[jt]s?(x)` — so counting them in the source ends the array inside the first pattern and reports *fewer* roots than there are. Fewer is the dangerous direction: it's the one that lets a widened scope pass. Pinned by a test.

## Coverage caught a real mistake, so I fixed the mistake

Writing `includeLiterals` as a second walk duplicated the comment and escape handling. Coverage found it immediately — the copy inside the new function was unreached, dropping branch coverage below the floor #114 set:

```
93.02% statements, 88.76% branches   → gate fails
```

The tempting fix is lowering the threshold. The right one was removing the duplication: one tokenizer that both `stringLiterals` and `includeLiterals` read through, so there is a single place that knows how to tell a quote from a comment from a bracket.

```
93.65% statements, 89.60% branches   → gate passes
```

That is the threshold doing its job on the very change that touched it.

## Verified in both directions

On the final implementation, not an earlier draft:

- A coverage block carrying `include` **and** `exclude` patterns → `Agent docs are consistent.`
- A widened test include → `collects from **, scripts rather than from app, scripts`

Both experiments reverted; `vitest.config.ts` is byte-identical to `main`.

## Deliberately not here

**Scoping the coverage configuration itself.** It changes what the thresholds measure and therefore what they should be, which is a decision of its own rather than something to fold into the change that makes it possible. #175 flagged it as the follow-on and that is where it belongs.

## Verification

`npm run validate` passes in full: 0 vulnerabilities, 472 unit tests across 30 files with thresholds met, 51 Playwright runs, lint, format, both checks, production build.

## Note on the workflow

Stated at step 6, per #153: this session cannot invoke sub-agents, so steps 6-8 were performed directly. No user-visible surface.

issues.title: test(e2e): cover complete search and recovery journeys
issues.body:
Closes #112.

## What was missing

The browser suite rendered each state well but crossed few boundaries. Six journeys close that, chosen for transitions a visitor actually performs rather than for more copy assertions.

| Journey | Why it earns a test |
| --- | --- |
| Success puts the handle in the URL; a new search takes it out and restores focus | The URL is the share link — a stale handle shares a search the visitor moved on from |
| Recent searches: appear → rerun → clear | Covered in `app/page.test.tsx`, but not across the boundary where one render writes and another reads back |
| `e2e-timeout`, `e2e-unknown` | No fixture existed for either |
| `e2e-validation` | A search GitHub itself refuses — unreachable from the client's own validation |
| Clipboard write fails | The fallback path is unreachable unless a test causes it |

Three new reserved usernames, documented in the AGENTS.md gotcha alongside the existing ones.

## Two judgment calls

**The validation failure asserts there is _no_ retry button.** Retrying an identical search gets an identical refusal, so the panel offers **Edit username** instead. That is the behaviour worth pinning — a retry there would look like recovery and never recover.

**The clipboard failure is forced, not hoped for.** The browser's own policy decides whether a real write succeeds, which is exactly why the existing WebKit test asserts only that *some* answer appears. This one overrides `navigator.clipboard` to reject, so the fallback message is reachable at all.

## These tests were checked against mutations

New tests for behaviour that already worked, so passing on the first run proved nothing. Each was verified by breaking the thing it covers:

- Removing `clearSharedSearchUrl()` from the new-search handler → the URL journey fails on `expect(page).not.toHaveURL(/[?&]user=/)`.

issues.title: refactor(types): make commit search results a discriminated union
issues.body:
Closes #118.

## The problem, concretely

`CommitData` let `found` be any boolean alongside optional error fields and a possibly-empty commit list. It could describe a successful search with no commits, or a success carrying a failure kind — states the server action never produces but the type permitted.

Consumers paid for that with defensive checks that could not fire:

- `app/page.tsx` — `result?.found && result.commits.length > 0`
- `app/_home/SearchResults.tsx` — `if (!firstCommit) return null`

Both are gone. `found` alone is now enough, because the type says so.

## The shape

```ts
type CommitSearchSuccess = { found: true;  commits: [CommitInfo, ...CommitInfo[]]; incomplete?: boolean }
type CommitSearchFailure = { found: false; commits: []; error: string; errorKind: CommitErrorKind; incomplete?: boolean }
type CommitData = CommitSearchSuccess | CommitSearchFailure
```

`incomplete` is on **both** variants deliberately: a search can time out before scanning every commit and return nothing, which the app reports as unfinished rather than as an absence of commits.

`error` and `errorKind` moved from optional to required on failures. Every failure the action produces already carried both; optional meant each reader deciding for itself what an absent kind meant. `getResultMessage`'s `result.error ?? fallback` is gone — the fallback could not fire.

## `toCommitSearchSuccess`

TypeScript does not narrow `CommitInfo[]` to a non-empty tuple from a `length === 0` check, so without a constructor every site would need its own assertion — and an assertion is a promise the compiler cannot keep. Putting the check and the construction in one call establishes the invariant in exactly one place. The real search path already had that guard; it now returns the value instead of guarding a separate literal, so the two cannot drift.

## Wire compatibility

**Unchanged, which is what makes this compatible rather than a migration.** Tuples are erased at runtime, so the Server Action serializes exactly the JSON it always did, and a result cached by an instance running the old code still deserializes.

## Two decisions worth reviewing

**The message helpers now take `CommitSearchFailure`, not `CommitData`.** They are only reached from the error panel and the failed-retry path. Taking the union meant each one deciding for itself what a success meant — which is precisely how `errorKind` came to be read off a successful result.

**The cache copies per variant** rather than spreading the union. `commits.map` returns a plain array that fits neither variant, and narrowing is what tells the compiler which shape it is rebuilding. Spreading and patching `commits` would have compiled only with a cast, and a cast is the thing this refactor removes.

## Fallout, found by looking

Per the rule added in #153, I searched for tests pinning the old contract rather than waiting for the gate: **36 type errors across nine test files**, nearly all fixtures constructing failures without an `error`, or reading a variant's fields off the bare union.

One test asserted on *a failure with no error kind at all* — a state the union makes unrepresentable. I kept it with an explicit cast and a comment, rather than deleting it: the runtime guard in `setCachedCommitSearch` still protects data the compiler cannot vouch for, such as a payload deserialized from an older cached result, and removing the test would leave that branch untested and looking dead.

## Verification

`npm run validate` passes in full: 0 vulnerabilities, 468 unit tests across 30 files, 45 Playwright runs, lint, format, both checks, production build. `npx tsc --noEmit` is clean with **no casts in production code**.

Coverage rose slightly — 93.68% → **93.82%** statements, 89.58% → **89.82%** branches. Removing branches that could never be taken removes uncovered branches.

## Note on the workflow

Stated at step 6, per #153: this session cannot invoke sub-agents, so steps 6-8 were performed directly. The ui-review equivalent found no user-visible surface: this is a type change with no rendering difference, which the browser suite confirms.

issues.title: chore(repo): document the strengthened main branch protection
issues.body:
Completes #120. The protection change is applied; this documents it.

## What changed on `main`

| Setting | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Branch up to date before merge (`strict`) | off | **on** |
| Required conversation resolution | off | **on** |
| Required linear history | off | **on** |
| Required approving reviews | 0 | 0 (unchanged) |
| Required checks | `validate` | `validate` (unchanged) |
| Enforced for admins | on | on |
| Force pushes / deletions | blocked | blocked |

**Approving reviews stay at zero, deliberately.** AGENTS.md step 11 permits self-merging a pull request with no assigned reviewer, and that is how this repository actually operates. Raising it to 1 would have made the documented policy unfollowable rather than enforced it.

**Vercel is not a required check.** `validate` already runs `next build`, so a build regression fails the gate on its own; adding the deployment status would mostly add a way for merges to block on an external service's reporting rather than on the code. Worth revisiting if a preview ever catches something the build does not.

## This pull request is also the test #120 asked for

The issue asks to "confirm pending, stale, failing, and approved states behave as intended". Rather than describe that, this branch was deliberately cut from `HEAD~1` so it is **behind `main` from the moment it opens** — the exact stale case the new `strict` setting is meant to catch. It should report `BEHIND` rather than `CLEAN`, refuse to merge, and only clear after its branch is updated and CI reruns against the current base.

If it merges without that, the setting is not doing what it claims and this PR should not have been mergeable.

## Documentation

Step 11 now says what to do about the up-to-date requirement rather than leaving the next agent to hit `BEHIND` and guess. It is the ordinary case whenever two pull requests are open at once — merging the first makes the second stale — and the important part is that **a green check from before the rebase does not carry over**, because it never saw the code that will land. That is the whole point of the setting.

`CONTRIBUTING.md` notes the same for Dependabot, where it bites hardest: several dependency PRs open together, each going stale as the one before it merges. `@dependabot rebase` is the cheap fix.

## Verification

`PASS (unread-paths)`. All three changed paths are `*.md`, enumerated from the branch diff plus `git status --short --untracked-files=all` with no unrelated work in the tree. Ran `npm run check:agent-docs` — the one gate command that reads them — and it reports the docs consistent. Skipped the other seven: no product code changed. CI still runs the complete gate here.

## Note on the workflow

issues.title: fix(ui): give the commit timeline list semantics and room to wrap
issues.body:
Closes #111.

## List semantics

The timeline was a run of `div`s, so assistive technology got repeated card-shaped groups with no count and no sense of sequence — for a result whose entire point is that the first item is the earliest. It is now an `ol` labelled "Earliest public commits", with the decorative markers, the connector line, and both icons hidden from it.

**`role="list"` on the `ol` is not redundant.** Tailwind's preflight sets `list-style: none`, and Safari with VoiceOver drops list semantics from a list styled that way. That is no longer a theoretical browser thanks to #113, so the test is tagged `@webkit` as well as `@mobile`.

## The overflow, and why nobody noticed

Long content was being **clipped rather than wrapped**, and the card's `overflow-hidden` is exactly why it went unseen: the page never scrolled, so a page-level overflow check passed while content was cut off inside the card. The new test asserts both — the page does not scroll *and* no card overruns its own box — which is what separates the two cases.

Three separate causes, each measured rather than guessed:

| Cause | Measurement |
| --- | --- |
| Repository header could not shrink — a flex item's automatic minimum size is its content | header pushed past the card until `min-w-0` + `wrap-anywhere` |
| Summary grid, same thing one level down, and worse: `truncate` is `white-space: nowrap`, which widened its track to the full name | **640px inside a 198px column** |
| Commit body with a long URL — `whitespace-pre-wrap` preserves newlines but does not break an unbroken token | clipped at the card edge |

I found these by instrumenting the page and listing every element whose `scrollWidth` exceeded its `clientWidth`, rather than reading the class lists and guessing.

## Two judgment calls

**The repository name in the summary grid now wraps instead of truncating.** Truncation relied on a `title` tooltip, which is unreachable by touch — so at exactly the width where the name stopped fitting, it also stopped being readable. That is the width the acceptance criteria are about.

**The header is one text flow rather than three flex items.** As flex items, the `/` separator wrapped onto a line of its own once a name was long, reading as a stray slash. Found by looking at the rendered page, not by a test — no assertion I would have written would have caught it.

## Dead animation classes

`animate-in`, `fade-in`, and `slide-in-from-bottom-4` come from a plugin this project does not install. Confirmed by grepping the compiled CSS: **zero rules**. The fade-and-rise they describe has never run, and `duration-500` was timing nothing. All four removed.

That also settles the reduced-motion criterion, and it is worth stating plainly rather than implying support was added: there is now no motion to honour a preference about.

## Tests

A new `e2e-long-data` fixture puts every field at a length with nowhere to wrap — a 39-character owner, a 61-character repository name, an unbroken subject, and a body carrying a long URL. The existing fixtures are all short, so they render identically whether or not the card handles long content, which is why this went unnoticed.

Per the rule added in #153, I searched for tests pinning the old behaviour and found one: `FirstCommitDisplay.test.tsx` queried the avatar by its accessible name, which the `alt=""` change removes. Updated to the new contract rather than left for the gate to catch.

## Verification

`npm run validate` passes in full: 0 vulnerabilities, 442 unit tests across 30 files, **45 Playwright runs** (up 3 — the new spec runs on all three projects), lint, format:check, check-agent-docs, check-labels, build.

Checked visually at 320px with the long fixture and at 1280px with normal data: everything wraps and stays readable, and ordinary content is unchanged.

## Note on the workflow

Stated at step 6, per #153: this session cannot invoke sub-agents, so steps 6-8 were performed directly. The ui-review equivalent was real work here rather than a formality — the stray-slash issue came out of it.

issues.body:
Closes #169. Prevents the class of failure that produced #166.

## The gap

Two workflows run the browser suite and each wrote its own install list by hand. Nothing tied those lists to `playwright.config.ts`, so #165 added the `webkit` project, updated `ci.yml`, and missed `deployed-smoke.yml`.

The gap surfaced as a **failed production health check after a deploy** — the most expensive place for it, and one no local command reaches, because that workflow only runs on a production `deployment_status`.

## The check

`scripts/browser-projects.mjs`, following the `ignore-entries.mjs` pattern: pure functions over source text, consumed by `check-agent-docs`.

**The mapping is project → engine, never project → name.** `mobile-chrome` is a Chromium project using the Galaxy S9+ descriptor, so a name-based reading would demand a browser called "mobile-chrome" that does not exist, while missing the one it actually needs. Engines are resolved from Playwright's own device table rather than a copy kept in this repo — a copy would be one more list to drift.

**It refuses what it cannot read.** A project whose browser resolves to neither a known device nor a `browserName` throws rather than contributing nothing, because silently skipping a project is precisely how a browser goes uninstalled. Same for an unknown device name, and for a config with no `projects` array at all.

**Both spellings of running the suite count.** `deployed-smoke.yml` runs `npm run test:e2e`; `ci.yml` runs `npm run validate`, which chains it. Checking only the first would have passed the very workflow that broke.

**An install naming no browser installs all of them**, so it satisfies any requirement — reported separately from having no install step, which is the opposite situation.

## Verified in both directions

Not argued — reproduced.

Reverting `deployed-smoke.yml` to chromium-only recreates #166, and the check now fails locally:

```
.github/workflows/deployed-smoke.yml installs chromium but the projects in playwright.config.ts
need chromium, webkit; webkit is missing. Playwright fails at browser launch rather than skipping
the project, and a workflow that runs only after a deploy reports that as a failed production
check rather than as a failed pull request.
```

Adding a `firefox` project without touching either workflow fails **both** workflows by name.

Both files were restored and are byte-identical to `main`.

## Bracket counting, not a lazy regex

Worth noting because it is the kind of thing that silently under-reports: a project's `use` object contains brackets of its own, so matching `projects: [ ... ]` to the first `]` stops inside the first project and misses every project after it. That failure direction is the dangerous one — fewer required browsers than there really are is exactly what lets a missing install through. Pinned by a test.

## Verification

`npm run validate` passes in full: 0 vulnerabilities, **442 unit tests across 30 files** (+14, exactly the new module's cases), 42 Playwright runs, lint, format:check, check-agent-docs, check-labels, build.

## Note on the workflow

Stated at step 6, per #153: this session cannot invoke sub-agents, so steps 6-8 were performed directly. No user-visible surface.

issues.title: refactor(app): separate route files from library modules
issues.body:
Closes #144. Last of the three layout refactors, after #142 and #143.

## Problem

`app/` held 23 files of which **15 were not routes** — the server action, the caches, the rate limiter, the logger, the types — sitting at the same level as `page.tsx` and `layout.tsx`. Listing the directory that defines what the app serves mostly showed things it does not serve.

`app/logger.ts` was the clearest case: imported by a route as `@/app/logger`, a module crossing route boundaries from inside the routes directory.

## Where it went, and why not `lib/`

Ten modules and their tests moved to `app/_lib/`.

The issue offered a root-level `lib/` as the alternative. I did not take it: **#143 had just deleted the root `components/` directory** in favour of colocation under `app/`, and adding a root `lib/` would reverse that direction a day later. Underscore-prefixed folders under `app/` are now the single rule the three refactors converge on:

- `app/_home/` — the feature
- `app/_components/` — what renders across features
- `app/_lib/` — what does not render

## The exception, named rather than hidden

`globals.css` and `favicon.ico` stay at the top level. The favicon is a Next.js metadata file. `globals.css` is the root layout's stylesheet, which Next.js convention places beside `layout.tsx` — moving it into `_lib/` would satisfy the letter of "only route files" and be stranger to every Next.js developer who goes looking for it.

`AGENTS.md` states that exception explicitly rather than leaving the rule looking absolute when it is not.

## One thing worth carrying forward

`npx tsc --noEmit` was clean, and every `from` specifier was correct, while **three test files were still broken.**

`vi.mock("./actions")` takes its path as a string. The compiler never checks it, and a grep for `from "..."` never finds it. Only running the suite caught it — 60 failing tests across three files, with a green typecheck.

Worth knowing before the next move of this kind: a rename verified by `tsc` alone is not verified.

## Verification

`npm run validate` passes in full: 0 vulnerabilities, **428 unit tests across 29 files — identical to before the move** — 42 Playwright runs across three projects, lint, format:check, check-agent-docs, check-labels, build.

The identical count is the proof for a relocation; a file dropping out of collection scope still shows a green suite, and only the count catches it. 17 files moved with `git mv` so history follows, and `docs/architecture.md`, `docs/production.md`, and `AGENTS.md` all track the new paths.

`ls app/` now returns route files, route directories, the three private folders, and the two documented exceptions.

## Note on the workflow

Stated at step 6, per #153: this session cannot invoke sub-agents, so steps 6-8 were performed directly. The ui-review equivalent found no user-visible surface — contents are unchanged, only locations.

# Product Guide

My First Commit turns GitHub's public commit search into a small origin story. A visitor enters a
GitHub username and sees the earliest public commit GitHub can find, followed by the next nine
results in chronological order.

## Product Principles

- **Focused:** one search task, without accounts, profiles, feeds, or a database.
- **Honest:** partial or unavailable GitHub results are described as such rather than presented as
  authoritative history.
- **Recoverable:** empty results, rate limits, timeouts, and upstream failures offer a useful next
  action.
- **Private by default:** recent searches stay in the browser, and searched usernames are excluded
  from analytics properties and analytics URLs.
- **Shareable:** a search can be sent as a URL or copied as a compact text summary.

## Capabilities

### Origin discovery

The app searches GitHub's public commit index by author, orders results from oldest to newest, and
requests the first ten matches. The first result receives a detailed summary; the following results
form the rest of the timeline.

### Search shortcuts

Known public profiles provide examples for a first visit and recovery from an empty result. After a
successful search, up to five recent usernames are kept in the visitor's browser as shortcuts. They
can be rerun or cleared without creating an account.

### Sharing

A completed search updates the page URL with the username. Opening that URL starts the same search,
and a copy action creates a short result summary with links back to the search and earliest commit.

### Failure handling

Validation errors, empty searches, rate limits, timeouts, GitHub outages, and unexpected failures
have distinct messages and recovery paths. When GitHub marks a search incomplete, the app labels
the timeline as partial, does not cache it, and offers another search without discarding the visible
results if that retry fails.

### Production visibility

The footer identifies the deployed release. GitHub Actions validates each change, a production
browser check exercises healthy deployments, and a release is promoted only after the deployed
commit passes both checks.

## Data and Privacy

- A searched username is sent to GitHub to retrieve public commit data.
- `GITHUB_TOKEN`, when configured, is used only by the server and is never exposed to the browser.
- Recent searches are stored in browser `localStorage` under
  `my-first-commit:recent-searches`.
- Successful and empty search results may be cached briefly in one server process to reduce
  repeated GitHub API calls. The cache is temporary and is not durable storage.
- Vercel Analytics receives product-health events without the searched username. Shared-search
  parameters are removed from analytics URLs before they are sent.
- The app has no accounts, database, or app-owned server-side search history.

The live [privacy page](https://my-first-commit-eta.vercel.app/privacy) is the visitor-facing notice.
The [architecture guide](architecture.md#data-boundaries) describes the implementation boundaries,
and the [production runbook](production.md#privacy-and-local-storage) covers operational details.

## Limitations

“First commit” means the earliest public commit GitHub's current search index returns for an author.
It is not a complete or immutable record of everything that person has authored.

- Only public commits indexed by GitHub are searchable. Private commits, deleted repositories, and
  private forks are not included.
- GitHub's index can lag behind new pushes, omit older history, or return the same commit through
  forks and mirrors.
- Squashed, rebased, rewritten, or force-pushed history can change the earliest visible result.
- Renamed accounts, changed author emails, bot-authored commits, and missing author metadata can
  affect which commits match a username.
- GitHub may return an incomplete result when a search takes too long. The app labels that result as
  partial rather than claiming it found the definitive first commit.
- Unauthenticated requests have stricter rate limits. A server-side token improves reliability but
  does not make private data searchable.

## Technology

My First Commit is a Next.js App Router application built with React, strict TypeScript, Tailwind
CSS, Octokit, and Vercel Analytics. It uses the visitor's system fonts and generated metadata images,
so builds do not depend on a font or image host. See the [architecture guide](architecture.md) for
the request flow and the [development guide](development.md) for the supported runtime and commands.

# Production Runbook

This runbook covers the production checks and levers for My First Commit.

## Production URLs

- Public app: https://my-first-commit-eta.vercel.app
- GitHub repository: https://github.com/scottdensmore/my-first-commit

Use the public app URL for production health checks. Vercel's generated deployment URLs can be protected and may return `401`.

The app also exposes a lightweight runtime health endpoint:

```text
https://my-first-commit-eta.vercel.app/api/health
```

It returns JSON status, deployment metadata, and whether the public site URL and `GITHUB_TOKEN` are configured. It does not expose server-side secrets or detailed runtime versions.

`checks.githubToken` reports presence only, never the value, a prefix, a length, or a hash. The endpoint is public and uncached, so nothing beyond a boolean belongs there. It confirms the variable is set; it does not prove the token is valid or unexpired.

## Required Configuration

Vercel environment variables:

```env
GITHUB_TOKEN=your_github_pat_here
NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL=https://my-first-commit-eta.vercel.app
```

GitHub Actions repository variables:

```env
PRODUCTION_BASE_URL=https://my-first-commit-eta.vercel.app
```

`GITHUB_TOKEN` is server-side only. Do not expose it as a public `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` variable.

### Rotating `GITHUB_TOKEN`

Vercel applies environment variable changes to new builds only, so a rotation does nothing until the
project is redeployed.

1. Add the new token in Vercel before revoking the old one, so production never falls back to
   unauthenticated requests at 60 requests per hour.
2. Redeploy production.
3. Confirm the variable reached the running deployment:

   ```bash
   curl -s https://my-first-commit-eta.vercel.app/api/health | grep -o '"githubToken":{"configured":[a-z]*}'
   ```

4. Run a search on the public app. `configured: true` only proves the variable is set; a search is
   what proves the token is accepted by GitHub.
5. Revoke the old token.

The app only reads public commit search data, so the token needs no scopes. An unscoped classic token
still raises the Search API limit from 60 to 5,000 requests per hour.

## Deployment Flow

1. Merge a green PR into `main`.
2. GitHub Actions runs `CI / validate`.
3. Vercel builds and deploys production.
4. GitHub receives a production `deployment_status` event.
5. The `Production Health Check` workflow runs Playwright against `PRODUCTION_BASE_URL`.
6. The `Promote Production Release` workflow creates the deployment tag and GitHub release only after the matching `main` CI run and production health check pass.

The production deploy is healthy when `CI / validate`, `Production Health Check`, and `Promote Production Release` pass on `main`.

### Skipped Promotions Are Normal

When two merges land close together, both queue a promotion. The older one runs after `main` has
already advanced, so its commit is no longer the deployed production commit. That run logs:

```text
main has advanced to <sha>.
<older-sha> is no longer the deployed production commit; skipping its release.
```

This is expected. The superseded commit intentionally gets no tag and no release, because the newer
commit is promoted in its place. Gaps in the deployment tag sequence are normal for the same reason.

Before this guard existed, the older promotion instead failed while pushing its tag, because
`GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot push a ref whose workflow files no longer match `main`:

```text
refusing to allow a GitHub App to create or update workflow `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
without `workflows` permission
```

A promotion that fails for any other reason is a real failure and should be investigated.

### Promotion Waits For CI

Vercel deploys in parallel with `CI / validate`, so a deployment and its health check can finish
before CI concludes on `main`. The promotion waits up to 15 minutes for the deployed commit's CI run
to reach a conclusion, logging one line per poll:

```text
CI run for <sha> is in_progress; waiting for it to finish.
```

Waiting is normal. A promotion fails only when CI concludes with something other than success, or
when no CI run reaches a conclusion inside the timeout.

## Release Checklist

See the [release guide](release.md). It owns the before-and-after-release checklist, moving
`CHANGELOG.md` entries into a dated section, and which workflow publishes which tag. Writing the
entry in the first place is a per-change step in [CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md).

## The Release Invariant

**A release tag names a commit that was proven healthy in production, not a commit that merely
merged and then something healthy was observed.** Two checks hold that up, and both exist because
the obvious version of each answers a subtly different question.

**The health run proves which commit it tested.** It points Playwright at a mutable alias, so a
green suite on its own means something healthy was serving that URL — not that the commit which
triggered the run was serving it. Before any spec runs,
`scripts/verify-deployed-commit.mjs` asks `/api/health` what commit is live and compares it to the
deployment's SHA. A deployment still in flight, or a failed one leaving the previous build live,
now fails here in seconds rather than producing a wall of results describing code that is not
deployed. The payload carries an abbreviated seven-character SHA, so the comparison is by prefix; a
run reporting `local` is refused, because that is what the route returns when
`VERCEL_GIT_COMMIT_SHA` is unset and it identifies no deployment at all.

Manual runs pass no expected SHA, since a URL given by hand has no commit to expect, and the step
is skipped.

**Promotion asks which commit is live, not which is newest.** The superseded guard resolves the
active deployment through the deployments API — the most recent one whose latest status is
`success` — rather than comparing against the tip of `main`. Those are different questions: `main`
advances at merge, while a deployment becomes live later and may never. Comparing against the tip
meant a newer commit still deploying, or one that failed, suppressed the release of the commit
genuinely in production, and that release was never cut at all. When no successful deployment can
be found, the guard stops rather than guessing.

Superseded deployments are still skipped, for the reason they always were: two deployments landing
close together queue two promotions, and the older one cannot push its tag once its workflow files
no longer match `main`.

To check the invariant by hand:

```bash
curl -s https://my-first-commit-eta.vercel.app/api/health | jq -r .commit
GITHUB_TOKEN=$(gh auth token) node scripts/resolve-active-deployment.mjs \
  scottdensmore/my-first-commit Production
```

The first prints an abbreviated SHA and the second a full one. They must agree; if they do not,
the alias and the deployment record disagree about what is live, and no release should be cut until
they do.

## The Production Search Canary

`tests/e2e/production-canary.spec.ts` is the only check that exercises the whole path against real
infrastructure: browser to Server Action to GitHub to a rendered commit. Every other search test
uses fixtures, which is what makes them deterministic and also what makes them blind to a revoked
token, a changed GitHub response, or a Server Action broken only in production. `/api/health`
reports that a token is *present*, never that it works.

It runs only where `PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL` is set, so it is automatically part of the production
health check and of any manual run against a deployed URL, and never part of local CI. No workflow
step configures it; the skip condition does that work.

**One search per deployment, deliberately.** It is a canary rather than a suite. It is untagged, so
it runs on Chromium only rather than once per browser project, and every additional search spends
the shared GitHub quota that the [burst bounding](#bounding-search-bursts) exists to protect.

**The handle is `torvalds` by default**, chosen for having the largest and most reliably indexed
history on the platform, and overridable with `E2E_CANARY_USERNAME`. Override it rather than editing
the spec if GitHub's commit search index ever stops returning results for it — the assertion depends
on that index, which is the one part of this check nothing in this repository controls.

**A partial result passes.** GitHub returning `incomplete_results` is its own load shedding, not a
fault of this app, and failing on it would make the canary flap for a reason no deploy can fix. What
it will not accept is an empty result, an error state, or a heading with no commit rendered.

To run it by hand:

```bash
PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL=https://my-first-commit-eta.vercel.app \
  npx playwright test --project=chromium production-canary
```

Confirmed to fail rather than pass vacuously: pointed at a handle with no indexed commits, it fails
on the missing result heading instead of reporting success.

## Production Health Check Alerts

When `Production Health Check` fails, GitHub Actions opens or updates a GitHub issue titled:

```text
Production health check failed
```

Use that issue as the incident record. It includes the health check target, workflow run, and commit SHA.

When responding to a health check failure:

1. Open the workflow run linked from the issue.
2. Confirm the health check target is the public production URL.
3. Open production manually and check whether the app renders.
4. Fix the deployment, configuration, or app regression.
5. Re-run `Production Health Check` or deploy a fix.
6. Close the issue after the production health check passes again.

## Manual Validation

Run `npm run validate`, the local [validation suite](development.md#validation), first.

Run a health check against production:

```bash
npm run test:e2e:deployed
```

The Production Health Check browser workflow covers the home page, branded 404 page, generated social assets, and `/api/health`.

Check the runtime health endpoint directly:

```bash
curl https://my-first-commit-eta.vercel.app/api/health
```

Run a health check against any deployed URL:

```bash
PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL=https://your-deployment.example npm run test:e2e
```

You can also start `Production Health Check` manually from GitHub Actions. Provide the public app URL as `base_url`.

Use the [manual QA checklist](manual-qa.md) for larger UI changes and Open Graph preview validation.

## Observability

This app intentionally uses Vercel-only observability. Do not add Sentry, GlitchTip, or another paid error-monitoring service unless the app grows beyond personal use.

Use these signals together:

- Vercel Analytics for traffic and page-level usage.
- Vercel Logs for runtime errors and server-side GitHub API failures.
- GitHub Actions for CI and production health check status.
- GitHub issues for production health check incidents.

### Vercel Analytics

Use Vercel Analytics to answer:

- Is anyone visiting the app?
- Which pages are getting traffic?
- Did usage change after a deploy?

If analytics look empty after a production deploy, confirm the app includes `@vercel/analytics` and that the latest production deploy completed.

### Vercel Logs

# Production Runbook

This runbook covers the production checks and levers for My First Commit.

## Production URLs

- Public app: https://my-first-commit-eta.vercel.app
- GitHub repository: https://github.com/scottdensmore/my-first-commit

Use the public app URL for production health checks. Vercel's generated deployment URLs can be protected and may return `401`.

The app also exposes a lightweight runtime health endpoint:

```text
https://my-first-commit-eta.vercel.app/api/health
```

It returns JSON status, deployment metadata, and whether the public site URL and `GITHUB_TOKEN` are configured. It does not expose server-side secrets or detailed runtime versions.

`checks.githubToken` reports presence only, never the value, a prefix, a length, or a hash. The endpoint is public and uncached, so nothing beyond a boolean belongs there. It confirms the variable is set; it does not prove the token is valid or unexpired.

## Required Configuration

Vercel environment variables:

```env

NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL=https://my-first-commit-eta.vercel.app
```

GitHub Actions repository variables:

```env
PRODUCTION_BASE_URL=https://my-first-commit-eta.vercel.app
```

`GITHUB_TOKEN` is server-side only. Do not expose it as a public `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` variable.

### Rotating `GITHUB_TOKEN`

Vercel applies environment variable changes to new builds only, so a rotation does nothing until the
project is redeployed.

1. Add the new token in Vercel before revoking the old one, so production never falls back to
   unauthenticated requests at 60 requests per hour.
2. Redeploy production.
3. Confirm the variable reached the running deployment:

   ```bash
   curl -s https://my-first-commit-eta.vercel.app/api/health | grep -o '"githubToken":{"configured":[a-z]*}'
   ```

4. Run a search on the public app. `configured: true` only proves the variable is set; a search is
   what proves the token is accepted by GitHub.
5. Revoke the old token.

The app only reads public commit search data, so the token needs no scopes. An unscoped classic token
still raises the Search API limit from 60 to 5,000 requests per hour.

## Deployment Flow

1. Merge a green PR into `main`.
2. GitHub Actions runs `CI / validate`.
3. Vercel builds and deploys production.
4. GitHub receives a production `deployment_status` event.
5. The `Production Health Check` workflow runs Playwright against `PRODUCTION_BASE_URL`.

The production deploy is healthy when `CI / validate`, `Production Health Check`, and `Promote Production Release` pass on `main`.

When two merges land close together, both queue a promotion. The older one runs after `main` has
already advanced, so its commit is no longer the deployed production commit. That run logs:

main has advanced to <sha>.
<older-sha> is no longer the deployed production commit; skipping its release.
```

This is expected. The superseded commit intentionally gets no tag and no release, because the newer
commit is promoted in its place. Gaps in the deployment tag sequence are normal for the same reason.

Before this guard existed, the older promotion instead failed while pushing its tag, because
`GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot push a ref whose workflow files no longer match `main`:

without `workflows` permission
```

A promotion that fails for any other reason is a real failure and should be investigated.

### Promotion Waits For CI

Vercel deploys in parallel with `CI / validate`, so a deployment and its health check can finish
before CI concludes on `main`. The promotion waits up to 15 minutes for the deployed commit's CI run
to reach a conclusion, logging one line per poll:

```text
CI run for <sha> is in_progress; waiting for it to finish.
```

Waiting is normal. A promotion fails only when CI concludes with something other than success, or
when no CI run reaches a conclusion inside the timeout.

# Architecture

My First Commit is a small Next.js App Router application. It has no database, no user accounts, and no server-side search storage.

## Request Flow

1. The browser renders the homepage from `app/page.tsx`.
2. The user enters a GitHub username in the search form.
3. The client validates the username format before submitting.
4. The client calls the `getCommits` server action in `app/_lib/actions.ts`.
5. The server action queries GitHub's public commit search through Octokit.
6. Successful and empty GitHub search results are cached briefly in memory by normalized username to reduce repeated API calls. Concurrent requests for the same username share one upstream search rather than each issuing their own, since the cache cannot help until the first one finishes. That sharing is per server instance, like the cache, so the ceiling is one concurrent search per username per instance rather than globally. Results GitHub marked `incomplete_results` are never cached, so a retry can reach a complete answer.
7. Searches that survive the cache are bounded per client by a rolling window of 30 a minute, keyed by a salted hash of the forwarded client address. Anything past the window is answered with the existing rate-limit result instead of reaching GitHub. The window lives in one server instance's memory and resets on a cold start, so it lowers what a burst from one client costs; it is not a global ceiling on the shared GitHub token. See the [rate-limit runbook section](production.md#bounding-search-bursts).
8. The server action maps GitHub results into the app's `CommitData` shape.
9. The client renders the first public commit and the next several commits in `FirstCommitDisplay`.
10. Successful searches are stored in browser `localStorage` as recent-search shortcuts.

## Data Boundaries

- `GITHUB_TOKEN` is server-side only and is used by Octokit in the server action.
- Usernames are sent to GitHub to search public commit data.
- GitHub username validation runs on both the client and server action boundary.
- Recent searches are stored only in the user's browser under `my-first-commit:recent-searches`.
- The app does not persist searches, users, commits, or analytics events in its own database.
- Rate limiting holds a salted SHA-256 hash of the forwarded client address in server memory, never the address itself, and never alongside the username that was searched. The salt is random per process and is never written down, so the hashes mean nothing outside the instance that made them or after it restarts. Entries are dropped once a client has been quiet for longer than the window, and the map is capped so a flood of distinct addresses cannot grow it without bound.
- Browsers post CSP violation reports to `/api/csp-report`. Only the two CSP report content types are read, bodies are rejected past 16 KB while they arrive rather than after buffering, at most ten reports are logged per request, http(s) URLs are reduced to origin and path and every other scheme to the scheme alone, and `original-policy` and `script-sample` are never read.

## Runtime Routes

- `/` renders the search experience.
- `/privacy` renders the static privacy page.
- Unknown routes keep the requested URL and render the custom `app/not-found.tsx` page with a `404` response.
- `/api/health` returns runtime health JSON for production checks.
- `/api/csp-report` accepts unauthenticated CSP violation reports posted by browsers and logs them as sanitized `csp_violation` events. See the [production runbook](production.md#csp-violation-reports).
- `/api/e2e-readiness` tells the Playwright preflight whether the server it found was started with the fixture mocks. It reports that one boolean and nothing else, and returns `404` whenever `NODE_ENV` is `production`, so it does not exist on a built or deployed server. See the [browser checks](development.md#validation).
- `/icon`, `/opengraph-image`, and `/twitter-image` are generated by App Router image routes.

## Failure Handling

GitHub API failures are normalized in `app/_lib/actions.ts`:

- Empty public search results show a polite empty state.
- GitHub sets `incomplete_results` when a commit search times out before scanning every commit, and still returns `200` with a partial item list. Those results carry `incomplete: true` through `CommitData`: the UI presents them as the earliest commit found so far rather than the first commit and offers a retry, and the cache refuses to store them so that a retry can reach a complete answer. A retry that fails keeps the partial result on screen rather than replacing it, since the visitor took an action the page offered. An incomplete search that returned no items is reported as an unfinished search, never as an absence of commits.
- Rate limits, timeouts, unavailable GitHub services, validation failures, and unknown errors show recovery-focused copy.
- A client past the per-client window gets the same `rate_limit` result GitHub's own rate limiting produces, so the screen, the retry, and the copy the visitor sees are identical. Only the unrendered `error` string and the log event differ, so neither claims GitHub refused a search the app refused itself.
- Server-side failures are logged with structured event names and sanitized fields only, without usernames, tokens, or raw Octokit error objects.

## Operational Checks

GitHub Actions and Vercel cover the main production path:

- `CI / validate` runs `npm run validate`: the dependency audit, unit tests, browser checks, lint, formatting, agent-document and label checks, and the production build. Contributors run the same script locally. See the [validation suite](development.md#validation).
- Vercel deploys previews and production.
- `Production Health Check` runs Playwright against the public production URL after successful production deployments.
- `Promote Production Release` creates a tag and GitHub release only after the matching `main` CI run and production health check pass.
- `/api/health` exposes runtime status without secrets.

GitHub API failures are normalized in `app/_lib/actions.ts`:

- Empty public search results show a polite empty state.
- GitHub sets `incomplete_results` when a commit search times out before scanning every commit, and still returns `200` with a partial item list. Those results carry `incomplete: true` through `CommitData`: the UI presents them as the earliest commit found so far rather than the first commit and offers a retry, and the cache refuses to store them so that a retry can reach a complete answer. A retry that fails keeps the partial result on screen rather than replacing it, since the visitor took an action the page offered. An incomplete search that returned no items is reported as an unfinished search, never as an absence of commits.
- Rate limits, timeouts, unavailable GitHub services, validation failures, and unknown errors show recovery-focused copy.
- A client past the per-client window gets the same `rate_limit` result GitHub's own rate limiting produces, so the screen, the retry, and the copy the visitor sees are identical. Only the unrendered `error` string and the log event differ, so neither claims GitHub refused a search the app refused itself.
- Server-side failures are logged with structured event names and sanitized fields only, without usernames, tokens, or raw Octokit error objects.

## Operational Checks

GitHub Actions and Vercel cover the main production path:

- `CI / validate` runs `npm run validate`: the dependency audit, unit tests, browser checks, lint, formatting, agent-document and label checks, and the production build. Contributors run the same script locally. See the [validation suite](development.md#validation).
- Vercel deploys previews and production.
- `Production Health Check` runs Playwright against the public production URL after successful production deployments.
- `Promote Production Release` creates a tag and GitHub release only after the matching `main` CI run and production health check pass.
- `/api/health` exposes runtime status without secrets.

name: Promote Production Release

on:
  workflow_run:
    workflows:
      - Production Health Check
    types:
      - completed

permissions:
  actions: read
  contents: write

concurrency:
  group: production-release-${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_sha }}
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  promote:
    name: Tag and release healthy production deployment
    if: >-
      github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'success' &&
      github.event.workflow_run.event == 'deployment_status' &&
      github.event.workflow_run.head_branch == 'main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Check out deployed commit
        uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_sha }}

      # Pinned rather than left to the runner's default, so the guard runs on the Node this
      # repository targets. The scripts it runs need no dependencies, so there is no install step.
      - name: Set up Node
        uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc

      # Two production deployments landing close together queue two promotions. The older one runs
      # after a newer deployment is already live, and pushing its tag is rejected when the deployed
      # commit's workflow files no longer match main:
      #   refusing to allow a GitHub App to create or update workflow `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
      #   without `workflows` permission
      # The superseded commit is no longer production, so skip it instead of failing the run. The
      # newer commit gets its own promotion.
      #
      # Resolved from the deployments API rather than from the tip of main, which answers a
      # different question. main advances at merge; a deployment becomes live later and may never.
      # Comparing against the tip meant a newer commit still deploying -- or one that failed --
      # suppressed the release of the commit genuinely in production, and that release was never
      # cut at all.
      - name: Skip superseded deployment
        id: guard
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          TARGET_SHA: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_sha }}
        run: |
          active="$(node scripts/resolve-active-deployment.mjs "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" Production)"

          if [ "$active" != "$TARGET_SHA" ]; then
            echo "${active} is the live production deployment."
            echo "${TARGET_SHA} has been overtaken; skipping its release."
            echo "superseded=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          else
            echo "${TARGET_SHA} is the live production deployment."
            echo "superseded=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          fi

      - name: Resolve release tag
        id: release
        if: steps.guard.outputs.superseded != 'true'
        run: |
          version="$(node -p "require('./package.json').version")"
          short_sha="$(printf '%s' "${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_sha }}" | cut -c1-7)"
          tag="v${version}-${short_sha}"

          echo "tag=$tag" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "short_sha=$short_sha" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: Confirm CI passed for deployed commit
        if: steps.guard.outputs.superseded != 'true'
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          TARGET_SHA: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_sha }}
        run: |
          # Vercel can deploy, and the health check can pass, before CI finishes on main. This query
          # used to filter on status=completed, which made "CI is still running" look identical to
          # "CI does not exist" — both returned an empty list and the step failed. A promotion was
          # lost that way after checking 8 seconds before CI concluded.
          #
          # Poll for a conclusion instead of taking a single snapshot. A missing run stays a failure,
          # but an unfinished one is simply not an answer yet.
          deadline=$(( SECONDS + 900 ))
          ci_conclusion=""

          while :; do
            ci_run="$(
              gh api "repos/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY}/actions/workflows/ci.yml/runs?head_sha=${TARGET_SHA}&branch=main&event=push&per_page=10" \
                --jq '(.workflow_runs[0] // {}) | "\(.status // "") \(.conclusion // "")"' || true
            )"
            ci_status="${ci_run%% *}"
            ci_conclusion="${ci_run#* }"

            if [ "$ci_status" = "completed" ]; then
              break
            fi

            if [ -z "$ci_status" ]; then
              echo "No CI run found yet for ${TARGET_SHA}."
            else
              echo "CI run for ${TARGET_SHA} is ${ci_status}; waiting for it to finish."
            fi

            if [ "$SECONDS" -ge "$deadline" ]; then
              echo "Timed out after 15 minutes waiting for CI to finish for ${TARGET_SHA}."
              echo "Last observed status: '${ci_status:-none}'."
              exit 1
            fi

            sleep 15
          done

          if [ "$ci_conclusion" != "success" ]; then
            echo "Expected successful CI run for ${TARGET_SHA}, got '${ci_conclusion:-none}'."
            exit 1
          fi

          echo "CI succeeded for ${TARGET_SHA}."

      - name: Create tag and GitHub release
        if: steps.guard.outputs.superseded != 'true'
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          TAG: ${{ steps.release.outputs.tag }}
          TARGET_SHA: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_sha }}
          RUN_URL: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.html_url }}
        run: |
          if gh release view "$TAG" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            echo "Release $TAG already exists."
            exit 0
          fi

          if git ls-remote --exit-code --tags origin "refs/tags/$TAG" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            echo "Tag $TAG already exists."
          else
            git tag "$TAG" "$TARGET_SHA"
            git push origin "$TAG"
          fi

          {
            echo "Production deployment release for $TAG."
            echo
            echo "This release was created automatically after Vercel deployed the commit and the Production Health Check passed."
            echo
            echo "- Commit: $TARGET_SHA"
            echo "- Production health check: $RUN_URL"
          } > release-notes.md

          # --latest=false is required. Without it the "Latest" pointer is chosen automatically from
          # date and version, and a fresh deployment tag always wins against the vX.Y.Z release it
          # was deployed from. A deployment tag is a deployment record, not the current version, so
          # /releases/latest must keep pointing at the version release.
          gh release create "$TAG" \
            --title "$TAG" \
            --notes-file release-notes.md \
            --target "$TARGET_SHA" \
            --latest=false \
            --verify-tag

      - name: Resolve release tag
        id: release
        if: steps.guard.outputs.superseded != 'true'
        run: |
          version="$(node -p "require('./package.json').version")"
          short_sha="$(printf '%s' "${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_sha }}" | cut -c1-7)"
          tag="v${version}-${short_sha}"

          echo "tag=$tag" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "short_sha=$short_sha" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: Confirm CI passed for deployed commit
        if: steps.guard.outputs.superseded != 'true'
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          TARGET_SHA: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_sha }}
        run: |
          # Vercel can deploy, and the health check can pass, before CI finishes on main. This query
          # used to filter on status=completed, which made "CI is still running" look identical to
          # "CI does not exist" — both returned an empty list and the step failed. A promotion was
          # lost that way after checking 8 seconds before CI concluded.
          #
          # Poll for a conclusion instead of taking a single snapshot. A missing run stays a failure,
          # but an unfinished one is simply not an answer yet.
          deadline=$(( SECONDS + 900 ))
          ci_conclusion=""

          while :; do
            ci_run="$(
              gh api "repos/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY}/actions/workflows/ci.yml/runs?head_sha=${TARGET_SHA}&branch=main&event=push&per_page=10" \
                --jq '(.workflow_runs[0] // {}) | "\(.status // "") \(.conclusion // "")"' || true
            )"
            ci_status="${ci_run%% *}"
            ci_conclusion="${ci_run#* }"

            if [ "$ci_status" = "completed" ]; then
              break
            fi

            if [ -z "$ci_status" ]; then
              echo "No CI run found yet for ${TARGET_SHA}."
            else
              echo "CI run for ${TARGET_SHA} is ${ci_status}; waiting for it to finish."
            fi

            if [ "$SECONDS" -ge "$deadline" ]; then
              echo "Timed out after 15 minutes waiting for CI to finish for ${TARGET_SHA}."
              echo "Last observed status: '${ci_status:-none}'."
              exit 1
            fi

            sleep 15
          done

          if [ "$ci_conclusion" != "success" ]; then
            echo "Expected successful CI run for ${TARGET_SHA}, got '${ci_conclusion:-none}'."
            exit 1
          fi

          echo "CI succeeded for ${TARGET_SHA}."

      - name: Create tag and GitHub release
        if: steps.guard.outputs.superseded != 'true'
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          TAG: ${{ steps.release.outputs.tag }}
          TARGET_SHA: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_sha }}
          RUN_URL: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.html_url }}
        run: |
          if gh release view "$TAG" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            echo "Release $TAG already exists."
            exit 0
          fi

          if git ls-remote --exit-code --tags origin "refs/tags/$TAG" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            echo "Tag $TAG already exists."
          else
            git tag "$TAG" "$TARGET_SHA"
            git push origin "$TAG"
          fi

          {
            echo "Production deployment release for $TAG."
            echo
            echo "This release was created automatically after Vercel deployed the commit and the Production Health Check passed."
            echo
            echo "- Commit: $TARGET_SHA"
            echo "- Production health check: $RUN_URL"
          } > release-notes.md

          # --latest=false is required. Without it the "Latest" pointer is chosen automatically from
          # date and version, and a fresh deployment tag always wins against the vX.Y.Z release it
          # was deployed from. A deployment tag is a deployment record, not the current version, so
          # /releases/latest must keep pointing at the version release.
          gh release create "$TAG" \
            --title "$TAG" \
            --notes-file release-notes.md \
            --target "$TARGET_SHA" \
            --latest=false \
            --verify-tag

name: Production Health Check

on:
  deployment_status:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      base_url:
        description: Fully qualified deployed app URL to health check.
        required: true

permissions:
  contents: read
  issues: write

jobs:
  production-health-check:
    name: Playwright production health check
    if: >-
      github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' ||
      (
        github.event.deployment_status.state == 'success' &&
        github.event.deployment.environment == 'Production'
      )
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL: ${{ github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' && inputs.base_url || vars.PRODUCTION_BASE_URL || github.event.deployment_status.environment_url }}
      # Empty for a manual run against an arbitrary URL, where there is no commit to expect. A
      # deployment_status run always has one, and that is the run a release is promoted from.
      EXPECTED_COMMIT_SHA: ${{ github.event_name == 'deployment_status' && github.event.deployment.sha || '' }}

    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Set up Node
        uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: npm

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      # Every browser `playwright.config.ts` declares a project for, because this job runs the
      # whole suite. Installing fewer fails at launch rather than skipping the project, and it
      # fails here — after a production deploy — rather than on the pull request that added one.
      - name: Install Playwright browsers
        run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium webkit

      - name: Validate health check target
        run: |
          if [ -z "$PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL" ]; then
            echo "PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL is required."
            echo "Set PRODUCTION_BASE_URL as a repository variable or provide base_url for manual runs."
            exit 1
          fi

          case "$PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL" in
            http://*|https://*) ;;
            *)
              echo "PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL must be an absolute http(s) URL."
              exit 1
              ;;
          esac

      # Before the suite, not after. A run against the wrong build otherwise produces a wall of
      # results describing code that is not deployed, and a pass that claims the triggering commit
      # is healthy on evidence gathered from a different one.
      - name: Verify the deployment is serving the expected commit
        if: env.EXPECTED_COMMIT_SHA != ''
        run: node scripts/verify-deployed-commit.mjs "$PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL" "$EXPECTED_COMMIT_SHA"

      - name: Run production browser health checks
        run: npm run test:e2e

      - name: Create or update health check failure issue
        if: failure() && github.event_name == 'deployment_status'
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          SMOKE_TARGET: ${{ env.PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL }}
          RUN_URL: ${{ github.server_url }}/${{ github.repository }}/actions/runs/${{ github.run_id }}
        run: |
          issue_title="Production health check failed"
          issue_body="$(cat <<BODY
          The production health check failed.

          - Target: ${SMOKE_TARGET}
          - Workflow run: ${RUN_URL}
          - Commit: ${GITHUB_SHA}

          Review the workflow logs, confirm the deployed app loads, and update this issue with the resolution.
          BODY
          )"

          issue_number="$(gh issue list --state open --search "${issue_title} in:title" --json number --jq '.[0].number // empty')"

          if [ -n "$issue_number" ]; then
            gh issue comment "$issue_number" --body "$issue_body"
          else
            gh issue create --title "$issue_title" --body "$issue_body"
          fi
