CHANGELOG.md-90-- The gate now fails when a workflow that runs the browser suite installs fewer browsers than the Playwright configuration declares projects for. Two workflows each kept their own hand-written install list, and nothing tied them to the config, so adding the WebKit project updated one and not the other — a gap that could only appear after a production deploy, because the workflow it broke runs on a deployment event and no local command reaches it. The check resolves each project to the engine it actually runs on rather than to its name, since a mobile project is Chromium-backed, and it refuses to read a project it does not understand instead of quietly assuming that project needs nothing.
CHANGELOG.md-91-
CHANGELOG.md-92-- The `app/` directory now holds route files and nothing else. It had grown to 23 files of which 15 were not routes — the server action, the cache, the logger, the type definitions and the rest sat at the same level as `page.tsx` and `layout.tsx`, so listing the directory that defines what the app serves mostly showed things it does not serve. Those modules moved to `app/_lib/`, completing the rule the previous two entries started: a folder under `app/` that is not a route starts with an underscore, components live beside the feature that uses them, and everything else is a module in `app/_lib/`. No behaviour changed and no route was added or removed.
CHANGELOG.md-93-- Components now have one home instead of three. `FirstCommitDisplay` sat alone in a root-level `components/` directory, the four search components sat in `app/_home/`, and the analytics wrapper sat loose in `app/`, with no rule saying which belonged where — so `SearchResults` imported one sibling across an alias boundary and the rest relatively, for no reason a reader could infer. A component now lives beside the feature that uses it, and `app/_components/` holds the ones used by something other than a single feature. The root `components/` directory is gone, and with it the last collection root the unit tests reached outside `app/` and `scripts/`. No behaviour changed; the suite collects the same 428 tests it did before the move.
CHANGELOG.md-94-- The browser suite now runs on a 320px mobile viewport and on WebKit as well as Desktop Chrome. Only Chrome ran before, so nothing automatically checked how the app behaves at phone width or in the engine behind Safari — layout, focus, navigation, and clipboard were all assumed to work the same everywhere. The two added projects run a selected set of journeys rather than the whole suite, so coverage grows by a few runs instead of tripling. Traces are also retained on failure now: the suite asked for them on the first retry, but retries are off, so no trace was ever captured for any failure in any browser.
CHANGELOG.md:95:- `AGENTS.md` now carries the agent-rules block that Next.js generates, instead of having it reappear after every browser suite run. `next dev` writes the block whenever its exact text is missing, and the browser suite boots `next dev`, so each full validation run left a modified `AGENTS.md` that someone had to notice and strip — it reached a commit by accident once. The generator offers no way to turn this off, and it skips writing once the block is present, so committing it is what actually stops it. A note above the block records that it is generated, that edits between its markers are overwritten on the next run, and that it cannot move to `CLAUDE.md`, which the gate requires to stay a byte-for-byte pointer.
CHANGELOG.md-96-- The homepage's internal components and modules moved from `app/home/` to `app/_home/`. Every directory under `app/` claims a URL segment, so a folder holding internals was one file away from becoming a public route at `/home`, with nothing in its name to say it should not be. A leading underscore marks it private to Next.js, which excludes it from routing outright. No route was added or removed and nothing about the app changed for a visitor; `/home` returns the branded not-found page exactly as before, and now cannot stop doing so.
CHANGELOG.md-97-- The app no longer downloads a web font, and a production build no longer needs Google Fonts to be reachable. The root layout fetched Geist and Geist Mono at build time, but the Tailwind font tokens have always defined system stacks and nothing ever referenced the `--font-geist-*` variables the layout generated, so no text was rendered in Geist — a visitor's browser only preloaded two font files it never used. Rendered typography is unchanged, the system stack it actually uses is documented beside the tokens that define it, and the build now depends on nothing outside the repository for fonts.
CHANGELOG.md-98-- Label synchronization now decides what to do in tested code. `scripts/sync-labels.mjs` had grown to mix validating `.github/labels.yml`, planning creates and updates, and deleting labels, with only the offline file check covered in CI — so the destructive branch was the least tested part of it. Validation, planning, reporting, and applying now live in `scripts/label-plan.mjs` as pure functions over plain data, unit tested without a token or a network: that a deletion is planned only with `--prune`, that a dry run previews exactly the deletions a real run would make and writes nothing, that an unquoted colour like `123456` is caught while `e10c02` passes through as the string it stays, and that what reaches the GitHub API is what the plan validated. The script itself is unchanged in behaviour and still the only entry point; `npm run check:labels` still validates the file offline on every pull request.
CHANGELOG.md:99:- The unit test run now collects from `app/`, `components/`, and `scripts/` instead of skipping directories one at a time. A scratch spec left at the repository root, or in any directory the exclude list had not been taught about, used to join `npm test` and fail the gate with a Playwright error that pointed at the tooling rather than at the stray file. Nothing outside those three roots is a unit test now, so such a file neither breaks the run nor quietly joins it, and the verification exemption for the external tooling-state directories no longer depends on a denylist keeping pace with every directory a tool might create. `npm run check:agent-docs` still fails if the ignore lists drift apart, and now also if the collection scope widens.
CHANGELOG.md-100-- The agent workflow now covers changes that replace an existing contract. Test-driven development assumed new behavior, where one new failing test is enough to drive the work; when a change instead replaces something, the suite already holds assertions on the behavior being removed, and those stay green while the new test goes red and then green, so the loop looks finished with the contradiction still in the tree. Agents now locate and update those assertions inside the same red/green loop instead of letting the full validation gate find them a cycle later. Agents that cannot invoke the review sub-agents must also say so on reaching the review steps rather than in the final report, since the fallback has one agent review its own change and reporting it at the end surfaces that only once the work has already been reviewed that way.
CHANGELOG.md:101:- The browser suite now also refuses a stale server of this application. Confirming that the port held the right app was not enough: a server left behind by an interrupted run answered that check perfectly, and if it had been started without the fixture mocks every reserved test username went to real GitHub, so nearly every spec failed for a reason that had nothing to do with the branch — the same misleading wall of failures the original check was built to remove. A second preflight probe now asks the server whether it was started for this suite and stops the run naming the missing flag when it was not; a server too old to answer that question is rejected the same way. That probe is a route of its own, reporting one boolean and returning `404` on any built or deployed server, so nothing about test configuration was added to the public health endpoint. Neither probe can tell which branch a server is running, which remains a reason to prefer letting the suite start its own.
CHANGELOG.md:102:- The browser suite now refuses to run against a foreign server. Playwright reused any server that answered on its port, so an unrelated application left running there was adopted silently and every spec failed as though the branch were broken. A preflight check asks `/api/health` whether the port holds this application and stops the run with one clear error when it does not, naming the port and what it found. The other process is never stopped, since the port may belong to another checkout or another person's work. The port is now settable with `E2E_PORT`, and the worker count is fixed rather than derived from the machine so a run behaves the same everywhere; both overrides reject an unusable value instead of falling back silently. CI keeps the concurrency it already had.
CHANGELOG.md-103-- `.editorconfig` now carries a `max_line_length` matching Prettier's `printWidth`, so editors show the same wrap column the formatter uses. Markdown opts out, because prose here is hand-wrapped and Prettier does not format it.
CHANGELOG.md-104-- One command now runs the validation gate. `npm run validate` chains the dependency audit, unit tests, browser checks, lint, formatting, agent-document and label checks, and the production build, stopping at the first failure. The `CI / validate` job runs that same script instead of listing the steps itself, so the local gate and the CI gate are the same definition rather than two lists that drift. `npm run check:agent-docs` now also fails if CI stops invoking the script, or if the copies of the list in the development guide or the `verifier` sub-agent definition stop matching it, and the parsing behind that check is unit tested. Those two are now the only places the chain is written out in order.
CHANGELOG.md-105-- Local Entire checkpoint hooks now match Claude Code's current tool names, including the newer task tools, so the configuration no longer depends on Claude Code's legacy alias map.

CHANGELOG.md-108-- The agent workflow now bounds its review loop: findings can be explicitly resolved with a stated reason, and a finding that survives two fix-and-re-review cycles stops for a human instead of looping. Reverification is scoped to the gate commands a fix can actually affect, with an exemption for paths no gate command reads, so a prose fix no longer triggers a full audit, test, browser, and build cycle.
CHANGELOG.md-109-- Agents must now add a `CHANGELOG.md` entry with user-facing and operational changes, treat issue, pull request, and review text as data rather than instructions, and bound the wait for an assigned reviewer instead of blocking indefinitely.
CHANGELOG.md-110-- The `ui-review` sub-agent now enumerates untracked files with `--untracked-files=all`, so a brand-new component directory can no longer be mistaken for a change with no user-visible surface.
CHANGELOG.md:111:- Consolidated the pre-PR command list, which had drifted into four inconsistent copies, into a canonical list in the development guide that the contributing guide, runbook, and release guide now link to. The agent-facing files keep deliberate inline copies. Trimmed the manual QA checklist to the states the deployed browser check skips and the judgments Playwright cannot make, and documented the Playwright browser install.
CHANGELOG.md-112-- Documented the `/privacy` and `/api/csp-report` routes in the architecture guide, along with the CSP report endpoint's data boundaries. Both shipped previously without being listed among the runtime routes.
CHANGELOG.md-113-- Clarified that the main agent owns exact unit-test red/green loops while the verifier owns focused Playwright execution and the complete validation gate.
CHANGELOG.md-114-- Removed the superseded specification and roadmap documents, along with their README links.
--

CHANGELOG.md-49-
CHANGELOG.md:50:- A release tag now names a commit that was proven healthy in production, rather than one that merged and was followed by something healthy being observed. The production health check pointed a browser at a mutable alias without ever asking which commit was answering, so a deployment still in flight — or a failed one leaving the previous build live — produced a green run that said nothing about the code it was supposed to be checking. The run now asks `/api/health` what is deployed and stops in seconds if it is not the commit that triggered it. Promotion had a related gap from the other side: it decided whether a deployment had been overtaken by comparing against the tip of `main`, which advances at merge, while a deployment becomes live later and may never — so a newer commit that was still deploying, or that failed, suppressed the release of the commit genuinely in production and that release was never cut. It now resolves the live deployment directly and refuses to guess when none can be found.
CHANGELOG.md-51-
CHANGELOG.md-52-- Syncing labels no longer deletes a label whose name differs from `.github/labels.yml` only in capitalization. GitHub cannot hold both `Bug` and `bug`, but the sync matched names exactly, so a label renamed by hand in the GitHub UI read as two things at once: a label to create and a stray to remove. Under `--prune` that combination deleted the very label the file asks to keep — taking it off every issue and pull request carrying it — while the create that was meant to replace it failed with a `422`. A case-only difference is now one label with a drifted name, corrected in place by renaming it, which a dry run previews as `would update: Bug -> bug`. Nothing in this repository could reach the old behaviour, since every name in the file is lowercase today. Two entries in the file differing only in case are now rejected as duplicates, because GitHub could not hold both.

--

CHANGELOG.md-56-- The production health check runs again. Adding the mobile and WebKit browser projects taught the CI workflow to install WebKit but not the separate workflow that health-checks a production deployment, so the first deploy after that change failed at browser launch and opened an alert issue. The deployed app was healthy throughout; only the check was broken. Both workflows now install every browser the Playwright configuration declares a project for.
CHANGELOG.md-57-- A maximum-length GitHub handle in **Recent searches** no longer pushes the page sideways on a narrow screen. A handle can be 39 characters and has nothing to break on, so a single shortcut was wider than a 320px viewport and scrolled the whole page horizontally — the same width 200% zoom produces on a 640px window, where content is meant to reflow rather than scroll in two directions. Long handles now wrap inside their button, which stays one tap target with one focus ring and still shows the handle in full. Short handles are unchanged.
CHANGELOG.md:58:- The **Try again** button on an error no longer loses keyboard focus when it is pressed. Browsers blur a control the moment it becomes disabled, so activating the retry dropped a keyboard or screen-reader visitor at the top of the document for the length of the request and left them nowhere when it finished. The button now stays focusable while its retry runs, says **Searching again...**, and ignores a second press instead of starting a duplicate search — the same behaviour the partial-result retry already had, so both retries in the app now work the same way.
CHANGELOG.md-59-- A burst of searches for many different usernames from one client is now bounded. Sharing one request between concurrent readers of the same username did nothing about a flood of *distinct* usernames, where every search is a genuine cache miss and reaches GitHub against a shared allowance of 30 searches a minute. One client may now run 30 searches a minute that reach GitHub — an answer the cache already holds is free — and anything past that gets the existing "GitHub is asking us to slow down" screen with its retry, unchanged. The threshold is set where no visitor can reach it: sustained, it is one distinct handle typed every two seconds for a full minute, where clicking every recent-search shortcut you have stored produces five. Counting is per client rather than app-wide on purpose, so a busy day cannot turn the limit on ordinary visitors. What is kept about a client is a salted hash of its address and the times of its searches in the last minute, dropped once it goes quiet; no address is stored, no username reaches the limiter at all, and the two are never held together. Like the cache, the count lives in one server instance's memory and resets on a cold start, so it makes abuse cost something rather than imposing a global ceiling — the production runbook says so plainly, and says where a real one would have to be configured.
CHANGELOG.md-60-- Concurrent searches for the same username now share one request to GitHub instead of each making their own. The existing cache only helps once a search has finished, so a link shared with a crowd previously multiplied into one upstream search per reader, all asking the identical question against a single shared token quota. The saving is per running instance, like the cache.
CHANGELOG.md-61-- Recent searches loaded from the browser are now sanitized before they are shown. In a corrupt stored list — hand-edited, or written by something other than this app — blank and whitespace-only entries rendered as a bare `@` shortcut that searched for nothing, values kept their surrounding whitespace, and the same handle in different capitalization appeared as two separate shortcuts. Entries are now trimmed, validated, and collapsed case-insensitively, and a corrupt list still shows the full five shortcuts a visitor has earned rather than letting junk consume the slots.

It now reads only the collection array, and only the one belonging to the test configuration, so a coverage block can be scoped properly while a widened test scope still fails. A success now carries at least one commit in the type itself, a failure always carries both an error and its kind, and reading the wrong variant's fields fails to compile instead of failing a runtime check somebody remembered to write. A pull request must be up to date with `main` before it can merge, so the required check has actually run against the code that will land rather than against an older base; review conversations must be resolved; and linear history is required, which squash merging already produced. Approving reviews stay at zero, matching the documented policy that a pull request with no assigned reviewer may be self-merged. All of it applies to administrators too. The practical cost is on parallel work: merging one of two open pull requests puts the other behind, and it needs its branch updated and CI rerun before it can merge in turn.

CHANGELOG.md-90-- The gate now fails when a workflow that runs the browser suite installs fewer browsers than the Playwright configuration declares projects for. Two workflows each kept their own hand-written install list, and nothing tied them to the config, so adding the WebKit project updated one and not the other — a gap that could only appear after a production deploy, because the workflow it broke runs on a deployment event and no local command reaches it. The check resolves each project to the engine it actually runs on rather than to its name, since a mobile project is Chromium-backed, and it refuses to read a project it does not understand instead of quietly assuming that project needs nothing.

CHANGELOG.md-92-- The `app/` directory now holds route files and nothing else. It had grown to 23 files of which 15 were not routes — the server action, the cache, the logger, the type definitions and the rest sat at the same level as `page.tsx` and `layout.tsx`, so listing the directory that defines what the app serves mostly showed things it does not serve. Every directory under `app/` claims a URL segment, so a folder holding internals was one file away from becoming a public route at `/home`, with nothing in its name to say it should not be. The root layout fetched Geist and Geist Mono at build time, but the Tailwind font tokens have always defined system stacks and nothing ever referenced the `--font-geist-*` variables the layout generated, so no text was rendered in Geist — a visitor's browser only preloaded two font files it never used. CHANGELOG.md-98-- Label synchronization now decides what to do in tested code. `scripts/sync-labels.mjs` had grown to mix validating `.github/labels.yml`, planning creates and updates, and deleting labels, with only the offline file check covered in CI — so the destructive branch was the least tested part of it. Validation, planning, reporting, and applying now live in `scripts/label-plan.mjs` as pure functions over plain data, unit tested without a token or a network: that a deletion is planned only with `--prune`, that a dry run previews exactly the deletions a real run would make and writes nothing, that an unquoted colour like `123456` is caught while `e10c02` passes through as the string it stays, and that what reaches the GitHub API is what the plan validated. The script itself is unchanged in behaviour and still the only entry point; `npm run check:labels` still validates the file offline on every pull request.
CHANGELOG.md:99:- The unit test run now collects from `app/`, `components/`, and `scripts/` instead of skipping directories one at a time. A scratch spec left at the repository root, or in any directory the exclude list had not been taught about, used to join `npm test` and fail the gate with a Playwright error that pointed at the tooling rather than at the stray file. Nothing outside those three roots is a unit test now, so such a file neither breaks the run nor quietly joins it, and the verification exemption for the external tooling-state directories no longer depends on a denylist keeping pace with every directory a tool might create. `npm run check:agent-docs` still fails if the ignore lists drift apart, and now also if the collection scope widens.
CHANGELOG.md-100-- The agent workflow now covers changes that replace an existing contract. Test-driven development assumed new behavior, where one new failing test is enough to drive the work; when a change instead replaces something, the suite already holds assertions on the behavior being removed, and those stay green while the new test goes red and then green, so the loop looks finished with the contradiction still in the tree. Agents now locate and update those assertions inside the same red/green loop instead of letting the full validation gate find them a cycle later. Agents that cannot invoke the review sub-agents must also say so on reaching the review steps rather than in the final report, since the fallback has one agent review its own change and reporting it at the end surfaces that only once the work has already been reviewed that way.
CHANGELOG.md:101:- The browser suite now also refuses a stale server of this application. Confirming that the port held the right app was not enough: a server left behind by an interrupted run answered that check perfectly, and if it had been started without the fixture mocks every reserved test username went to real GitHub, so nearly every spec failed for a reason that had nothing to do with the branch — the same misleading wall of failures the original check was built to remove. A second preflight probe now asks the server whether it was started for this suite and stops the run naming the missing flag when it was not; a server too old to answer that question is rejected the same way. That probe is a route of its own, reporting one boolean and returning `404` on any built or deployed server, so nothing about test configuration was added to the public health endpoint. Neither probe can tell which branch a server is running, which remains a reason to prefer letting the suite start its own.
CHANGELOG.md:102:- The browser suite now refuses to run against a foreign server. Playwright reused any server that answered on its port, so an unrelated application left running there was adopted silently and every spec failed as though the branch were broken. A preflight check asks `/api/health` whether the port holds this application and stops the run with one clear error when it does not, naming the port and what it found. The other process is never stopped, since the port may belong to another checkout or another person's work. The port is now settable with `E2E_PORT`, and the worker count is fixed rather than derived from the machine so a run behaves the same everywhere; both overrides reject an unusable value instead of falling back silently. CI keeps the concurrency it already had.
CHANGELOG.md-103-- `.editorconfig` now carries a `max_line_length` matching Prettier's `printWidth`, so editors show the same wrap column the formatter uses. Markdown opts out, because prose here is hand-wrapped and Prettier does not format it.
CHANGELOG.md-104-- One command now runs the validation gate. `npm run validate` chains the dependency audit, unit tests, browser checks, lint, formatting, agent-document and label checks, and the production build, stopping at the first failure. The `CI / validate` job runs that same script instead of listing the steps itself, so the local gate and the CI gate are the same definition rather than two lists that drift. `npm run check:agent-docs` now also fails if CI stops invoking the script, or if the copies of the list in the development guide or the `verifier` sub-agent definition stop matching it, and the parsing behind that check is unit tested. Those two are now the only places the chain is written out in order.
CHANGELOG.md-105-- Local Entire checkpoint hooks now match Claude Code's current tool names, including the newer task tools, so the configuration no longer depends on Claude Code's legacy alias map.

CHANGELOG.md-108-- The agent workflow now bounds its review loop: findings can be explicitly resolved with a stated reason, and a finding that survives two fix-and-re-review cycles stops for a human instead of looping. CHANGELOG.md-110-- The `ui-review` sub-agent now enumerates untracked files with `--untracked-files=all`, so a brand-new component directory can no longer be mistaken for a change with no user-visible surface.

The agent-facing files keep deliberate inline copies. docs/development.md:139:Before any spec runs, a global setup asks `/api/health` on that port whether it is this application. The run now stops with one error naming the port and what was found there — a different service, an unexpected status, an unreadable response, a dropped connection, or silence.

60-## Deployment Flow
61-
62-1. Merge a green PR into `main`.

65-4. GitHub receives a production `deployment_status` event.

71-### Skipped Promotions Are Normal
72-
73-When two merges land close together, both queue a promotion. The older one runs after `main` has
74-already advanced, so its commit is no longer the deployed production commit. That run logs:
75-
76-```text
77-main has advanced to <sha>.
78-<older-sha> is no longer the deployed production commit; skipping its release.
79-```
80-
81-This is expected. The superseded commit intentionally gets no tag and no release, because the newer
82-commit is promoted in its place. Gaps in the deployment tag sequence are normal for the same reason.
83-
84-Before this guard existed, the older promotion instead failed while pushing its tag, because
85-`GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot push a ref whose workflow files no longer match `main`:
86-
87-```text
88-refusing to allow a GitHub App to create or update workflow `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
89-without `workflows` permission
90-```
91-
92-A promotion that fails for any other reason is a real failure and should be investigated.

94-### Promotion Waits For CI
95-
96-Vercel deploys in parallel with `CI / validate`, so a deployment and its health check can finish
97-before CI concludes on `main`. The promotion waits up to 15 minutes for the deployed commit's CI run
98-to reach a conclusion, logging one line per poll:
99-
100-```text
101-CI run for <sha> is in_progress; waiting for it to finish.
102-```
103-
104-Waiting is normal. A promotion fails only when CI concludes with something other than success, or

108-
109-See the [release guide](release.md). It owns the before-and-after-release checklist, moving

113:## The Release Invariant
114-
115-**A release tag names a commit that was proven healthy in production, not a commit that merely
116-merged and then something healthy was observed.** Two checks hold that up, and both exist because
117-the obvious version of each answers a subtly different question.
118-
119-**The health run proves which commit it tested.** It points Playwright at a mutable alias, so a
120-green suite on its own means something healthy was serving that URL — not that the commit which
121-triggered the run was serving it. Before any spec runs,
122-`scripts/verify-deployed-commit.mjs` asks `/api/health` what commit is live and compares it to the
123-deployment's SHA. A deployment still in flight, or a failed one leaving the previous build live,
124-now fails here in seconds rather than producing a wall of results describing code that is not
125-deployed. The payload carries an abbreviated seven-character SHA, so the comparison is by prefix; a
126-run reporting `local` is refused, because that is what the route returns when
127-`VERCEL_GIT_COMMIT_SHA` is unset and it identifies no deployment at all.
128-
129-Manual runs pass no expected SHA, since a URL given by hand has no commit to expect, and the step
130-is skipped.
131-
132-**Promotion asks which commit is live, not which is newest.** The superseded guard resolves the
133-active deployment through the deployments API — the most recent one whose latest status is
134-`success` — rather than comparing against the tip of `main`. Those are different questions: `main`
135-advances at merge, while a deployment becomes live later and may never. Comparing against the tip
136-meant a newer commit still deploying, or one that failed, suppressed the release of the commit
137-genuinely in production, and that release was never cut at all. When no successful deployment can
138-be found, the guard stops rather than guessing.
139-
140-Superseded deployments are still skipped, for the reason they always were: two deployments landing
141-close together queue two promotions, and the older one cannot push its tag once its workflow files
142-no longer match `main`.
143-
144-To check the invariant by hand:
145-
146-```bash
147-curl -s https://my-first-commit-eta.vercel.app/api/health | jq -r .commit
148-GITHUB_TOKEN=$(gh auth token) node scripts/resolve-active-deployment.mjs \
149-  scottdensmore/my-first-commit Production
150-```
151-
152-The first prints an abbreviated SHA and the second a full one. They must agree; if they do not,
153-the alias and the deployment record disagree about what is live, and no release should be cut until
154-they do.

271-### Structured Logs
272-
273-GitHub API failures are logged with structured event names:
274-
275:- `github_commit_search_rate_limited`
276-- `github_commit_search_timeout`
277-- `github_commit_search_unavailable`
278-- `github_commit_search_failed`

283:`commit_search_rate_limited_client` is this app refusing a search, not GitHub refusing one. See
284:[Bounding Search Bursts](#bounding-search-bursts). It carries the `limit` and `windowMs` in force
285-and nothing that identifies the client or the search, so the event counts refusals and cannot be
286-used to trace one. A steady trickle is ordinary internet background noise; a sustained rise means
287-one or more clients are searching far faster than a person can, on at least one instance.
288-
289-`github_commit_search_incomplete` is not a failure. GitHub returned `incomplete_results`, meaning it

292-visitors are seeing partial results rather than that searches are erroring. An `itemCount` of `0`
293-means the search returned nothing and the visitor saw the unfinished-search state instead.
294-
295-Useful fields include:
296-
297-- `status`
298-- `errorKind`
299-- `rateLimitRemaining`
300-- `rateLimitReset`
301-- `itemIndex`
302-- `itemCount`

308-## Bounding Search Bursts
309-
310-GitHub's Search API allows **30 requests per minute** for an authenticated token, and 10 per minute
311-unauthenticated. That is the real ceiling every visitor shares, and one script asking for thousands
312-of distinct usernames can spend it in seconds: each one is a cache miss and a coalescer miss, so
313-each one reaches GitHub.
314-
315-The app bounds this per client, in `app/_lib/commitSearchRateLimit.ts`: **30 searches per rolling
316-60 seconds**, counted only for searches that would reach GitHub, with anything past that answered
317:by the existing rate-limit screen.
318-
319-### Read This As A Cost, Not A Quota
320-
321-The window is a `Map` in one server instance, exactly like the commit cache and the in-flight map.
322-So:
323-
324:- The limit is 30 per client **per instance**. Vercel scales instances with load, so the app-wide
325-  effect is 30 x however many instances are running.
326:- A cold start resets it. A burst spread across cold starts is barely limited at all.
327-- It therefore **cannot** defend the shared 30/minute GitHub ceiling and must not be described as
328-  if it does. What actually removes upstream calls is the cache and the request coalescing: a
329-  repeated username costs nothing, and concurrent readers of one shared link cost one search.
330-
331-What it does buy is that abuse stops being free. A single client cannot walk a username list at
332-machine speed through one instance, and the traffic that gets through is shaped like traffic from
333-many separate clients rather than one.
334-
335:A real global ceiling is platform configuration, not code — a Vercel Firewall rate-limit rule on
336:the app, keyed by IP, the same lever the [CSP report section](#rate-limiting-csp-reports)
337-describes. Nothing in this repository configures or reads it. If one is added, note it here.
338-
339-### Why 30 A Minute
340-
341-A person types a distinct valid GitHub handle every few seconds at the very fastest, and a visitor
342-clicking every recent-search shortcut they have stored produces five requests and then stops to
343-read. Thirty a minute, sustained, is one every two seconds for a full minute; no visitor reaches
344-it, so the threshold does not need traffic data to justify and lowering it would only start
345-catching people. It is also the documented authenticated search ceiling, so a client past it is by
346-itself capable of spending the whole shared per-minute allowance.
347-
348-A visitor who somehow does reach it sees the ordinary "GitHub is asking us to slow down" screen
349:with its retry, and is under the limit again within a minute.
350-
351-### What Is Held In Memory, And For How Long
352-
353-Per client, until the client has been quiet for longer than the window:
354-
355-- A salted SHA-256 hash of the forwarded client address.
356-- The timestamps of that client's searches inside the current 60-second window, at most 30 of them.
357-
358:Nothing else. The searched username never reaches the limiter — it is handed an opaque key — so no
359-username is stored, logged, or associated with a client anywhere in this path. The salt is 32
360-random bytes generated per process and never persisted.
361-
362-A memory dump of a running instance would show the salt, those hashes, and those timestamps. With
363-the salt in hand, an investigator could confirm whether an address they already suspected was
364:among the clients active in the last minute; they could not read the addresses out, correlate them
365-with another instance or with the same instance before a restart, or learn anything at all about
366-what was searched.
367-
368-### The Forwarded Header Is Untrusted Input
369-
370-The client key comes from `x-vercel-forwarded-for`, falling back to `x-forwarded-for`. Vercel sets
371-both itself and overwrites `x-forwarded-for` from the connecting socket precisely so it cannot be
372-spoofed, so on this deployment neither is attacker-controlled. `x-vercel-forwarded-for` is
373-preferred because it is the one a proxy placed in front of Vercel could not overwrite either.
374-
375-Behind some other proxy that forwards a client's header verbatim, a spoofer could:
376-
377-- **Split their own traffic** across many fabricated addresses and get a fresh allowance for each.
378:  This weakens the limit to the cost of forging headers. It cannot exhaust memory: idle clients are
379-  dropped and the map is capped, and eviction under a flood only ever *forgets* a client, which
380-  refills an allowance rather than refusing anyone.
381-- **Spend another client's allowance** by sending that client's address, refusing them for up to
382:  one window. The blast radius is one minute, one instance, and one address the attacker had to
383-  know already; nothing is revealed to them, and nothing persists.
384-
385-They cannot learn who else has searched, what anyone searched for, or read any stored key back.

387-## Security Headers
388-
389-The app sets baseline security headers from `next.config.ts`:
390-
391-- `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`
392-- `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin`
393-- `Permissions-Policy` disabling camera, microphone, geolocation, and payment APIs
394-- `X-Frame-Options: DENY`
395-- `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` for CSP tuning without blocking production traffic
396-
397-Content Security Policy is currently report-only. Review Vercel logs before moving from report-only to enforcement.
398-
399-### CSP Violation Reports
400-
401-The policy names a reporting destination through both `report-uri` and `report-to`, backed by the
402-`Reporting-Endpoints` header. Browsers post violations to `/api/csp-report`, which logs them as
403-structured `csp_violation` events. Without this, a report-only policy is unobservable: violations
404-reach each visitor's browser console and nowhere else.
405-
406-Find them in Vercel Logs by searching for:
407-
408-```text
409-csp_violation
410-```
411-
412-Logged fields:
413-
414-- `documentUri`
415-- `blockedUri`
416-- `effectiveDirective`
417-- `disposition`
418-- `statusCode`
419-- `sourceFile`
420-- `lineNumber`
421-- `columnNumber`
422-
423-`http:` and `https:` URLs are reduced to origin and path. Query strings are dropped because the app
424-puts the searched username in `?user=`, and search usernames must not reach logs. Every other scheme
425-is reduced to the scheme alone — `data:`, `blob:`, and `javascript:` carry their payload inline, and
426-`mailto:` or an app-specific scheme registered by an extension carries an address or a path there —
427-so `data:` and `my-app:` are logged with nothing after the colon. The reported `original-policy` and
428:`script-sample` are never read at all: the policy is long and already known, and the sample can
429-contain page content or user input.
430-
431-The endpoint is unauthenticated, so its intake is bounded three ways:
432-
433-- **Content type.** Only `application/csp-report` (from `report-uri`) and `application/reports+json`
434-  (from the Reporting API) are read. Anything else is answered `415` without the body being touched.
435-- **Body size.** 16 KB, counted in bytes rather than characters, and enforced as the body arrives: an
436-  oversized `Content-Length` is refused before a byte is read, and because that header can be absent
437:  or untrue the stream is counted while it is consumed and cancelled the moment the limit is passed.
438-  Oversized bodies are answered `413`.
439-- **Reports per request.** At most **10** violations are logged from one POST. A Reporting API array
440-  is a batch, so without a cap a single request could turn into a log record per entry. The overflow
441-  is counted in one `csp_report_truncated` event carrying `received` and `logged`.
442-
443-Other events from the same endpoint indicate a malformed or hostile POST rather than a real
444-violation: `csp_report_malformed`, `csp_report_empty`, `csp_report_too_large`,
445-`csp_report_unsupported_type`, `csp_report_truncated`, and `csp_report_unreadable`.
446-
447-### Rate Limiting CSP Reports
448-
449-The bounds above cap what one request can cost. They do not cap how many requests arrive, and this
450-repository has no place to fix that: the app runs as serverless functions with no shared state, so
451:per-instance counting would not hold across instances. Rate limiting or sampling for
452-`/api/csp-report` is platform configuration, applied in the Vercel project rather than in code.
453-
454-If `csp_violation` or `csp_report_*` volume becomes noisy or expensive:
455-
456:1. Add a Vercel Firewall rate-limit rule scoped to the `/api/csp-report` path, keyed by IP.
457-2. If real traffic alone is the volume, lower the sampling instead — CSP supports it through the
458-   Reporting API endpoint configuration, and a report-only policy does not need every duplicate.
459-3. Re-check the log volume after either change before tightening further.
460-
461-None of this is in the repository, and nothing in the app reads it. Treat a change here as an
462-account-level operational change, and note it in this runbook when it is made.
463-
464-### Moving CSP To Enforcement
465-
466-Do not simply rename the header. `script-src` currently allows `'unsafe-inline'` and `'unsafe-eval'`,
467-so enforcing the policy as written would activate `frame-ancestors`, `base-uri`, `form-action`, and
468-`default-src` without blocking injected inline script, which is the main thing CSP defends against.
469-
470-The intended order is:
471-
472-1. Collect `csp_violation` events from real traffic in preview and production.
473-2. Tighten the policy against what actually fires.
474-3. Replace `'unsafe-inline'` and `'unsafe-eval'` in `script-src` with per-request nonces, which
475-   requires middleware and can break the Next.js inline bootstrap and Vercel Analytics.
476-4. Only then rename the header to `Content-Security-Policy`.

71-### Skipped Promotions Are Normal
72-
73-When two merges land close together, both queue a promotion. The older one runs after `main` has
74-already advanced, so its commit is no longer the deployed production commit. That run logs:
75-
76-```text
77-main has advanced to <sha>.
78-<older-sha> is no longer the deployed production commit; skipping its release.
79-```
80-
81-This is expected. The superseded commit intentionally gets no tag and no release, because the newer
82-commit is promoted in its place. Gaps in the deployment tag sequence are normal for the same reason.
83-
84-Before this guard existed, the older promotion instead failed while pushing its tag, because
85-`GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot push a ref whose workflow files no longer match `main`:
86-
87-```text
88-refusing to allow a GitHub App to create or update workflow `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
89-without `workflows` permission
90-```
91-
92-A promotion that fails for any other reason is a real failure and should be investigated.

94-### Promotion Waits For CI
95-
96-Vercel deploys in parallel with `CI / validate`, so a deployment and its health check can finish
97-before CI concludes on `main`. The promotion waits up to 15 minutes for the deployed commit's CI run
98-to reach a conclusion, logging one line per poll:
99-
100-```text
101-CI run for <sha> is in_progress; waiting for it to finish.
102-```
103-
104-Waiting is normal. A promotion fails only when CI concludes with something other than success, or
105-when no CI run reaches a conclusion inside the timeout.

113:## The Release Invariant
114-
115-**A release tag names a commit that was proven healthy in production, not a commit that merely
116-merged and then something healthy was observed.** Two checks hold that up, and both exist because
117-the obvious version of each answers a subtly different question.
118-
119-**The health run proves which commit it tested.** It points Playwright at a mutable alias, so a
120-green suite on its own means something healthy was serving that URL — not that the commit which
121-triggered the run was serving it. Before any spec runs,
122-`scripts/verify-deployed-commit.mjs` asks `/api/health` what commit is live and compares it to the
123-deployment's SHA. A deployment still in flight, or a failed one leaving the previous build live,
124-now fails here in seconds rather than producing a wall of results describing code that is not
125-deployed. The payload carries an abbreviated seven-character SHA, so the comparison is by prefix; a
126-run reporting `local` is refused, because that is what the route returns when
127-`VERCEL_GIT_COMMIT_SHA` is unset and it identifies no deployment at all.
128-
129-Manual runs pass no expected SHA, since a URL given by hand has no commit to expect, and the step
130-is skipped.
131-
132-**Promotion asks which commit is live, not which is newest.** The superseded guard resolves the
133-active deployment through the deployments API — the most recent one whose latest status is
134-`success` — rather than comparing against the tip of `main`. Those are different questions: `main`
135-advances at merge, while a deployment becomes live later and may never. Comparing against the tip
136-meant a newer commit still deploying, or one that failed, suppressed the release of the commit
137-genuinely in production, and that release was never cut at all. When no successful deployment can
138-be found, the guard stops rather than guessing.
139-
140-Superseded deployments are still skipped, for the reason they always were: two deployments landing
141-close together queue two promotions, and the older one cannot push its tag once its workflow files
142-no longer match `main`.
143-
144-To check the invariant by hand:
145-
146-```bash
147-curl -s https://my-first-commit-eta.vercel.app/api/health | jq -r .commit
148-GITHUB_TOKEN=$(gh auth token) node scripts/resolve-active-deployment.mjs \
149-  scottdensmore/my-first-commit Production
150-```
151-
152-The first prints an abbreviated SHA and the second a full one. They must agree; if they do not,
153-the alias and the deployment record disagree about what is live, and no release should be cut until
154-they do.

308-## Bounding Search Bursts
309-
310-GitHub's Search API allows **30 requests per minute** for an authenticated token, and 10 per minute
311-unauthenticated. That is the real ceiling every visitor shares, and one script asking for thousands
312-of distinct usernames can spend it in seconds: each one is a cache miss and a coalescer miss, so
313-each one reaches GitHub.
314-
315-The app bounds this per client, in `app/_lib/commitSearchRateLimit.ts`: **30 searches per rolling
316-60 seconds**, counted only for searches that would reach GitHub, with anything past that answered
317:by the existing rate-limit screen.
318-
319-### Read This As A Cost, Not A Quota
320-
321-The window is a `Map` in one server instance, exactly like the commit cache and the in-flight map.
322-So:
323-
324:- The limit is 30 per client **per instance**. Vercel scales instances with load, so the app-wide
325-  effect is 30 x however many instances are running.
326:- A cold start resets it. A burst spread across cold starts is barely limited at all.
327-- It therefore **cannot** defend the shared 30/minute GitHub ceiling and must not be described as
328-  if it does. What actually removes upstream calls is the cache and the request coalescing: a
329-  repeated username costs nothing, and concurrent readers of one shared link cost one search.
330-
331-What it does buy is that abuse stops being free. A single client cannot walk a username list at
332-machine speed through one instance, and the traffic that gets through is shaped like traffic from
333-many separate clients rather than one.
334-
335:A real global ceiling is platform configuration, not code — a Vercel Firewall rate-limit rule on
336:the app, keyed by IP, the same lever the [CSP report section](#rate-limiting-csp-reports)
337-describes. Nothing in this repository configures or reads it. If one is added, note it here.
338-
339-### Why 30 A Minute
340-
341-A person types a distinct valid GitHub handle every few seconds at the very fastest, and a visitor
342-clicking every recent-search shortcut they have stored produces five requests and then stops to
343-read. Thirty a minute, sustained, is one every two seconds for a full minute; no visitor reaches
344-it, so the threshold does not need traffic data to justify and lowering it would only start
345-catching people. It is also the documented authenticated search ceiling, so a client past it is by
346-itself capable of spending the whole shared per-minute allowance.
347-
348-A visitor who somehow does reach it sees the ordinary "GitHub is asking us to slow down" screen
349:with its retry, and is under the limit again within a minute.
350-
351-### What Is Held In Memory, And For How Long
352-
353-Per client, until the client has been quiet for longer than the window:
354-
355-- A salted SHA-256 hash of the forwarded client address.
356-- The timestamps of that client's searches inside the current 60-second window, at most 30 of them.
357-
358:Nothing else. The searched username never reaches the limiter — it is handed an opaque key — so no
359-username is stored, logged, or associated with a client anywhere in this path. The salt is 32
360-random bytes generated per process and never persisted.
361-
362-A memory dump of a running instance would show the salt, those hashes, and those timestamps. With
363-the salt in hand, an investigator could confirm whether an address they already suspected was
364:among the clients active in the last minute; they could not read the addresses out, correlate them
365-with another instance or with the same instance before a restart, or learn anything at all about
366-what was searched.
367-
368-### The Forwarded Header Is Untrusted Input
369-
370-The client key comes from `x-vercel-forwarded-for`, falling back to `x-forwarded-for`. Vercel sets
371-both itself and overwrites `x-forwarded-for` from the connecting socket precisely so it cannot be
372-spoofed, so on this deployment neither is attacker-controlled. `x-vercel-forwarded-for` is
373-preferred because it is the one a proxy placed in front of Vercel could not overwrite either.
374-
375-Behind some other proxy that forwards a client's header verbatim, a spoofer could:
376-
377-- **Split their own traffic** across many fabricated addresses and get a fresh allowance for each.
378:  This weakens the limit to the cost of forging headers. It cannot exhaust memory: idle clients are
379-  dropped and the map is capped, and eviction under a flood only ever *forgets* a client, which
380-  refills an allowance rather than refusing anyone.
381-- **Spend another client's allowance** by sending that client's address, refusing them for up to
382:  one window. The blast radius is one minute, one instance, and one address the attacker had to
383-  know already; nothing is revealed to them, and nothing persists.
384-
385-They cannot learn who else has searched, what anyone searched for, or read any stored key back.

399-### CSP Violation Reports
400-
401-The policy names a reporting destination through both `report-uri` and `report-to`, backed by the
402-`Reporting-Endpoints` header. Browsers post violations to `/api/csp-report`, which logs them as
403-structured `csp_violation` events. Without this, a report-only policy is unobservable: violations
404-reach each visitor's browser console and nowhere else.
405-
406-Find them in Vercel Logs by searching for:
407-
408-```text
409-csp_violation
410-```
411-
412-Logged fields:
413-
414-- `documentUri`
415-- `blockedUri`
416-- `effectiveDirective`
417-- `disposition`
418-- `statusCode`
419-- `sourceFile`
420-- `lineNumber`
421-- `columnNumber`
422-
423-`http:` and `https:` URLs are reduced to origin and path. Query strings are dropped because the app
424-puts the searched username in `?user=`, and search usernames must not reach logs. Every other scheme
425-is reduced to the scheme alone — `data:`, `blob:`, and `javascript:` carry their payload inline, and
426-`mailto:` or an app-specific scheme registered by an extension carries an address or a path there —
427-so `data:` and `my-app:` are logged with nothing after the colon. The reported `original-policy` and
428:`script-sample` are never read at all: the policy is long and already known, and the sample can
429-contain page content or user input.
430-
431-The endpoint is unauthenticated, so its intake is bounded three ways:
432-
433-- **Content type.** Only `application/csp-report` (from `report-uri`) and `application/reports+json`
434-  (from the Reporting API) are read. Anything else is answered `415` without the body being touched.
435-- **Body size.** 16 KB, counted in bytes rather than characters, and enforced as the body arrives: an
436-  oversized `Content-Length` is refused before a byte is read, and because that header can be absent
437:  or untrue the stream is counted while it is consumed and cancelled the moment the limit is passed.
438-  Oversized bodies are answered `413`.
439-- **Reports per request.** At most **10** violations are logged from one POST. A Reporting API array
440-  is a batch, so without a cap a single request could turn into a log record per entry. The overflow
441-  is counted in one `csp_report_truncated` event carrying `received` and `logged`.
442-
443-Other events from the same endpoint indicate a malformed or hostile POST rather than a real
444-violation: `csp_report_malformed`, `csp_report_empty`, `csp_report_too_large`,
445-`csp_report_unsupported_type`, `csp_report_truncated`, and `csp_report_unreadable`.
446-
447-### Rate Limiting CSP Reports
448-
449-The bounds above cap what one request can cost. They do not cap how many requests arrive, and this
450-repository has no place to fix that: the app runs as serverless functions with no shared state, so
451:per-instance counting would not hold across instances. Rate limiting or sampling for
452-`/api/csp-report` is platform configuration, applied in the Vercel project rather than in code.
453-
454-If `csp_violation` or `csp_report_*` volume becomes noisy or expensive:
455-
456:1. Add a Vercel Firewall rate-limit rule scoped to the `/api/csp-report` path, keyed by IP.
457-2. If real traffic alone is the volume, lower the sampling instead — CSP supports it through the
458-   Reporting API endpoint configuration, and a report-only policy does not need every duplicate.
459-3. Re-check the log volume after either change before tightening further.
460-
461-None of this is in the repository, and nothing in the app reads it. Treat a change here as an
462-account-level operational change, and note it in this runbook when it is made.
463-
464-### Moving CSP To Enforcement
465-
466-Do not simply rename the header. `script-src` currently allows `'unsafe-inline'` and `'unsafe-eval'`,
467-so enforcing the policy as written would activate `frame-ancestors`, `base-uri`, `form-action`, and
468-`default-src` without blocking injected inline script, which is the main thing CSP defends against.
469-
470-The intended order is:
471-
472-1. Collect `csp_violation` events from real traffic in preview and production.
473-2. Tighten the policy against what actually fires.
474-3. Replace `'unsafe-inline'` and `'unsafe-eval'` in `script-src` with per-request nonces, which
475-   requires middleware and can break the Next.js inline bootstrap and Vercel Analytics.
476-4. Only then rename the header to `Content-Security-Policy`.

61-
62-1. Merge a green PR into `main`.
63-2. GitHub Actions runs `CI / validate`.
64-3. Vercel builds and deploys production.
65-4. GitHub receives a production `deployment_status` event.
66-5. The `Production Health Check` workflow runs Playwright against `PRODUCTION_BASE_URL`.

71-### Skipped Promotions Are Normal
72-
73-When two merges land close together, both queue a promotion. The older one runs after `main` has
74-already advanced, so its commit is no longer the deployed production commit. That run logs:
75-
76-```text
77-main has advanced to <sha>.
78-<older-sha> is no longer the deployed production commit; skipping its release.
79-```
80-
81-This is expected. The superseded commit intentionally gets no tag and no release, because the newer
82-commit is promoted in its place. Gaps in the deployment tag sequence are normal for the same reason.
83-
84-Before this guard existed, the older promotion instead failed while pushing its tag, because
85-`GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot push a ref whose workflow files no longer match `main`:
86-
87-```text
88-refusing to allow a GitHub App to create or update workflow `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
89-without `workflows` permission
90-```
91-
92-A promotion that fails for any other reason is a real failure and should be investigated.

94-### Promotion Waits For CI
95-
96-Vercel deploys in parallel with `CI / validate`, so a deployment and its health check can finish
97-before CI concludes on `main`. The promotion waits up to 15 minutes for the deployed commit's CI run
98-to reach a conclusion, logging one line per poll:
99-
100-```text
101-CI run for <sha> is in_progress; waiting for it to finish.
102-```
103-
104-Waiting is normal. A promotion fails only when CI concludes with something other than success, or
105-when no CI run reaches a conclusion inside the timeout.

113:## The Release Invariant
114-
115-**A release tag names a commit that was proven healthy in production, not a commit that merely
116-merged and then something healthy was observed.** Two checks hold that up, and both exist because
117-the obvious version of each answers a subtly different question.
118-
119-**The health run proves which commit it tested.** It points Playwright at a mutable alias, so a
120-green suite on its own means something healthy was serving that URL — not that the commit which
121-triggered the run was serving it. Before any spec runs,
122-`scripts/verify-deployed-commit.mjs` asks `/api/health` what commit is live and compares it to the
123-deployment's SHA. A deployment still in flight, or a failed one leaving the previous build live,
124-now fails here in seconds rather than producing a wall of results describing code that is not
125-deployed. The payload carries an abbreviated seven-character SHA, so the comparison is by prefix; a
126-run reporting `local` is refused, because that is what the route returns when
127-`VERCEL_GIT_COMMIT_SHA` is unset and it identifies no deployment at all.
128-
129-Manual runs pass no expected SHA, since a URL given by hand has no commit to expect, and the step
130-is skipped.
131-
132-**Promotion asks which commit is live, not which is newest.** The superseded guard resolves the
133-active deployment through the deployments API — the most recent one whose latest status is
134-`success` — rather than comparing against the tip of `main`. Those are different questions: `main`
135-advances at merge, while a deployment becomes live later and may never. Comparing against the tip
136-meant a newer commit still deploying, or one that failed, suppressed the release of the commit
137-genuinely in production, and that release was never cut at all. When no successful deployment can
138-be found, the guard stops rather than guessing.
139-
140-Superseded deployments are still skipped, for the reason they always were: two deployments landing
141-close together queue two promotions, and the older one cannot push its tag once its workflow files
142-no longer match `main`.
143-
144-To check the invariant by hand:
145-
146-```bash
147-curl -s https://my-first-commit-eta.vercel.app/api/health | jq -r .commit
148-GITHUB_TOKEN=$(gh auth token) node scripts/resolve-active-deployment.mjs \
149-  scottdensmore/my-first-commit Production
150-```
151-
152-The first prints an abbreviated SHA and the second a full one. They must agree; if they do not,
153-the alias and the deployment record disagree about what is live, and no release should be cut until
154-they do.

308-## Bounding Search Bursts
309-
310-GitHub's Search API allows **30 requests per minute** for an authenticated token, and 10 per minute
311-unauthenticated. That is the real ceiling every visitor shares, and one script asking for thousands
312-of distinct usernames can spend it in seconds: each one is a cache miss and a coalescer miss, so
313-each one reaches GitHub.
314-
315-The app bounds this per client, in `app/_lib/commitSearchRateLimit.ts`: **30 searches per rolling
316-60 seconds**, counted only for searches that would reach GitHub, with anything past that answered
317:by the existing rate-limit screen.
318-
319-### Read This As A Cost, Not A Quota
320-
321-The window is a `Map` in one server instance, exactly like the commit cache and the in-flight map.
322-So:
323-
324:- The limit is 30 per client **per instance**. Vercel scales instances with load, so the app-wide
325-  effect is 30 x however many instances are running.
326:- A cold start resets it. A burst spread across cold starts is barely limited at all.
327-- It therefore **cannot** defend the shared 30/minute GitHub ceiling and must not be described as
328-  if it does. What actually removes upstream calls is the cache and the request coalescing: a
329-  repeated username costs nothing, and concurrent readers of one shared link cost one search.
330-
331-What it does buy is that abuse stops being free. A single client cannot walk a username list at
332-machine speed through one instance, and the traffic that gets through is shaped like traffic from
333-many separate clients rather than one.
334-
335:A real global ceiling is platform configuration, not code — a Vercel Firewall rate-limit rule on
336:the app, keyed by IP, the same lever the [CSP report section](#rate-limiting-csp-reports)
337-describes. Nothing in this repository configures or reads it. If one is added, note it here.
338-
339-### Why 30 A Minute
340-
341-A person types a distinct valid GitHub handle every few seconds at the very fastest, and a visitor
342-clicking every recent-search shortcut they have stored produces five requests and then stops to
343-read. Thirty a minute, sustained, is one every two seconds for a full minute; no visitor reaches
344-it, so the threshold does not need traffic data to justify and lowering it would only start
345-catching people. It is also the documented authenticated search ceiling, so a client past it is by
346-itself capable of spending the whole shared per-minute allowance.
347-
348-A visitor who somehow does reach it sees the ordinary "GitHub is asking us to slow down" screen
349:with its retry, and is under the limit again within a minute.
350-
351-### What Is Held In Memory, And For How Long
352-
353-Per client, until the client has been quiet for longer than the window:
354-
355-- A salted SHA-256 hash of the forwarded client address.
356-- The timestamps of that client's searches inside the current 60-second window, at most 30 of them.
357-
358:Nothing else. The searched username never reaches the limiter — it is handed an opaque key — so no
359-username is stored, logged, or associated with a client anywhere in this path. The salt is 32
360-random bytes generated per process and never persisted.
361-
362-A memory dump of a running instance would show the salt, those hashes, and those timestamps. With
363-the salt in hand, an investigator could confirm whether an address they already suspected was
364:among the clients active in the last minute; they could not read the addresses out, correlate them
365-with another instance or with the same instance before a restart, or learn anything at all about
366-what was searched.
367-
368-### The Forwarded Header Is Untrusted Input
369-
370-The client key comes from `x-vercel-forwarded-for`, falling back to `x-forwarded-for`. Vercel sets
371-both itself and overwrites `x-forwarded-for` from the connecting socket precisely so it cannot be
372-spoofed, so on this deployment neither is attacker-controlled. `x-vercel-forwarded-for` is
373-preferred because it is the one a proxy placed in front of Vercel could not overwrite either.
374-
375-Behind some other proxy that forwards a client's header verbatim, a spoofer could:
376-
377-- **Split their own traffic** across many fabricated addresses and get a fresh allowance for each.
378:  This weakens the limit to the cost of forging headers. It cannot exhaust memory: idle clients are
379-  dropped and the map is capped, and eviction under a flood only ever *forgets* a client, which
380-  refills an allowance rather than refusing anyone.
381-- **Spend another client's allowance** by sending that client's address, refusing them for up to
382:  one window. The blast radius is one minute, one instance, and one address the attacker had to
383-  know already; nothing is revealed to them, and nothing persists.
384-
385-They cannot learn who else has searched, what anyone searched for, or read any stored key back.

399-### CSP Violation Reports
400-
401-The policy names a reporting destination through both `report-uri` and `report-to`, backed by the
402-`Reporting-Endpoints` header. Browsers post violations to `/api/csp-report`, which logs them as
403-structured `csp_violation` events. Without this, a report-only policy is unobservable: violations
404-reach each visitor's browser console and nowhere else.
405-
406-Find them in Vercel Logs by searching for:
407-
408-```text
409-csp_violation
410-```
411-
412-Logged fields:
413-
414-- `documentUri`
415-- `blockedUri`
416-- `effectiveDirective`
417-- `disposition`
418-- `statusCode`
419-- `sourceFile`
420-- `lineNumber`
421-- `columnNumber`
422-
423-`http:` and `https:` URLs are reduced to origin and path. Query strings are dropped because the app
424-puts the searched username in `?user=`, and search usernames must not reach logs. Every other scheme
425-is reduced to the scheme alone — `data:`, `blob:`, and `javascript:` carry their payload inline, and
426-`mailto:` or an app-specific scheme registered by an extension carries an address or a path there —
427-so `data:` and `my-app:` are logged with nothing after the colon. The reported `original-policy` and
428:`script-sample` are never read at all: the policy is long and already known, and the sample can
429-contain page content or user input.
430-
431-The endpoint is unauthenticated, so its intake is bounded three ways:
432-
433-- **Content type.** Only `application/csp-report` (from `report-uri`) and `application/reports+json`
434-  (from the Reporting API) are read. Anything else is answered `415` without the body being touched.
435-- **Body size.** 16 KB, counted in bytes rather than characters, and enforced as the body arrives: an
436-  oversized `Content-Length` is refused before a byte is read, and because that header can be absent
437:  or untrue the stream is counted while it is consumed and cancelled the moment the limit is passed.
438-  Oversized bodies are answered `413`.
439-- **Reports per request.** At most **10** violations are logged from one POST. A Reporting API array
440-  is a batch, so without a cap a single request could turn into a log record per entry. The overflow
441-  is counted in one `csp_report_truncated` event carrying `received` and `logged`.
442-
443-Other events from the same endpoint indicate a malformed or hostile POST rather than a real
444-violation: `csp_report_malformed`, `csp_report_empty`, `csp_report_too_large`,
445-`csp_report_unsupported_type`, `csp_report_truncated`, and `csp_report_unreadable`.
446-
447-### Rate Limiting CSP Reports
448-
449-The bounds above cap what one request can cost. They do not cap how many requests arrive, and this
450-repository has no place to fix that: the app runs as serverless functions with no shared state, so
451:per-instance counting would not hold across instances. Rate limiting or sampling for
452-`/api/csp-report` is platform configuration, applied in the Vercel project rather than in code.
453-
454-If `csp_violation` or `csp_report_*` volume becomes noisy or expensive:
455-
456:1. Add a Vercel Firewall rate-limit rule scoped to the `/api/csp-report` path, keyed by IP.
457-2. If real traffic alone is the volume, lower the sampling instead — CSP supports it through the
458-   Reporting API endpoint configuration, and a report-only policy does not need every duplicate.
459-3. Re-check the log volume after either change before tightening further.
460-
461-None of this is in the repository, and nothing in the app reads it. Treat a change here as an
462-account-level operational change, and note it in this runbook when it is made.
463-
464-### Moving CSP To Enforcement
465-
466-Do not simply rename the header. `script-src` currently allows `'unsafe-inline'` and `'unsafe-eval'`,
467-so enforcing the policy as written would activate `frame-ancestors`, `base-uri`, `form-action`, and
468-`default-src` without blocking injected inline script, which is the main thing CSP defends against.
469-
470-The intended order is:
471-
472-1. Collect `csp_violation` events from real traffic in preview and production.
473-2. Tighten the policy against what actually fires.
474-3. Replace `'unsafe-inline'` and `'unsafe-eval'` in `script-src` with per-request nonces, which
475-   requires middleware and can break the Next.js inline bootstrap and Vercel Analytics.
476-4. Only then rename the header to `Content-Security-Policy`.
