# Changelog

All notable changes to My First Commit are documented here.

This project follows a lightweight, human-curated changelog. Keep the newest changes at the top and move items from `Unreleased` into a dated release section when cutting a release.

## Unreleased

### Added

- The production health check now performs one real commit search and asserts a commit renders, rather than only checking that the app responds. Every other search test uses fixtures, so a revoked token, a changed GitHub response, or a Server Action broken only in production could pass production health and be promoted to a release — `/api/health` reports that a token is present, never that it works. One search per deployment on one browser, because each one spends the shared GitHub quota the burst limiting exists to protect. A partial result from GitHub counts as a pass, since that is GitHub shedding load rather than a fault of this app; an empty result, an error state, or a heading with no commit does not.

- Unit test coverage is now measured, reported, and enforced. The gate's unit step runs with V8 coverage, so one command produces the numbers locally and in CI, and a text summary plus an HTML report in the ignored `coverage/` directory. The thresholds are a non-regression floor rather than a target: they were set a whole percent below a measurement of the suite as it stands — 93% statements, 89% branches, 98% functions, 94% lines against 93.68, 89.58, 98.30, and 94.66 — so a change that leaves new code untested fails the gate while a refactor does not fail on rounding. Coverage counts the files the suite loads, which means the floors cannot catch a module no test imports at all; the development guide says so rather than leaving the number to imply more than it measures.
- Two time-based contracts that nothing exercised are now tested on a fake clock, in milliseconds rather than in real waiting. The five-minute cache lifetime is pinned at both sides of its boundary — served one millisecond before the deadline, gone once it is reached — along with the rules about what may be cached: an empty result is stored so a handle with no public commits is not searched again, while a rate limit, timeout, outage, or any other failure never is, and a read inside the window refreshes eviction order without extending the lifetime. The ten-second search deadline is now proved by a request that hangs: it is still outstanding at 9,999 milliseconds and aborted at 10,000, where the previous test injected the abort itself and so could not tell a working timer from a missing one.

- Partial commit results now offer a **Search again** button in place. A retry that succeeds replaces the partial result, one that comes back partial again says so, and one that fails leaves the commits on screen and explains why instead of replacing them with an error screen. Each outcome is announced to assistive technology.

### Changed

- Every Entire CLI Codex hook now has up to 300 seconds to finish before Codex terminates it,
  increased from 30 seconds for larger sessions and checkpoint operations that need longer to
  finalize.

- The repository front door now leads with the live product, current build and release status, an
  accurate screenshot, a concise local quick start, and a compact guide to the rest of the
  documentation. Detailed capabilities, privacy boundaries, and GitHub search limitations moved to
  a dedicated product guide, and contributor recognition now links to GitHub's automatically
  maintained history instead of duplicating it in a hand-maintained file. The initial screenshot
  showed a profile-heavy interface the current app no longer renders; it has been replaced with the
  actual commit-results experience.

- Development dependencies updated: `eslint-config-next` to 16.3.1 and `@testing-library/user-event` to 14.6.4. The lint config is the half of the Next.js 16.3.1 release that governs linting, and is pinned to the same exact version as Next.js itself, so it moves with it rather than drifting a release behind. The testing library fixes the `repeat` property on synthesized keyboard events, which no test here reads. Neither package ships in the application, so nothing a visitor loads changed; `npm run lint` passes unchanged against the new config, which is the check a lint-config bump can actually break.

- Next.js updated from 16.3.0 to 16.3.1, a patch release of backported fixes. Two of them reach this app: `headers()` regains its live view of the incoming request, which is what the per-client search limit reads to identify a caller, and image optimization preserves the response it produced, which is how commit author avatars are served. The rest of the release covers Turbopack internals and features this app does not use — `'use cache'`, `unstable_cache`, middleware, i18n, and the Pages Router. The full validation suite passes on the new version, including the browser journeys that exercise both changed paths, and the version bump carried no unrelated lockfile churn: only Next.js itself, its platform build binaries, and its own transitive helpers moved.

- The agent instructions now describe the import convention the code actually follows. They said imports were "relative within a feature, aliased with `@/` only across a boundary", which matched neither half of the codebase: all 29 relative imports of a shared module cross out of their own folder, and the 3 aliased ones are exactly the route files under `app/api/`. What decides the form is depth, not the boundary crossed — a route file sits three levels down, where the relative path counts directories instead of naming anything and quietly means a different module if the route moves. The rule now says that, so it can be checked against the code rather than read as a principle nothing obeys.

- Analytics moved out of the homepage feature folder. `analytics.ts` sat in `app/_home/`, the directory for things only the homepage uses, while the root layout's analytics component imported it from outside — so every page load pulled a module out of the homepage feature to do something with no connection to searching for a commit. It now sits in `app/_lib/` with the other shared modules, which leaves `app/_home/` meaning what its name claims. The agent instructions gained the rule that decides this for the next module, and their layout list picked up the two files it had fallen behind on. Documentation and file locations only; no behaviour changed and the analytics events themselves are untouched.

### Removed

- Dropped the `clsx` and `tailwind-merge` dependencies, which nothing imported. Both are conventional in a Tailwind project and both arrived with the initial commit, but no revision since has ever imported either one: every component in this app composes `className` with a template literal, so neither package had a single call site in any version of this code. They shipped nothing, while each remained a package the audit gate had to keep clearing and Dependabot had to keep proposing upgrades for. Nothing else in the tree depended on them, so removing the two declarations removed them outright. No behaviour and no styling changed; a future need for conditional class composition can add one back deliberately.

- The structured logger can no longer be handed a raw error object. `logger.error` accepted an optional second argument of any type and passed it straight to `console.error`, which is the one thing this module exists to prevent — an Octokit error carries the request URL, and a commit-search URL carries the username being searched. No caller ever passed one, so nothing was being logged that should not have been; what is gone is the supported way to start. Callers already pull out the scalars they need, such as the status code and the error kind, and log those.

- Deleted two unreachable branches and nine unused design tokens. The share-text builder took a whole search result and carried a fallback for one with no commits, though its only caller reaches it from behind a `found` check that guarantees at least one — narrowing the parameter to the success type made the compiler reject the test that had been pinning the dead branch, and reject nothing else, which is what proved it unreachable rather than merely untested. Separately, the stylesheet mapped nine `--color-*` tokens into Tailwind's theme, generating utilities such as `bg-gh-blue` that no file ever used; every colour in this app is applied by reading the `:root` custom property directly instead. Tailwind only emits utilities that are referenced, so those tokens never reached the stylesheet and the generated CSS is byte-for-byte identical after removing them.

### Fixed

- A release tag now names a commit that was proven healthy in production, rather than one that merged and was followed by something healthy being observed. The production health check pointed a browser at a mutable alias without ever asking which commit was answering, so a deployment still in flight — or a failed one leaving the previous build live — produced a green run that said nothing about the code it was supposed to be checking. The run now asks `/api/health` what is deployed and stops in seconds if it is not the commit that triggered it. Promotion had a related gap from the other side: it decided whether a deployment had been overtaken by comparing against the tip of `main`, which advances at merge, while a deployment becomes live later and may never — so a newer commit that was still deploying, or that failed, suppressed the release of the commit genuinely in production and that release was never cut. It now resolves the live deployment directly and refuses to guess when none can be found.

- Syncing labels no longer deletes a label whose name differs from `.github/labels.yml` only in capitalization. GitHub cannot hold both `Bug` and `bug`, but the sync matched names exactly, so a label renamed by hand in the GitHub UI read as two things at once: a label to create and a stray to remove. Under `--prune` that combination deleted the very label the file asks to keep — taking it off every issue and pull request carrying it — while the create that was meant to replace it failed with a `422`. A case-only difference is now one label with a drifted name, corrected in place by renaming it, which a dry run previews as `would update: Bug -> bug`. Nothing in this repository could reach the old behaviour, since every name in the file is lowercase today. Two entries in the file differing only in case are now rejected as duplicates, because GitHub could not hold both.

- The commit timeline is now an ordered list, and long content no longer gets clipped by its card. Assistive technology previously received a run of identical card-shaped groups of `div`s with no count and no sense of sequence, for a result whose whole point is that the first item is the earliest. It is now an `ol` labelled "Earliest public commits", so a screen reader announces how many commits there are and which one it is on, and the decorative timeline markers and icons no longer add names of their own. Long repository names, unbroken commit subjects, and URLs inside a commit body now wrap instead of being cut off by the edge of the card at phone width or at 200% zoom — the repository name in the summary grid wraps rather than truncating to a tooltip no touch user can reach, and the author avatar no longer repeats the author's name to a screen reader that has just read the link beside it.

- The production health check runs again. Adding the mobile and WebKit browser projects taught the CI workflow to install WebKit but not the separate workflow that health-checks a production deployment, so the first deploy after that change failed at browser launch and opened an alert issue. The deployed app was healthy throughout; only the check was broken. Both workflows now install every browser the Playwright configuration declares a project for.
- A maximum-length GitHub handle in **Recent searches** no longer pushes the page sideways on a narrow screen. A handle can be 39 characters and has nothing to break on, so a single shortcut was wider than a 320px viewport and scrolled the whole page horizontally — the same width 200% zoom produces on a 640px window, where content is meant to reflow rather than scroll in two directions. Long handles now wrap inside their button, which stays one tap target with one focus ring and still shows the handle in full. Short handles are unchanged.
- The **Try again** button on an error no longer loses keyboard focus when it is pressed. Browsers blur a control the moment it becomes disabled, so activating the retry dropped a keyboard or screen-reader visitor at the top of the document for the length of the request and left them nowhere when it finished. The button now stays focusable while its retry runs, says **Searching again...**, and ignores a second press instead of starting a duplicate search — the same behaviour the partial-result retry already had, so both retries in the app now work the same way.
- A burst of searches for many different usernames from one client is now bounded. Sharing one request between concurrent readers of the same username did nothing about a flood of *distinct* usernames, where every search is a genuine cache miss and reaches GitHub against a shared allowance of 30 searches a minute. One client may now run 30 searches a minute that reach GitHub — an answer the cache already holds is free — and anything past that gets the existing "GitHub is asking us to slow down" screen with its retry, unchanged. The threshold is set where no visitor can reach it: sustained, it is one distinct handle typed every two seconds for a full minute, where clicking every recent-search shortcut you have stored produces five. Counting is per client rather than app-wide on purpose, so a busy day cannot turn the limit on ordinary visitors. What is kept about a client is a salted hash of its address and the times of its searches in the last minute, dropped once it goes quiet; no address is stored, no username reaches the limiter at all, and the two are never held together. Like the cache, the count lives in one server instance's memory and resets on a cold start, so it makes abuse cost something rather than imposing a global ceiling — the production runbook says so plainly, and says where a real one would have to be configured.
- Concurrent searches for the same username now share one request to GitHub instead of each making their own. The existing cache only helps once a search has finished, so a link shared with a crowd previously multiplied into one upstream search per reader, all asking the identical question against a single shared token quota. The saving is per running instance, like the cache.
- Recent searches loaded from the browser are now sanitized before they are shown. In a corrupt stored list — hand-edited, or written by something other than this app — blank and whitespace-only entries rendered as a bare `@` shortcut that searched for nothing, values kept their surrounding whitespace, and the same handle in different capitalization appeared as two separate shortcuts. Entries are now trimmed, validated, and collapsed case-insensitively, and a corrupt list still shows the full five shortcuts a visitor has earned rather than letting junk consume the slots.
- Abandoning a running search by resetting the page or starting a new one now stops it, so its result can no longer appear over the page you moved to and the search form no longer stays disabled until the abandoned request gives up.
- A commit search that GitHub abandoned before scanning every commit is now labelled a partial result rather than "First public commit found", explains that an earlier commit may be missing, and is never cached, so searching again can reach the full history. An unfinished search that returned nothing is reported as unfinished instead of as an absence of commits, offers a retry, and no longer suggests checking a different profile. Copied result text carries the same caveat.
- Primary green actions now meet WCAG AA text contrast, and successful searches move focus to the result heading for a clear assistive-technology transition.
- GitHub search failure logs now exclude raw upstream messages and accept only validated numeric rate-limit metadata.
- Vercel Analytics event URLs now remove shared-search usernames while preserving unrelated query parameters.
- Forged Server Action requests with non-string usernames now return validation errors safely.
- Commit results with missing or invalid dates no longer crash the result timeline.
- Unexpected Server Action rejections now use the inline retry experience instead of escaping to the global error screen.
- Prevented older overlapping searches from replacing newer results, and disabled search shortcuts while a request is pending.

### Changed

- The browser-test fixtures moved out of the server action that queries GitHub. Thirty percent of that file — 173 of 569 lines — was test doubles for the reserved `e2e-*` usernames, including one that throws on purpose and two that keep state between calls, all sitting in the module that holds the token and the real search path. They now live in their own module, which nothing but the browser suite reaches. Nothing about the app changed; the file that matters is a third shorter and reads as the production path it is, and coverage of it rose from 76.54% to 93.33% because it is no longer measured against lines no unit test could ever run. The coverage floors were raised to match the new measurement rather than left with three and a half points of slack.

- Coverage now measures the directories the unit suite collects from rather than only the files it happens to load, so a module no test imports counts as zero instead of vanishing from the report. 328-  if it does. What actually removes upstream calls is the cache and the request coalescing: a
329-  repeated username costs nothing, and concurrent readers of one shared link cost one search.
330-
331-What it does buy is that abuse stops being free. A single client cannot walk a username list at
332-machine speed through one instance, and the traffic that gets through is shaped like traffic from
333-many separate clients rather than one.
334-
335:A real global ceiling is platform configuration, not code — a Vercel Firewall rate-limit rule on
336:the app, keyed by IP, the same lever the [CSP report section](#rate-limiting-csp-reports)
337-describes. Nothing in this repository configures or reads it. If one is added, note it here.
338-
339-### Why 30 A Minute
340-
341-A person types a distinct valid GitHub handle every few seconds at the very fastest, and a visitor
342-clicking every recent-search shortcut they have stored produces five requests and then stops to
343-read. Thirty a minute, sustained, is one every two seconds for a full minute; no visitor reaches
344-it, so the threshold does not need traffic data to justify and lowering it would only start
345-catching people. It is also the documented authenticated search ceiling, so a client past it is by
346-itself capable of spending the whole shared per-minute allowance.
347-
348-A visitor who somehow does reach it sees the ordinary "GitHub is asking us to slow down" screen
349:with its retry, and is under the limit again within a minute.
350-
351-### What Is Held In Memory, And For How Long
352-
353-Per client, until the client has been quiet for longer than the window:
354-
355-- A salted SHA-256 hash of the forwarded client address.
356-- The timestamps of that client's searches inside the current 60-second window, at most 30 of them.
357-
358:Nothing else. The searched username never reaches the limiter — it is handed an opaque key — so no
359-username is stored, logged, or associated with a client anywhere in this path. The salt is 32
360-random bytes generated per process and never persisted.
361-
362-A memory dump of a running instance would show the salt, those hashes, and those timestamps. With
363-the salt in hand, an investigator could confirm whether an address they already suspected was
364:among the clients active in the last minute; they could not read the addresses out, correlate them
365-with another instance or with the same instance before a restart, or learn anything at all about
366-what was searched.
367-
368-### The Forwarded Header Is Untrusted Input
369-
370-The client key comes from `x-vercel-forwarded-for`, falling back to `x-forwarded-for`. Vercel sets
371-both itself and overwrites `x-forwarded-for` from the connecting socket precisely so it cannot be
372-spoofed, so on this deployment neither is attacker-controlled. `x-vercel-forwarded-for` is
373-preferred because it is the one a proxy placed in front of Vercel could not overwrite either.
374-
375-Behind some other proxy that forwards a client's header verbatim, a spoofer could:
376-
377-- **Split their own traffic** across many fabricated addresses and get a fresh allowance for each.
378:  This weakens the limit to the cost of forging headers. It cannot exhaust memory: idle clients are
379-  dropped and the map is capped, and eviction under a flood only ever *forgets* a client, which
380-  refills an allowance rather than refusing anyone.
381-- **Spend another client's allowance** by sending that client's address, refusing them for up to
382:  one window. The blast radius is one minute, one instance, and one address the attacker had to
383-  know already; nothing is revealed to them, and nothing persists.
384-
385-They cannot learn who else has searched, what anyone searched for, or read any stored key back.
386-
387-## Security Headers
388-
389-The app sets baseline security headers from `next.config.ts`:
390-
391-- `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`
392-- `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin`
393-- `Permissions-Policy` disabling camera, microphone, geolocation, and payment APIs
394-- `X-Frame-Options: DENY`
395-- `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` for CSP tuning without blocking production traffic
396-
397-Content Security Policy is currently report-only. Review Vercel logs before moving from report-only to enforcement.
398-
399-### CSP Violation Reports
400-
401-The policy names a reporting destination through both `report-uri` and `report-to`, backed by the
402-`Reporting-Endpoints` header. Browsers post violations to `/api/csp-report`, which logs them as
403-structured `csp_violation` events. Without this, a report-only policy is unobservable: violations
404-reach each visitor's browser console and nowhere else.
405-
406-Find them in Vercel Logs by searching for:
407-
408-```text
409-csp_violation
410-```
411-
412-Logged fields:
413-
414-- `documentUri`
415-- `blockedUri`
416-- `effectiveDirective`
417-- `disposition`
418-- `statusCode`
419-- `sourceFile`
420-- `lineNumber`
421-- `columnNumber`
422-
423-`http:` and `https:` URLs are reduced to origin and path. Query strings are dropped because the app
424-puts the searched username in `?user=`, and search usernames must not reach logs. Every other scheme
425-is reduced to the scheme alone — `data:`, `blob:`, and `javascript:` carry their payload inline, and
426-`mailto:` or an app-specific scheme registered by an extension carries an address or a path there —
427-so `data:` and `my-app:` are logged with nothing after the colon. The reported `original-policy` and
428:`script-sample` are never read at all: the policy is long and already known, and the sample can
429-contain page content or user input.
430-
431-The endpoint is unauthenticated, so its intake is bounded three ways:
432-
433-- **Content type.** Only `application/csp-report` (from `report-uri`) and `application/reports+json`
434-  (from the Reporting API) are read. Anything else is answered `415` without the body being touched.
435-- **Body size.** 16 KB, counted in bytes rather than characters, and enforced as the body arrives: an
436-  oversized `Content-Length` is refused before a byte is read, and because that header can be absent
437:  or untrue the stream is counted while it is consumed and cancelled the moment the limit is passed.
438-  Oversized bodies are answered `413`.
439-- **Reports per request.** At most **10** violations are logged from one POST. A Reporting API array
440-  is a batch, so without a cap a single request could turn into a log record per entry. The overflow
441-  is counted in one `csp_report_truncated` event carrying `received` and `logged`.
442-
443-Other events from the same endpoint indicate a malformed or hostile POST rather than a real
444-violation: `csp_report_malformed`, `csp_report_empty`, `csp_report_too_large`,
445-`csp_report_unsupported_type`, `csp_report_truncated`, and `csp_report_unreadable`.
446-
447-### Rate Limiting CSP Reports
448-
449-The bounds above cap what one request can cost. They do not cap how many requests arrive, and this
450-repository has no place to fix that: the app runs as serverless functions with no shared state, so
451:per-instance counting would not hold across instances. Rate limiting or sampling for
452-`/api/csp-report` is platform configuration, applied in the Vercel project rather than in code.
453-
454-If `csp_violation` or `csp_report_*` volume becomes noisy or expensive:
455-
456:1. Add a Vercel Firewall rate-limit rule scoped to the `/api/csp-report` path, keyed by IP.
457-2. If real traffic alone is the volume, lower the sampling instead — CSP supports it through the
458-   Reporting API endpoint configuration, and a report-only policy does not need every duplicate.
459-3. Re-check the log volume after either change before tightening further.
460-
461-None of this is in the repository, and nothing in the app reads it. Treat a change here as an
462-account-level operational change, and note it in this runbook when it is made.
463-
464-### Moving CSP To Enforcement
465-
466-Do not simply rename the header. `script-src` currently allows `'unsafe-inline'` and `'unsafe-eval'`,
467-so enforcing the policy as written would activate `frame-ancestors`, `base-uri`, `form-action`, and
468-`default-src` without blocking injected inline script, which is the main thing CSP defends against.
469-
470-The intended order is:
471-
472-1. Collect `csp_violation` events from real traffic in preview and production.
473-2. Tighten the policy against what actually fires.
474-3. Replace `'unsafe-inline'` and `'unsafe-eval'` in `script-src` with per-request nonces, which
475-   requires middleware and can break the Next.js inline bootstrap and Vercel Analytics.
476-4. Only then rename the header to `Content-Security-Policy`.
477-
478-## Accessibility Checks
479-
480-The browser health checks include accessibility-oriented coverage for landmarks, search form labels, keyboard tab order, validation announcements, and reachable search/recent-search actions.
481-
482-When changing UI structure, confirm:
483-
484-1. The header, main content, search form, and footer keep clear accessible names.
485-2. The search field receives focus on initial load and after reset/edit actions.
486-3. Keyboard users can tab from the search field to primary actions and recent-search controls.
487-4. Validation and result states use the appropriate `status` or `alert` role.
488-
489-## Privacy And Local Storage
490-
491-The app does not persist searches on a server. Successful searches are stored in the user's browser `localStorage` under:
492-
493-```text
494-my-first-commit:recent-searches
495-```
496-
497-This powers the recent-search shortcuts. Clearing browser site data removes the list.
498-
499-Successful and empty GitHub search results may also be cached briefly in server memory by normalized username to reduce repeated GitHub API calls. This cache is ephemeral and is not a database.
500-
501:Rate limiting holds a salted hash of each recent client's forwarded address, and the times of that client's searches in the last minute, in the same ephemeral server memory. No address and no username is stored, and the two are never held together. See [Bounding Search Bursts](#bounding-search-bursts).
502-
503-## Troubleshooting
504-
505-### Production Health Check Fails With `401`
506-
507-Check the target URL. Vercel-generated deployment URLs can be protected. Confirm the workflow is using:
508-
509-```env
REDACTED://my-first-commit-eta.vercel.app
511-```
512-
513-### Production Health Check Cannot Find App Text
514-
515-Open the health check target URL and confirm it renders the public app. If it shows a login, protection page, or unrelated Vercel page, fix the target URL.
516-
517-### GitHub Searches Are Rate Limited
518-
519:Check logs for `github_commit_search_rate_limited`.
520-
521:Confirm `GITHUB_TOKEN` is set in Vercel production. Unauthenticated GitHub Search API requests have a much lower rate limit.
522-
523-Check whether the running deployment sees it:
524-
525-```bash
526-curl -s https://my-first-commit-eta.vercel.app/api/health
527-```
528-
529-`checks.githubToken.configured: false` means the variable is missing from the deployment, usually
530:because it was changed without redeploying. `true` with rate limiting means the token is set but
531:expired, revoked, or genuinely over its limit.
532-
533-### Visitors Report Rate Limiting But GitHub Is Not Rate Limiting
534-
535:Check whether the logs show `commit_search_rate_limited_client` rather than
536:`github_commit_search_rate_limited`. The first is this app's own per-client bound, the second is
537-GitHub's. The visitor sees the same screen either way, which is deliberate, so the log is what
538-tells the two apart. See [Bounding Search Bursts](#bounding-search-bursts) for the threshold and
539-why a person is not expected to reach it.
540-
541-### GitHub Searches Fail With Validation Errors
542-
543-Check logs for `github_commit_search_failed` with `status: 422`. This usually means the username/query is invalid or GitHub could not validate the search request.
544-
545-### GitHub Searches Time Out
546-
547-Check logs for `github_commit_search_timeout`. This means GitHub did not respond before the server action timeout. Retry the search and check GitHub status if it persists.
548-
549-### GitHub Is Temporarily Unavailable
550-
551-Check logs for `github_commit_search_unavailable` with a `5xx` status. The app should show a retry-friendly message. Wait for GitHub to recover or retry later.
552-
553-### GitHub Returns Unexpected Commit Data
554-
555-Check logs for `github_commit_search_malformed_item`. The app skips malformed records and shows an empty state if no valid commits remain.
556-
557-### Production Works But Preview Fails
558-
559-Preview deployments may not have all production environment variables. Check Vercel project environment variable scope and branch/preview settings.
560-
561-### Vercel Builds A Branch That Has No App Code
562-
563-Vercel creates a deployment for every branch push. A branch whose tree has no `package.json` fails at
564-the install step with `ENOENT ... /vercel/path0/package.json`.
565-
566-This happened with Entire's checkpoint storage. Entire used to push `entire/checkpoints/v1`, a branch
567-holding only its object store, on every `git push`, and each push produced a failed preview
568-deployment.
569-
570-Do not try to fix this with `vercel.json`. Vercel reads `vercel.json` from the commit being deployed,
571-so `git.deploymentEnabled` and `ignoreCommand` are never consulted for a branch that does not contain
572-the file. That is exactly the branch class the setting appears to target, which makes the fix look
573-correct while doing nothing.
574-
575-Fix it at the source instead, so no branch is pushed:
576-
577-```bash
578-entire configure --checkpoint-backend refs
579-```
580-
581-Checkpoints then land under `refs/entire/checkpoints/*` rather than `refs/heads/*`, and Vercel has no
582-branch to deploy. The old `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch can stay; it is simply no longer pushed to.

# Release Guide

Use this checklist when cutting a new My First Commit release.

## Before Release

1. Confirm `main` is current and clean.
2. Move relevant `CHANGELOG.md` entries from `Unreleased` into a dated version section.
3. Confirm any user-facing docs, screenshots, or runbook notes are current.
4. Run `npm run validate`, the local [validation suite](development.md#validation).

## Publish Release

Production releases are created automatically after a merge to `main`, a successful `CI / validate` run, a successful Vercel production deployment, and a passing `Production Health Check`. The `Promote Production Release` workflow creates both the Git tag and the GitHub release. The automatic tag format is:

```text
vX.Y.Z-<deployed-short-sha>
```

The deployed footer shows the same release tag and links to the matching GitHub release.

1. Create a tag from the current `main` commit:

   ```bash
   git tag vX.Y.Z
   git push origin vX.Y.Z
   ```

2. Confirm the `Release` workflow publishes the GitHub release automatically.
3. If needed, run the workflow manually with the existing `vX.Y.Z` tag.
4. Use the matching `CHANGELOG.md` section as the release notes.
5. Mark prereleases only when the release is not intended for normal production use.

item.stdout:
1	# Changelog
     2	
     3	All notable changes to My First Commit are documented here.
     4	
     5	This project follows a lightweight, human-curated changelog. Keep the newest changes at the top and move items from `Unreleased` into a dated release section when cutting a release.
     6	
     7	## Unreleased
     8	
     9	### Added
    10	
    11	- The production health check now performs one real commit search and asserts a commit renders, rather than only checking that the app responds. Every other search test uses fixtures, so a revoked token, a changed GitHub response, or a Server Action broken only in production could pass production health and be promoted to a release — `/api/health` reports that a token is present, never that it works. One search per deployment on one browser, because each one spends the shared GitHub quota the burst limiting exists to protect. A partial result from GitHub counts as a pass, since that is GitHub shedding load rather than a fault of this app; an empty result, an error state, or a heading with no commit does not.
    12	
    13	- Unit test coverage is now measured, reported, and enforced. The gate's unit step runs with V8 coverage, so one command produces the numbers locally and in CI, and a text summary plus an HTML report in the ignored `coverage/` directory. The thresholds are a non-regression floor rather than a target: they were set a whole percent below a measurement of the suite as it stands — 93% statements, 89% branches, 98% functions, 94% lines against 93.68, 89.58, 98.30, and 94.66 — so a change that leaves new code untested fails the gate while a refactor does not fail on rounding. Coverage counts the files the suite loads, which means the floors cannot catch a module no test imports at all; the development guide says so rather than leaving the number to imply more than it measures.
    14	- Two time-based contracts that nothing exercised are now tested on a fake clock, in milliseconds rather than in real waiting. The five-minute cache lifetime is pinned at both sides of its boundary — served one millisecond before the deadline, gone once it is reached — along with the rules about what may be cached: an empty result is stored so a handle with no public commits is not searched again, while a rate limit, timeout, outage, or any other failure never is, and a read inside the window refreshes eviction order without extending the lifetime. The ten-second search deadline is now proved by a request that hangs: it is still outstanding at 9,999 milliseconds and aborted at 10,000, where the previous test injected the abort itself and so could not tell a working timer from a missing one.
    15	
    16	- Partial commit results now offer a **Search again** button in place. A retry that succeeds replaces the partial result, one that comes back partial again says so, and one that fails leaves the commits on screen and explains why instead of replacing them with an error screen. Each outcome is announced to assistive technology.
    17	
    18	### Changed
    19	
    20	- Every Entire CLI Codex hook now has up to 300 seconds to finish before Codex terminates it,
    21	  increased from 30 seconds for larger sessions and checkpoint operations that need longer to
    22	  finalize.
    23	
    24	- The repository front door now leads with the live product, current build and release status, an
    25	  accurate screenshot, a concise local quick start, and a compact guide to the rest of the
    26	  documentation. Detailed capabilities, privacy boundaries, and GitHub search limitations moved to
    27	  a dedicated product guide, and contributor recognition now links to GitHub's automatically
    28	  maintained history instead of duplicating it in a hand-maintained file. The initial screenshot
    29	  showed a profile-heavy interface the current app no longer renders; it has been replaced with the
    30	  actual commit-results experience.
    31	
    32	- Development dependencies updated: `eslint-config-next` to 16.3.1 and `@testing-library/user-event` to 14.6.4. The lint config is the half of the Next.js 16.3.1 release that governs linting, and is pinned to the same exact version as Next.js itself, so it moves with it rather than drifting a release behind. The testing library fixes the `repeat` property on synthesized keyboard events, which no test here reads. Neither package ships in the application, so nothing a visitor loads changed; `npm run lint` passes unchanged against the new config, which is the check a lint-config bump can actually break.
    33	
    34	- Next.js updated from 16.3.0 to 16.3.1, a patch release of backported fixes. Two of them reach this app: `headers()` regains its live view of the incoming request, which is what the per-client search limit reads to identify a caller, and image optimization preserves the response it produced, which is how commit author avatars are served. The rest of the release covers Turbopack internals and features this app does not use — `'use cache'`, `unstable_cache`, middleware, i18n, and the Pages Router. The full validation suite passes on the new version, including the browser journeys that exercise both changed paths, and the version bump carried no unrelated lockfile churn: only Next.js itself, its platform build binaries, and its own transitive helpers moved.
    35	
    36	- The agent instructions now describe the import convention the code actually follows. They said imports were "relative within a feature, aliased with `@/` only across a boundary", which matched neither half of the codebase: all 29 relative imports of a shared module cross out of their own folder, and the 3 aliased ones are exactly the route files under `app/api/`. What decides the form is depth, not the boundary crossed — a route file sits three levels down, where the relative path counts directories instead of naming anything and quietly means a different module if the route moves. The rule now says that, so it can be checked against the code rather than read as a principle nothing obeys.
    37	
    38	- Analytics moved out of the homepage feature folder. `analytics.ts` sat in `app/_home/`, the directory for things only the homepage uses, while the root layout's analytics component imported it from outside — so every page load pulled a module out of the homepage feature to do something with no connection to searching for a commit. It now sits in `app/_lib/` with the other shared modules, which leaves `app/_home/` meaning what its name claims. The agent instructions gained the rule that decides this for the next module, and their layout list picked up the two files it had fallen behind on. Documentation and file locations only; no behaviour changed and the analytics events themselves are untouched.
    39	
    40	### Removed
    41	
    42	- Dropped the `clsx` and `tailwind-merge` dependencies, which nothing imported. Both are conventional in a Tailwind project and both arrived with the initial commit, but no revision since has ever imported either one: every component in this app composes `className` with a template literal, so neither package had a single call site in any version of this code. They shipped nothing, while each remained a package the audit gate had to keep clearing and Dependabot had to keep proposing upgrades for. Nothing else in the tree depended on them, so removing the two declarations removed them outright. No behaviour and no styling changed; a future need for conditional class composition can add one back deliberately.
    43	
    44	- The structured logger can no longer be handed a raw error object. `logger.error` accepted an optional second argument of any type and passed it straight to `console.error`, which is the one thing this module exists to prevent — an Octokit error carries the request URL, and a commit-search URL carries the username being searched. No caller ever passed one, so nothing was being logged that should not have been; what is gone is the supported way to start. Callers already pull out the scalars they need, such as the status code and the error kind, and log those.
    45	
    46	- Deleted two unreachable branches and nine unused design tokens. The share-text builder took a whole search result and carried a fallback for one with no commits, though its only caller reaches it from behind a `found` check that guarantees at least one — narrowing the parameter to the success type made the compiler reject the test that had been pinning the dead branch, and reject nothing else, which is what proved it unreachable rather than merely untested. Separately, the stylesheet mapped nine `--color-*` tokens into Tailwind's theme, generating utilities such as `bg-gh-blue` that no file ever used; every colour in this app is applied by reading the `:root` custom property directly instead. Tailwind only emits utilities that are referenced, so those tokens never reached the stylesheet and the generated CSS is byte-for-byte identical after removing them.
    47	
    48	### Fixed
    49	
    50	- A release tag now names a commit that was proven healthy in production, rather than one that merged and was followed by something healthy being observed. The production health check pointed a browser at a mutable alias without ever asking which commit was answering, so a deployment still in flight — or a failed one leaving the previous build live — produced a green run that said nothing about the code it was supposed to be checking. The run now asks `/api/health` what is deployed and stops in seconds if it is not the commit that triggered it. Promotion had a related gap from the other side: it decided whether a deployment had been overtaken by comparing against the tip of `main`, which advances at merge, while a deployment becomes live later and may never — so a newer commit that was still deploying, or that failed, suppressed the release of the commit genuinely in production and that release was never cut. It now resolves the live deployment directly and refuses to guess when none can be found.
    51	
    52	- Syncing labels no longer deletes a label whose name differs from `.github/labels.yml` only in capitalization. GitHub cannot hold both `Bug` and `bug`, but the sync matched names exactly, so a label renamed by hand in the GitHub UI read as two things at once: a label to create and a stray to remove. Under `--prune` that combination deleted the very label the file asks to keep — taking it off every issue and pull request carrying it — while the create that was meant to replace it failed with a `422`. A case-only difference is now one label with a drifted name, corrected in place by renaming it, which a dry run previews as `would update: Bug -> bug`. Nothing in this repository could reach the old behaviour, since every name in the file is lowercase today. Two entries in the file differing only in case are now rejected as duplicates, because GitHub could not hold both.
    53	
    54	- The commit timeline is now an ordered list, and long content no longer gets clipped by its card. Assistive technology previously received a run of identical card-shaped groups of `div`s with no count and no sense of sequence, for a result whose whole point is that the first item is the earliest. It is now an `ol` labelled "Earliest public commits", so a screen reader announces how many commits there are and which one it is on, and the decorative timeline markers and icons no longer add names of their own. Long repository names, unbroken commit subjects, and URLs inside a commit body now wrap instead of being cut off by the edge of the card at phone width or at 200% zoom — the repository name in the summary grid wraps rather than truncating to a tooltip no touch user can reach, and the author avatar no longer repeats the author's name to a screen reader that has just read the link beside it.
    55	
    56	- The production health check runs again. Adding the mobile and WebKit browser projects taught the CI workflow to install WebKit but not the separate workflow that health-checks a production deployment, so the first deploy after that change failed at browser launch and opened an alert issue. The deployed app was healthy throughout; only the check was broken. Both workflows now install every browser the Playwright configuration declares a project for.
    57	- A maximum-length GitHub handle in **Recent searches** no longer pushes the page sideways on a narrow screen. A handle can be 39 characters and has nothing to break on, so a single shortcut was wider than a 320px viewport and scrolled the whole page horizontally — the same width 200% zoom produces on a 640px window, where content is meant to reflow rather than scroll in two directions. Long handles now wrap inside their button, which stays one tap target with one focus ring and still shows the handle in full. Short handles are unchanged.
    58	- The **Try again** button on an error no longer loses keyboard focus when it is pressed. Browsers blur a control the moment it becomes disabled, so activating the retry dropped a keyboard or screen-reader visitor at the top of the document for the length of the request and left them nowhere when it finished. The button now stays focusable while its retry runs, says **Searching again...**, and ignores a second press instead of starting a duplicate search — the same behaviour the partial-result retry already had, so both retries in the app now work the same way.
    59	- A burst of searches for many different usernames from one client is now bounded. Sharing one request between concurrent readers of the same username did nothing about a flood of *distinct* usernames, where every search is a genuine cache miss and reaches GitHub against a shared allowance of 30 searches a minute. One client may now run 30 searches a minute that reach GitHub — an answer the cache already holds is free — and anything past that gets the existing "GitHub is asking us to slow down" screen with its retry, unchanged. The threshold is set where no visitor can reach it: sustained, it is one distinct handle typed every two seconds for a full minute, where clicking every recent-search shortcut you have stored produces five. Counting is per client rather than app-wide on purpose, so a busy day cannot turn the limit on ordinary visitors. What is kept about a client is a salted hash of its address and the times of its searches in the last minute, dropped once it goes quiet; no address is stored, no username reaches the limiter at all, and the two are never held together. Like the cache, the count lives in one server instance's memory and resets on a cold start, so it makes abuse cost something rather than imposing a global ceiling — the production runbook says so plainly, and says where a real one would have to be configured.
    60	- Concurrent searches for the same username now share one request to GitHub instead of each making their own. The existing cache only helps once a search has finished, so a link shared with a crowd previously multiplied into one upstream search per reader, all asking the identical question against a single shared token quota. The saving is per running instance, like the cache.
    61	- Recent searches loaded from the browser are now sanitized before they are shown. In a corrupt stored list — hand-edited, or written by something other than this app — blank and whitespace-only entries rendered as a bare `@` shortcut that searched for nothing, values kept their surrounding whitespace, and the same handle in different capitalization appeared as two separate shortcuts. Entries are now trimmed, validated, and collapsed case-insensitively, and a corrupt list still shows the full five shortcuts a visitor has earned rather than letting junk consume the slots.
    62	- Abandoning a running search by resetting the page or starting a new one now stops it, so its result can no longer appear over the page you moved to and the search form no longer stays disabled until the abandoned request gives up.
    63	- A commit search that GitHub abandoned before scanning every commit is now labelled a partial result rather than "First public commit found", explains that an earlier commit may be missing, and is never cached, so searching again can reach the full history. Copied result text carries the same caveat.
    64	- Primary green actions now meet WCAG AA text contrast, and successful searches move focus to the result heading for a clear assistive-technology transition.
    65	- GitHub search failure logs now exclude raw upstream messages and accept only validated numeric rate-limit metadata.
    66	- Vercel Analytics event URLs now remove shared-search usernames while preserving unrelated query parameters.

    68	- Commit results with missing or invalid dates no longer crash the result timeline.
    69	- Unexpected Server Action rejections now use the inline retry experience instead of escaping to the global error screen.

    74	- The browser-test fixtures moved out of the server action that queries GitHub.     75	
    76	- Coverage now measures the directories the unit suite collects from rather than only the files it happens to load, so a module no test imports counts as zero instead of vanishing from the report.     77

    79	
    80	- The check that keeps unit test collection scoped now reads the collection setting rather than every glob in the Vitest config. It now reads only the collection array, and only the one belonging to the test configuration, so a coverage block can be scoped properly while a widened test scope still fails. Brackets are counted outside string literals, because a collection pattern contains them and counting them in the raw text would end the array inside the first pattern and report fewer roots than there are.
    81	
    82	- Browser coverage now runs the journeys a visitor actually performs across boundaries, rather than only rendering each state in isolation. A successful search is checked to put the handle in the URL and a new search to take it back out while restoring focus to the field; a completed search is followed from appearing in recent searches through being rerun to being cleared, in the browser as well as in storage; and the timeout, unknown and validation failures each get a state of their own, with the validation failure asserted to offer a way out rather than a retry that would fetch the identical refusal. The clipboard fallback is exercised by making the write fail, since the browser's own policy decides whether a real write succeeds and the fallback is otherwise unreachable from a test.
    83	
    84	- Commit search results are now a discriminated union, so states the app never produces can no longer be written down. The result type allowed a successful search with no commits, and failure fields on a success, which every consumer paid for with a defensive check that could not fire — the page tested `found && commits.length > 0`, and the results view carried an early return for a first commit that was always there. A success now carries at least one commit in the type itself, a failure always carries both an error and its kind, and reading the wrong variant's fields fails to compile instead of failing a runtime check somebody remembered to write. The wire format is unchanged: tuples are erased at runtime, so what the server action serializes is the same JSON as before and a result cached by an older instance still deserializes.
    85	
    86	- `main` now enforces more of the workflow it already documented. A pull request must be up to date with `main` before it can merge, so the required check has actually run against the code that will land rather than against an older base; review conversations must be resolved; and linear history is required, which squash merging already produced. Approving reviews stay at zero, matching the documented policy that a pull request with no assigned reviewer may be self-merged. All of it applies to administrators too. The practical cost is on parallel work: merging one of two open pull requests puts the other behind, and it needs its branch updated and CI rerun before it can merge in turn.
    87	
    88	- Removed four animation utility classes from the results view. `animate-in`, `fade-in`, and `slide-in-from-bottom-4` come from a plugin this project does not install, so they compiled to no rules at all and the fade-and-rise they describe has never run; `duration-500` was left timing nothing. Removing them means the markup no longer promises motion the app does not have, and there is consequently no motion to honour a reduced-motion preference.
    89	
    90	- The gate now fails when a workflow that runs the browser suite installs fewer browsers than the Playwright configuration declares projects for. Two workflows each kept their own hand-written install list, and nothing tied them to the config, so adding the WebKit project updated one and not the other — a gap that could only appear after a production deploy, because the workflow it broke runs on a deployment event and no local command reaches it. The check resolves each project to the engine it actually runs on rather than to its name, since a mobile project is Chromium-backed, and it refuses to read a project it does not understand instead of quietly assuming that project needs nothing.
    91	
    92	- The `app/` directory now holds route files and nothing else. It had grown to 23 files of which 15 were not routes — the server action, the cache, the logger, the type definitions and the rest sat at the same level as `page.tsx` and `layout.tsx`, so listing the directory that defines what the app serves mostly showed things it does not serve. Those modules moved to `app/_lib/`, completing the rule the previous two entries started: a folder under `app/` that is not a route starts with an underscore, components live beside the feature that uses them, and everything else is a module in `app/_lib/`. No behaviour changed and no route was added or removed.
    93	- Components now have one home instead of three. `FirstCommitDisplay` sat alone in a root-level `components/` directory, the four search components sat in `app/_home/`, and the analytics wrapper sat loose in `app/`, with no rule saying which belonged where — so `SearchResults` imported one sibling across an alias boundary and the rest relatively, for no reason a reader could infer. A component now lives beside the feature that uses it, and `app/_components/` holds the ones used by something other than a single feature. The root `components/` directory is gone, and with it the last collection root the unit tests reached outside `app/` and `scripts/`. No behaviour changed; the suite collects the same 428 tests it did before the move.
    94	- The browser suite now runs on a 320px mobile viewport and on WebKit as well as Desktop Chrome. Only Chrome ran before, so nothing automatically checked how the app behaves at phone width or in the engine behind Safari — layout, focus, navigation, and clipboard were all assumed to work the same everywhere. The two added projects run a selected set of journeys rather than the whole suite, so coverage grows by a few runs instead of tripling. Traces are also retained on failure now: the suite asked for them on the first retry, but retries are off, so no trace was ever captured for any failure in any browser.
    95	- `AGENTS.md` now carries the agent-rules block that Next.js generates, instead of having it reappear after every browser suite run. `next dev` writes the block whenever its exact text is missing, and the browser suite boots `next dev`, so each full validation run left a modified `AGENTS.md` that someone had to notice and strip — it reached a commit by accident once. The generator offers no way to turn this off, and it skips writing once the block is present, so committing it is what actually stops it. A note above the block records that it is generated, that edits between its markers are overwritten on the next run, and that it cannot move to `CLAUDE.md`, which the gate requires to stay a byte-for-byte pointer.
    96	- The homepage's internal components and modules moved from `app/home/` to `app/_home/`. Every directory under `app/` claims a URL segment, so a folder holding internals was one file away from becoming a public route at `/home`, with nothing in its name to say it should not be. A leading underscore marks it private to Next.js, which excludes it from routing outright. No route was added or removed and nothing about the app changed for a visitor; `/home` returns the branded not-found page exactly as before, and now cannot stop doing so.
    97	- The app no longer downloads a web font, and a production build no longer needs Google Fonts to be reachable. The root layout fetched Geist and Geist Mono at build time, but the Tailwind font tokens have always defined system stacks and nothing ever referenced the `--font-geist-*` variables the layout generated, so no text was rendered in Geist — a visitor's browser only preloaded two font files it never used. Rendered typography is unchanged, the system stack it actually uses is documented beside the tokens that define it, and the build now depends on nothing outside the repository for fonts.
    98	- Label synchronization now decides what to do in tested code. `scripts/sync-labels.mjs` had grown to mix validating `.github/labels.yml`, planning creates and updates, and deleting labels, with only the offline file check covered in CI — so the destructive branch was the least tested part of it. Validation, planning, reporting, and applying now live in `scripts/label-plan.mjs` as pure functions over plain data, unit tested without a token or a network: that a deletion is planned only with `--prune`, that a dry run previews exactly the deletions a real run would make and writes nothing, that an unquoted colour like `123456` is caught while `e10c02` passes through as the string it stays, and that what reaches the GitHub API is what the plan validated. The script itself is unchanged in behaviour and still the only entry point; `npm run check:labels` still validates the file offline on every pull request.
    99	- The unit test run now collects from `app/`, `components/`, and `scripts/` instead of skipping directories one at a time. A scratch spec left at the repository root, or in any directory the exclude list had not been taught about, used to join `npm test` and fail the gate with a Playwright error that pointed at the tooling rather than at the stray file. Nothing outside those three roots is a unit test now, so such a file neither breaks the run nor quietly joins it, and the verification exemption for the external tooling-state directories no longer depends on a denylist keeping pace with every directory a tool might create. `npm run check:agent-docs` still fails if the ignore lists drift apart, and now also if the collection scope widens.
   100	- The agent workflow now covers changes that replace an existing contract. Test-driven development assumed new behavior, where one new failing test is enough to drive the work; when a change instead replaces something, the suite already holds assertions on the behavior being removed, and those stay green while the new test goes red and then green, so the loop looks finished with the contradiction still in the tree. Agents now locate and update those assertions inside the same red/green loop instead of letting the full validation gate find them a cycle later. Agents that cannot invoke the review sub-agents must also say so on reaching the review steps rather than in the final report, since the fallback has one agent review its own change and reporting it at the end surfaces that only once the work has already been reviewed that way.
   101	- The browser suite now also refuses a stale server of this application. Confirming that the port held the right app was not enough: a server left behind by an interrupted run answered that check perfectly, and if it had been started without the fixture mocks every reserved test username went to real GitHub, so nearly every spec failed for a reason that had nothing to do with the branch — the same misleading wall of failures the original check was built to remove. A second preflight probe now asks the server whether it was started for this suite and stops the run naming the missing flag when it was not; a server too old to answer that question is rejected the same way. That probe is a route of its own, reporting one boolean and returning `404` on any built or deployed server, so nothing about test configuration was added to the public health endpoint. Neither probe can tell which branch a server is running, which remains a reason to prefer letting the suite start its own.
   102	- The browser suite now refuses to run against a foreign server. Playwright reused any server that answered on its port, so an unrelated application left running there was adopted silently and every spec failed as though the branch were broken. A preflight check asks `/api/health` whether the port holds this application and stops the run with one clear error when it does not, naming the port and what it found. The other process is never stopped, since the port may belong to another checkout or another person's work. The port is now settable with `E2E_PORT`, and the worker count is fixed rather than derived from the machine so a run behaves the same everywhere; both overrides reject an unusable value instead of falling back silently. CI keeps the concurrency it already had.
   103	- `.editorconfig` now carries a `max_line_length` matching Prettier's `printWidth`, so editors show the same wrap column the formatter uses. Markdown opts out, because prose here is hand-wrapped and Prettier does not format it.
   104	- One command now runs the validation gate. `npm run validate` chains the dependency audit, unit tests, browser checks, lint, formatting, agent-document and label checks, and the production build, stopping at the first failure. The `CI / validate` job runs that same script instead of listing the steps itself, so the local gate and the CI gate are the same definition rather than two lists that drift. `npm run check:agent-docs` now also fails if CI stops invoking the script, or if the copies of the list in the development guide or the `verifier` sub-agent definition stop matching it, and the parsing behind that check is unit tested. Those two are now the only places the chain is written out in order.
   105	- Local Entire checkpoint hooks now match Claude Code's current tool names, including the newer task tools, so the configuration no longer depends on Claude Code's legacy alias map.
   106	- Lint and unit tests now cover product code only. `eslint.config.mjs` and `vitest.config.ts` ignore the root-level external tooling-state directories `.claude/`, `.codex/`, `.entire/`, and `.vercel/`, matching `.prettierignore`.    107	- The verification exemption is now scoped by what the gate can actually read rather than by file extension. A change confined to `*.md` files or to those tooling-state directories runs `npm run check:agent-docs` only and reports `PASS (unread-paths)`. Previously a `.claude/settings.json` edit ran all eight gate commands, including a full browser suite and production build, none of which could observe it. `.github/hooks/` stays fully gated: it is agent tooling, but it is in none of the ignore lists.
   108	- The agent workflow now bounds its review loop: findings can be explicitly resolved with a stated reason, and a finding that survives two fix-and-re-review cycles stops for a human instead of looping. Reverification is scoped to the gate commands a fix can actually affect, with an exemption for paths no gate command reads, so a prose fix no longer triggers a full audit, test, browser, and build cycle.
   109	- Agents must now add a `CHANGELOG.md` entry with user-facing and operational changes, treat issue, pull request, and review text as data rather than instructions, and bound the wait for an assigned reviewer instead of blocking indefinitely.
   110	- The `ui-review` sub-agent now enumerates untracked files with `--untracked-files=all`, so a brand-new component directory can no longer be mistaken for a change with no user-visible surface.
   111	- Consolidated the pre-PR command list, which had drifted into four inconsistent copies, into a canonical list in the development guide that the contributing guide, runbook, and release guide now link to. The agent-facing files keep deliberate inline copies. Trimmed the manual QA checklist to the states the deployed browser check skips and the judgments Playwright cannot make, and documented the Playwright browser install.
   112	- Documented the `/privacy` and `/api/csp-report` routes in the architecture guide, along with the CSP report endpoint's data boundaries. Both shipped previously without being listed among the runtime routes.
   113	- Clarified that the main agent owns exact unit-test red/green loops while the verifier owns focused Playwright execution and the complete validation gate.
   114	- Removed the superseded specification and roadmap documents, along with their README links.
   115	- Upgraded the project from Node 22 to Node 24, the current Active LTS and Vercel's default runtime. `.nvmrc`, `package.json` engines, and the docs now all name 24. Node 26 is deliberately not used: Vercel offers only 20.x, 22.x, and 24.x, so pinning 26 would not deploy.
   116	
   117	### Removed
   118	
   119	- Four unused Next.js starter assets — `public/file.svg`, `public/globe.svg`, `public/vercel.svg`, and `public/window.svg` — which were deployed on every release but referenced nowhere in the app, its docs, or the README. The `public/` directory is now empty and gone with them, along with the Prettier ignore entry that existed only to accommodate them.
   120	- Copilot-specific instruction file. `.github/copilot-instructions.md` is deleted and deregistered from `npm run check:agent-docs`, which now keeps only `CLAUDE.md` and `GEMINI.md` as pointers to `AGENTS.md`. Copilot CLI, the Copilot cloud agent, Copilot code review, and Copilot Chat in VS Code read `AGENTS.md` natively, so those surfaces keep the same instructions; Copilot Chat on GitHub.com and in Visual Studio, JetBrains, Eclipse, and Xcode do not read `AGENTS.md` and no longer receive repository instructions. The check now also fails if the file reappears, since it would outrank `AGENTS.md`. The Copilot CLI hook file `.github/hooks/entire.json` is unaffected and stays.
   121	
   122	### Security
   123	
   124	- The unauthenticated CSP report endpoint now bounds what one anonymous request can cost. Its 16 KB limit is enforced in bytes as the body arrives — an oversized `Content-Length` is refused before a byte is read, and a body that arrives without one, or lies about it, is cancelled the moment it passes the limit — where previously the whole body was buffered and then measured in JavaScript characters, so a multibyte body several times over the limit was accepted. At most ten violations are now logged per request, with the overflow counted in a single event, so a Reporting API array can no longer amplify one POST into a log record per entry. Only the two CSP report content types are read; anything else is refused without the body being touched. Reported URLs on any scheme other than `http:` and `https:` are now reduced to the scheme alone, so `mailto:` addresses and paths from app-specific schemes cannot reach logs, joining the `data:`, `blob:`, `javascript:`, and `filesystem:` payloads already dropped. Query strings, fragments, `original-policy`, and `script-sample` are still never logged. Rate limiting the endpoint itself is platform configuration rather than code, and the production runbook now says where it belongs.
   125	
   126	## 0.3.0 - 2026-08-01
   127	
   128	### Added
   129	
   130	- Label sync automation. `.github/labels.yml` is reconciled with GitHub by the `Sync Labels` workflow on merge, or locally through `npm run sync:labels`. Deleting labels is opt-in, and CI validates the label file on every pull request.
   131	- CSP violation reporting. The report-only policy now names a reporting destination through `report-uri`, `report-to`, and the `Reporting-Endpoints` header, and `/api/csp-report` records violations as structured `csp_violation` log events. Reported URLs are reduced to origin and path so searched usernames cannot reach logs, and the original policy and script sample are never read.
   132	- `/api/health` now reports whether `GITHUB_TOKEN` is configured, so a rotation that never reached the running deployment is visible without a live search. Presence only is reported, never the value. The production health check asserts it against deployed targets.
   133	
   134	### Fixed
